fields.title: The Five Disciplines of Learning Organizations
fields.summary: This resource introduces Peter Senge's five disciplines of the learning organization — adapted for DSD's context — and examines what it would mean for DSD to function as a genuinely learning organization. The five disciplines offer both an individual leadership framework and an organizational aspiration that is directly relevant to DSD's equity and effectiveness commitments.
fields.body:
What this is for

This resource introduces Peter Senge's five disciplines of the learning organization — adapted for DSD's context — and examines what it would mean for DSD to function as a genuinely learning organization. The five disciplines offer both an individual leadership framework and an organizational aspiration that is directly relevant to DSD's equity and effectiveness commitments.

Why this matters in DSD work

DSD's work is complex enough that no single individual, team, or program can hold all the knowledge it requires. The field of disability services is evolving — in policy, in equity understanding, in community context, in technology — faster than any static knowledge base can keep up with. A learning organization is not a luxury; it is the organizational form that DSD's context demands.

Peter Senge's The Fifth Discipline (1990) remains the foundational text on learning organizations. Its five disciplines provide a coherent framework for building organizational learning capacity that is practically accessible and deeply relevant to human services contexts.

Core concepts

The five disciplines

Discipline 1: Personal Mastery

Personal mastery is the individual discipline — the ongoing commitment to developing oneself, clarifying what matters, and maintaining the creative tension between current reality and vision. It is not achievement or expertise; it is a practice of continuous learning and honest assessment.

For DSD: Personal mastery shows up in staff who hold learning conversations in supervision, pursue IDPs with genuine intent, engage reflective practice, and remain open to revising their understanding. An organization where personal mastery is practiced is an organization where people are genuinely developing — not just accumulating tenure.

Connection to other assets: Personal mastery connects directly to the Leading Self section of this hub: self-awareness (Asset 1), reflective practice (Asset 2), seeking feedback (Asset 5), and personal and professional growth (Asset 8).

Discipline 2: Mental Models

Mental models are the assumptions, beliefs, and generalizations that shape how we see the world and how we act in it. They are largely invisible — we don't usually examine them, we simply act from them. The discipline of mental models is the practice of surfacing, examining, and revising those assumptions.

For DSD: Mental models are particularly consequential in the context of disability and cultural difference. Staff who hold unchecked mental models about what disability looks like, about what families in specific cultural communities value, or about what good service looks like will act from those models without awareness. Surfacing and examining mental models is an equity practice.

The discipline of mental models is practiced through conversations that surface assumptions, through culturally humble inquiry rather than expert certainty, and through the deliberate use of frameworks like the IDI Continuum to reveal the shape of one's own orientations.

Discipline 3: Building Shared Vision

A shared vision is more than an organizational statement posted in a conference room. It is a genuine commitment to a desired future that is held by enough of the organization's members that it becomes a guide for action, a source of motivation, and a standard for accountability.

For DSD: DSD's six program goals provide the content for a shared vision. But content is not the same as genuine commitment. Shared vision is built through participatory processes, honest conversation about what the vision actually requires of people, and sustained connection between daily work and larger purpose. Leaders at every level build or erode shared vision through the consistency between what they say and what they do.

For equity work: Shared vision in a diverse organization requires explicit attention to whose voices shaped the vision. A vision developed by dominant groups and extended to others is not genuinely shared. Building shared vision across DSD's full staff diversity requires deliberate participatory design.

Discipline 4: Team Learning

Team learning is the capacity of a group to learn together — to achieve results that no individual could achieve alone, and to develop shared understanding and capability through collective work. It is grounded in the practice of dialogue: genuine inquiry in which people suspend their assumptions and think together rather than presenting positions and defending them.

For DSD: Team learning is what happens when a supervision team genuinely examines why a service approach is producing inequitable outcomes, rather than defending the approach. It is what happens when an equity champion convenes a learning conversation rather than a training. It is what happens when mistakes are treated as organizational learning opportunities rather than individual failures.

The discipline of team learning requires psychological safety (see Asset 9) — people who do not feel safe cannot think together; they can only manage impressions.

Discipline 5: Systems Thinking

Systems thinking is the integrating discipline — the capacity to see how the parts of a system relate to each other and to the whole, rather than seeing only individual parts in isolation. It is the "fifth discipline" because without it, the other four remain disconnected practices rather than a coherent organizational capability.

Systems thinking in human services means understanding how a decision made in one part of the service system affects other parts, how incentive structures shape behaviors that produce outcomes no one intended, and how the same problem keeps recurring because its systemic drivers have not been addressed.

For DSD: Systems thinking is what allows leaders to see not just the individual who is not receiving a needed service, but the system-level factors that produce that gap. It is what distinguishes between a practice that is broken and a policy that generates that practice, between a staff member who is struggling and an organizational design that makes their work unnecessarily difficult.

Adapting the five disciplines for DSD

Discipline — DSD application

Personal Mastery — IDPs, reflective practice, honest self-assessment, development vs. improvement
Mental Models — IDI work, equity analysis, cultural humility, surfacing assumptions in case review
Shared Vision — DSD six program goals, participatory strategic planning, community-centered planning
Team Learning — Learning-focused supervision, equity conversations, post-action reviews, reading groups
Systems Thinking — EAT application, equity data analysis, Cascade Crosswalk, Olmstead implementation

Practical application

Assess your team's learning organization capacity. For each of the five disciplines, rate your team on a simple scale: Where are you genuinely practicing this? Where is the aspiration stronger than the reality?

Start with systems thinking on a recurring problem. Take a problem your team keeps encountering and examine it through a systems lens: What drives this pattern? What in the broader system produces this outcome? What would have to change at the system level — not just the individual case level — to address it?

Build dialogue into team meetings. Replace some of the advocacy (presenting positions) in your team's conversations with genuine inquiry (exploring together). Practice saying "I wonder what's driving this" rather than "I think the problem is."

Connect personal mastery to the organizational mission. In supervision and team conversations, explicitly link individual development to organizational purpose. Staff whose personal growth is connected to the mission they care about develop faster and more durably than staff who develop in isolation from organizational purpose.

Common challenges

"Learning organizations sound great in theory but are unrealistic in a government agency." The disciplines are scalable — they can be practiced at the team level, the program level, and the division level, even when the broader organizational culture is not yet a learning organization. Start where you can.

"We don't have time for dialogue; we have work to do." The distinction between dialogue (thinking together) and debate (presenting positions) is primarily one of orientation, not time investment. A team meeting can include genuine dialogue without being longer — it requires a different facilitator orientation, not additional hours.

"Systems thinking is too abstract for daily practice." Systems thinking at a practical level asks one question: What else is this connected to? That question — asked regularly — is accessible in daily conversations, case reviews, and program discussions.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

All five disciplines serve DSD's program goals, but particularly:
• Equitable and effective service delivery requires systems thinking to understand and address systemic gaps
• Inclusive workforce culture requires team learning and shared vision
• Continuous quality improvement requires personal mastery and mental model examination

Connection to other leadership competencies

• Reflective Practice Walk-Through (Asset 2): Personal mastery through reflection
• Inclusive Supervision Foundations (Asset 9): Team learning requires psychological safety
• Strategic Planning Foundations (Asset 16): Shared vision feeds into strategic planning
• Vision, Strategy, and Structure (Asset 18): Systems thinking connects structure to strategy

Reflective questions

1. Which of the five disciplines is most alive in your team right now? Which is most underdeveloped?
2. What is a mental model you hold about the people DSD serves that you have never examined out loud? What would happen if you did?
3. When have you experienced genuine team learning — a conversation in which the group arrived somewhere none of the individuals could have reached alone? What made that possible?
4. What recurring problem in your team or program has a system-level driver that has not been addressed? What would addressing it at the system level require?
5. How would DSD be different if staff at every level approached their daily work with personal mastery — genuine development commitment connected to organizational purpose?

Sources

• Senge, P. M. (1990). The fifth discipline: The art and practice of the learning organization. Doubleday/Currency. https://www.toolshero.com/management/five-disciplines-learning-organizations/ (https://www.toolshero.com/management/five-disciplines-learning-organizations/)
• Senge, P. M., Kleiner, A., Roberts, C., Ross, R., & Smith, B. (1994). The fifth discipline fieldbook. Currency/Doubleday.
• Adaptconsultingcompany.com. (2024). Senge's five disciplines model. https://www.adaptconsultingcompany.com/2024/09/19/senges-five-disciplines-model/ (https://www.adaptconsultingcompany.com/2024/09/19/senges-five-disciplines-model/)
• One DSD L05 Inclusive Leadership Library. One DSD People, Equity and Culture Program.
• One DSD L08 Emotional Intelligence Library. One DSD People, Equity and Culture Program.

fields.body:
Accessible Meetings Checklist

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Accessibility
Library home: L09 Accessibility & Plain Language Library
Companion to: WCAG 2.2 AA Flagship Module; Accessible Communications Checklist; Sensory Accommodations Walk-Through; Effective Communication for People with Communication Disabilities
Standards reference: WCAG 2.2 AA; Title II ADA (Effective Communication); §504 Rehabilitation Act; Minnesota Human Rights Act (MHRA); DSD Equity and Inclusion principles

What this is

A comprehensive checklist for making DSD meetings accessible — covering virtual meetings, in-person meetings, and hybrid formats. This checklist addresses captioning, ASL interpretation requests, materials distributed in advance, accessible venue criteria, sensory accommodations, breaks, and the full arc from pre-meeting planning through follow-up. It is organized in three phases: Before the Meeting, During the Meeting, and After the Meeting.

Why this matters for DSD

DSD staff facilitate hundreds of meetings every year — service planning meetings, team meetings, trainings, public forums, stakeholder engagements, and individual consultations. When meetings are not accessible:

• Staff with hearing disabilities cannot follow the discussion
• Staff with visual disabilities cannot access visual materials shared in the meeting
• People with cognitive disabilities are overwhelmed by dense, unstructured presentations
• People who use sign language and do not read lips well are excluded without ASL interpretation
• People with sensory sensitivities are physically unable to attend or participate comfortably
• People with mobility disabilities cannot access venues with barriers

The ADA's Title II Effective Communication requirement applies to DSD's meetings. When a person with a communication disability needs an auxiliary aid or service to communicate effectively, DSD must provide it — at no cost to the individual — unless it would impose an undue burden or fundamentally alter the program. The person's preference for the type of aid must receive primary consideration.

Meeting accessibility is not a courtesy — it is a legal and ethical obligation.

The core requirements

All DSD meetings must:
1. Include an accessibility accommodation request process in all invitations
2. Allow sufficient advance notice for accommodation requests
3. Use captioning for all virtual meetings and large in-person meetings
4. Provide meeting materials in advance (at least 48 hours)
5. Use accessible document formats for all shared materials
6. Follow a clear, predictable agenda structure
7. Offer breaks in meetings longer than 60 minutes
8. Use inclusive facilitation practices
9. Provide follow-up materials in accessible formats

Before the Meeting

Step 1: Include an Accommodation Request Notice in All Invitations

Every meeting invitation — whether for a large public forum or a small team meeting — must include a way for participants to request accommodations.

Minimum required text in invitations:
"If you need an accommodation to participate in this meeting, please contact [name] at [phone] or [email] by [date — at least 5 business days before the meeting]. Accommodations may include ASL interpretation, CART captioning, materials in alternative formats, a sign language interpreter, or other supports. Requests submitted with less than [5] business days' notice will be honored if possible; the more advance notice you provide, the more easily we can arrange what you need."

Key elements:
• Named contact person (not just a general inbox)
• Both phone and email options
• Deadline for requests that allows planning time (5 business days is a minimum; 10 business days or more is better for complex accommodations)
• Non-exhaustive examples of accommodations (do not limit what people can request)
• A note that last-minute requests will be made in good faith

Common error: Putting accommodation request information at the bottom of an invitation in small print. Fix: Make the accommodation notice a clearly visible section near the top of every invitation.

Step 2: Process Accommodation Requests

When an accommodation request comes in:
1. Acknowledge receipt within one business day
2. Confirm what can be provided and by when
3. If the specific accommodation cannot be provided, engage the person in finding an effective alternative
4. Do not assume what accommodation a person needs — let them specify
5. Never ask for a diagnosis or medical documentation for reasonable accommodations — ask only for information about what is needed to participate effectively
6. Log accommodation requests in your meeting file for continuity and planning purposes

Step 3: Arrange ASL Interpretation

ASL interpretation is a common and legally required accommodation for meetings involving Deaf people who use American Sign Language.

Key steps:
1. Contact a qualified ASL interpreter service as soon as you receive the request — qualified interpreters book quickly, especially for specialized or technical content
2. Provide the interpreter with the meeting agenda, key terminology, and any documents that will be discussed, at least 24 hours in advance
3. For virtual meetings: arrange for the interpreter to be on camera at all times; use Spotlight in Microsoft Teams or Zoom to pin the interpreter's video
4. For in-person meetings: position the interpreter in the signer's direct line of sight, near the primary speaker, with good lighting — never against a window
5. For meetings longer than 90 minutes: arrange two interpreters who rotate every 30 minutes (interpreting is cognitively intense and accuracy declines with fatigue)

Minnesota resources for ASL interpretation:
• DSD's contract interpretation services (contact the DSD Equity Team for current contractors)
• Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind & Hard of Hearing: https://mn.gov/deaf-commission/
• Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf (RID): https://rid.org/

Note on video relay interpreting (VRI): VRI (video-based remote interpreting) is an alternative when an in-person interpreter is not available. It is not always equally effective — it can fail when the participant has difficulty seeing the screen, when lighting is poor, or when the content is very technical. Always discuss VRI suitability with the participant.

Step 4: Arrange CART Captioning

CART (Communication Access Realtime Translation) provides real-time text transcription of spoken content. It is essential for people who are deaf or hard of hearing but do not use sign language, and beneficial for many others.

Key steps:
1. Contact a qualified CART provider as soon as you receive the request
2. Provide the CART provider with the agenda, glossary of key terms, proper nouns (names, programs, legislation), and any prepared remarks
3. For virtual meetings: share the CART stream URL with the participant; many CART providers can also integrate with Teams or Zoom
4. For in-person meetings: arrange a display screen for the participant to view the CART output; position it in their line of sight
5. Request a transcript of the CART output for post-meeting follow-up

Auto-generated captions vs. CART:
Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and Google Meet all offer auto-generated live captions. These are not a substitute for CART when a participant has requested CART as an accommodation. Auto-captions have error rates that vary with accents, technical vocabulary, and audio quality. CART captioners achieve accuracy rates above 98% and can be corrected in real time. Use auto-captions as a supplemental tool; use CART as the accommodation.

Step 5: Prepare and Distribute Materials in Advance

All meeting materials — agendas, presentations, documents, reports — must be distributed to participants at least 48 hours before the meeting. For participants using screen readers or Braille displays, earlier distribution (5–7 days) is better — navigating complex documents with assistive technology takes more time.

Material requirements:
• All documents in accessible formats (Word with accessibility checked, tagged PDF — not scanned PDFs or images)
• Presentation slides shared as accessible PowerPoint or accessible PDF — not as an image or a printed handout only
• Agendas formatted with clear headings and times
• If video will be shown, provide captioned versions in advance

Why in advance matters: Participants with visual disabilities, cognitive disabilities, or processing differences need time to review materials before the meeting. Handing out a complex report at the start of a meeting and immediately discussing it excludes people who cannot absorb complex information in real time.

Step 6: Assess Venue Accessibility (In-Person Meetings)

For in-person meetings, verify the following before confirming the location:

Physical access:
• [ ] Building entrance is accessible (no steps, or step-free alternative is clearly marked and not a service entrance)
• [ ] Accessible parking within reasonable proximity
• [ ] Path from parking to meeting room is accessible (no stairs, no heavy doors without automatic openers)
• [ ] Elevator available if meeting room is not on ground floor (and elevator is working — check day-of)
• [ ] Meeting room door is wide enough for wheelchairs (minimum 32 inches clear; 36 inches preferred)
• [ ] Accessible restroom on the same floor as the meeting room

Meeting room:
• [ ] Table and chair setup allows wheelchair users to sit at the table with all other participants — not at the side or end
• [ ] Assistive listening system (hearing loop/induction loop, or FM system) available and working — required for groups of 50 or more under ADA standards; recommended for smaller groups when requested
• [ ] Lighting is adequate (not fluorescent flicker; not too dim; natural light supplemented)
• [ ] Space is quiet — not adjacent to loud machinery, HVAC units, or high-traffic areas
• [ ] Room temperature is comfortable and adjustable
• [ ] Accessible seating options (chairs with armrests, chairs at different heights)

Common error: Booking a venue without checking for elevators or accessible restrooms, and discovering barriers on the day of the meeting. Fix: Always do a physical accessibility walk-through or request an accessibility confirmation from the venue in writing before booking.

Step 7: Plan the Agenda for Accessibility

Accessible agendas:
• Are shared in advance in accessible format
• List start and end times for the meeting and for each major item
• Identify who will speak on each item
• Include scheduled breaks (for meetings over 60 minutes)
• Note when materials will be distributed or demonstrated
• Are simple and clear — no abbreviations or internal shorthand without explanation

During the Meeting

Step 8: Open with Accessibility Orientation

Begin every meeting with a brief accessibility orientation (30–60 seconds):
• Confirm that CART, ASL interpretation, or other accommodations are functioning
• Identify the interpreter and captioner to all participants
• Remind participants to speak one at a time (for captioning accuracy and interpretation clarity)
• Share how participants can signal that they want to speak (raise hand button, physical hand raise, or unmute)
• Note the location of accessible restrooms (in-person meetings)
• Remind participants of the break schedule

Step 9: Inclusive Facilitation Practices

Speaking practices:
• Speak clearly, at a moderate pace
• Face the group — do not speak while turned to the whiteboard or screen
• Identify yourself before speaking ("This is [Name]") in large virtual meetings where screen readers cannot identify speakers
• Do not talk over each other — wait for the previous speaker to finish before speaking
• Repeat or summarize audience questions and comments before responding (improves captioning and allows remote participants to hear)

Visual practices:
• Describe all visual content verbally: "The slide shows a bar chart comparing enrollment across five programs. The highest enrollment is in CDCS, with 1,240 participants."
• Do not reference visuals with only spatial language: "as you can see here" or "the thing on the left" — describe what it shows
• Read key text from slides or documents aloud

Participation practices:
• Use multiple modes for participation: verbal, chat, written questions
• Give processing time before expecting responses — do not rush people
• Use the raise-hand function in virtual meetings consistently
• Allow participants who use AAC (Augmentative and Alternative Communication) devices adequate time to compose and share their message

Step 10: Manage Sensory Environment (In-Person)

• Keep the room at a comfortable, stable temperature
• Dim or adjust overhead lighting if requested by a participant with sensory sensitivity — provide reading lights as supplemental lighting
• Minimize background noise (close doors, turn off HVAC noise where possible)
• Do not use scented sprays, strong air fresheners, or perfumed products in or near the meeting room (request this from all participants in the invitation)
• Have a designated quiet space nearby if participants need a sensory break

Step 11: Take and Track Breaks

For meetings over 60 minutes:
• Schedule a 10-minute break at the 60-minute mark
• For meetings over 2 hours: schedule breaks every 60 minutes
• Break times should be clearly communicated at the start of the meeting and on the agenda
• Breaks support cognitive accessibility (sustained attention has limits for everyone, particularly for people with ADHD, autism, or traumatic brain injuries), physical accessibility (people who need to move, stretch, or use medical devices), and interpreter and captioner sustainability

After the Meeting

Step 12: Distribute Accessible Follow-Up Materials

Within 24–48 hours of the meeting, send:
• Meeting summary or minutes in accessible Word or tagged PDF format
• Any presentations shared during the meeting in accessible PowerPoint or PDF
• Any action items with clear ownership and due dates
• CART transcript (if applicable) for participants who requested it or who missed content

For participants who missed part of the meeting due to an accessibility barrier: Follow up individually and offer to walk through key decisions or content.

Step 13: Follow Up on Accommodation Quality

After the meeting, check in briefly with participants who received accommodations:
• Did the interpretation or captioning meet your needs?
• Were there any barriers we should address for the next meeting?
• Is there anything we can do better?

This feedback improves future meetings and demonstrates that DSD takes accessibility seriously as an ongoing practice, not a one-time checkbox.

ASL Interpretation Request Process Summary

Step — Action — Timeline

1 — Participant requests ASL interpretation in the accommodation notice — ≥5 business days before meeting
2 — DSD staff acknowledges request within 1 business day — Within 1 business day of request
3 — DSD contacts interpreter service and books qualified interpreter — As soon as possible after request
4 — DSD provides interpreter with advance materials — ≥24 hours before meeting
5 — DSD confirms interpreter logistics with participant — ≥48 hours before meeting
6 — Meeting opens with accessibility orientation — First 2 minutes of meeting
7 — DSD follow up with participant on quality — Within 24 hours after meeting

Common Errors and How to Fix Them

Error — Impact — Fix

No accommodation request notice in invitation — Participants cannot request what they need — Add accommodation notice to every invitation template
Short notice for accommodation requests — Interpreters and CART providers unavailable — Build 5–10 business day lead time into invitation templates
Materials distributed at meeting start — Screen reader/Braille users excluded from real-time discussion — Send accessible materials 48+ hours in advance
Auto-captions treated as CART — Accuracy too low for substantive meetings — Arrange qualified CART when requested; use auto-captions as supplement
Venue not checked for accessibility — Physical barriers prevent attendance — Do accessibility walk-through or get written confirmation before booking
No breaks in long meetings — Participants with fatigue, pain, or cognitive needs cannot sustain participation — Schedule 10-minute breaks every 60 minutes
Visuals not described verbally — Blind and low-vision participants miss content — Describe all slides and visual content in words during the meeting
ASL interpreter not spotted in virtual meeting — Deaf participants cannot see interpreter — Use Spotlight/Pin to fix interpreter video on screen
No follow-up materials — Participants who missed content cannot catch up — Send accessible summary within 24–48 hours of every meeting

Where to Get Help

• ADA National Network — Meeting Accessibility: https://adata.org/
• ADA.gov — Effective Communication: https://www.ada.gov/resources/effective-communication/
• Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind & Hard of Hearing: https://mn.gov/deaf-commission/
• Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf: https://rid.org/
• Microsoft Teams Accessibility Features: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/accessibility-overview-of-microsoft-teams
• One DSD Equity Team: Accommodation request support, interpreter and CART coordination

Connection to DSD's Six Program Goals

DSD Program Goal — Accessible Meetings Connection

Equity and inclusion — Accessible meetings ensure all staff and community members can participate fully
Cultural and linguistic competence — Interpretation and multilingual accommodation support diverse linguistic communities
Olmstead implementation — Service planning meetings for people with disabilities must themselves be accessible
Workforce development — Staff with disabilities need accessible team meetings, trainings, and all-staff events
Quality improvement — Accessible meetings produce better decisions because all perspectives are heard
Leadership and accountability — Leaders are accountable for the accessibility of every meeting they facilitate

Sources

• ADA.gov — Effective Communication: https://www.ada.gov/resources/effective-communication/
• ADA National Network — Accessible Meetings Fact Sheet: https://adata.org/
• Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind & Hard of Hearing: https://mn.gov/deaf-commission/
• Section508.gov — Creating Accessible Meetings: https://www.section508.gov/
• Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, W3C, December 2024: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
• DOJ ADA Title Two Web and Mobile App Accessibility Final Rule, April 2024: https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/
• Microsoft Teams Accessibility: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/accessibility-overview-of-microsoft-teams

Accessibility is everyone's responsibility. When in doubt, ask people with disabilities what works for them.

fields.title: ADA Title Two (State & Local Government) — Compliance Guide
fields.summary: ADA Title Two is the part of the Americans with Disabilities Act that applies to us. It covers state and local government — every program, service, and activity a public entity provides. For the Disability Services Division it is not an outside rule to satisfy; it is the floor under everything we do.
fields.body:
ADA Title Two is the part of the Americans with Disabilities Act that applies to us. It covers state and local government — every program, service, and activity a public entity provides. For the Disability Services Division it is not an outside rule to satisfy; it is the floor under everything we do.

What Title Two requires, in plain terms:
• Equal opportunity. People with disabilities must have the same real chance to take part in and benefit from our programs as anyone else.
• Effective communication. We must communicate with people with disabilities as effectively as with everyone else — which can mean interpreters, captions, large print, Braille, or accessible electronic formats, at no cost to the person.
• Reasonable modifications. We adjust our policies, practices, and procedures when needed so a person with a disability can take part — unless the change would fundamentally alter the program.
• Accessible facilities and services. Physical spaces, and the way services are delivered, must be usable by people with disabilities.

The web and mobile accessibility rule (2024). The U.S. Department of Justice set a specific technical standard for Title Two: state and local government websites and mobile apps must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. "Guidelines" is in the name, but meeting WCAG 2.1 AA is required, not optional. The compliance dates were later adjusted — public entities serving 50,000 or more people must comply by April 26, 2027, and smaller entities and special districts by April 26, 2028. Narrow exceptions exist for certain content, but even then, if a person with a disability needs that content, we still must provide it in a format they can use.

What this means for your work. When you build a form, write a notice, post a document, host a meeting, or stand up an online service, accessibility is part of the assignment from the start — not a fix added at the end. Captions on video. Real text, not pictures of text. Forms you can operate with a keyboard. Color contrast that meets the standard. A clear way to request another format. Build it in, and the service works better for everyone — older adults, people with low vision, people on phones or slow connections, and the Minnesotans with disabilities we serve.

This is a working summary for staff, not legal advice. For a specific legal question, route it to the consultant, who will refer it to the appropriate office.

fields.title: Inclusive Recruitment and Hiring
fields.summary: Inclusive hiring means building a process that reaches a wide range of candidates and judges each one fairly. It is one of the most direct ways the division can reduce disparities, because who we hire shapes who we are and how well we serve.
fields.body:
Inclusive hiring means building a process that reaches a wide range of candidates and judges each one fairly. It is one of the most direct ways the division can reduce disparities, because who we hire shapes who we are and how well we serve.

Reach more people.
• Post beyond the usual places. Share openings through community organizations, cultural media, and partner networks, not only the standard lists.
• Write inclusive job postings. Use plain, gender-neutral language. List the real essential functions. Avoid jargon and inflated requirements that screen people out for no good reason.
• Name the commitment. Say plainly that you welcome a wide pool and will provide accommodations during the process.

Judge candidates fairly.
• Decide criteria first. Agree on what matters before you read applications, and apply it consistently.
• Use diverse, prepared panels. A mix of perspectives, with shared questions and a simple scoring guide, reduces bias.
• Watch for unspoken filters. Culture fit can quietly mean people like us. Look for what the person brings, not how familiar they feel.
• Make the process accessible. Use accessible application tools and a clear, easy way to request accommodation.

Handle demographic data with care. If you track who applies to see whether outreach is working, keep that information separate from the hiring decision and review it only after the hire is made.

Inclusive hiring is not about lowering the bar. It is about removing the barriers that kept good people from reaching it.

fields.title: Disability Etiquette and Respectful Interaction
fields.summary: Respectful interaction with people with disabilities is mostly common sense and good manners, with a few habits worth naming. The goal is simple: treat the person as a person, and follow their lead.
fields.body:
Respectful interaction with people with disabilities is mostly common sense and good manners, with a few habits worth naming. The goal is simple: treat the person as a person, and follow their lead.

General habits.
• Talk to the person directly, not to their companion, interpreter, or aide.
• Use People First language: a person with a disability, not a disabled person.
• Ask before helping, and accept the answer. Do not assume someone needs help, and do not help without asking.
• Do not touch a person's wheelchair, cane, or service animal. They are part of the person's space.

A few specifics.
• If someone uses a wheelchair, try to position yourself at eye level for a longer conversation.
• With someone who is blind or has low vision, say who you are when you arrive and when you leave, and offer your arm rather than grabbing theirs.
• With someone who is Deaf or hard of hearing, face them, speak naturally, and use a qualified interpreter for anything important.
• With someone who has a speech difference, be patient, do not finish their sentences, and ask them to repeat rather than pretending you understood.
• With someone who has a cognitive or intellectual disability, use plain language, allow time, and check understanding respectfully.

When in doubt, ask. The person is the expert on what works for them. A simple how can I best work with you today is worth more than any list.

Respect is the whole point. Lead with it, follow the person's preferences, and the etiquette takes care of itself.

fields.title: Microsoft PowerPoint Accessibility Checklist
fields.summary: A step-by-step checklist for creating accessible Microsoft PowerPoint presentations. This checklist covers slide layouts versus custom text boxes, reading order, alt text, slide titles, color contrast, animations and transitions, accessible video and audio embeds, and how to use the built-in Accessibility Checker. It also covers the most common errors and how to fix them.
fields.body:
Microsoft PowerPoint Accessibility Checklist

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Accessibility
Library home: L09 Accessibility & Plain Language Library
Companion to: WCAG 2.2 AA Flagship Module; Microsoft Word Accessibility Checklist; Accessible Meetings Checklist
Standards reference: WCAG 2.2 AA; §508 Rehabilitation Act; Title II ADA; Microsoft Accessibility documentation

What this is

A step-by-step checklist for creating accessible Microsoft PowerPoint presentations. This checklist covers slide layouts versus custom text boxes, reading order, alt text, slide titles, color contrast, animations and transitions, accessible video and audio embeds, and how to use the built-in Accessibility Checker. It also covers the most common errors and how to fix them.

Use this checklist whenever you create a presentation for a staff meeting, training, public event, or online sharing — including presentations that will be exported to PDF or recorded as video.

Why this matters for DSD

Presentations are a primary vehicle for training, policy communication, and meeting facilitation in DSD. When a presentation is not accessible:

• Staff or clients with vision disabilities cannot access the content via screen readers
• People who are deaf or hard of hearing cannot access embedded audio or video without captions
• People with cognitive disabilities are overwhelmed by slides with too much text and poor structure
• When presented virtually, poor accessibility compounds — someone using a screen reader through a Zoom screen share cannot navigate the presentation at all if reading order is not set

Title II ADA compliance applies to presentations DSD shares digitally. WCAG 2.2 AA is DSD's operating standard.

The core requirements

Accessible PowerPoint presentations must:
1. Use built-in slide layouts (not custom text boxes dropped onto blank slides)
2. Give every slide a unique, descriptive title
3. Set the reading order for each slide
4. Add alt text to every image, chart, and graphic
5. Mark decorative visuals as decorative
6. Meet color contrast requirements (4.5:1 for text)
7. Not rely on color alone to convey meaning
8. Caption all embedded video; provide audio descriptions where needed
9. Make animations and transitions keyboard-accessible and avoid strobing effects
10. Pass the built-in Accessibility Checker before sharing

Step-by-Step Checklist

Step 1: Use Built-In Slide Layouts (Not Custom Text Boxes)

This is the single most important PowerPoint accessibility step. When you use a built-in slide layout (from the Layout menu), the reading order is automatically set in a logical sequence that screen readers and keyboard navigation follow. When you add custom text boxes by inserting them manually onto a blank slide, the reading order is arbitrary — usually the order in which items were inserted — which is rarely the intended reading order.

How to use slide layouts:
1. When adding a new slide, go to Home > New Slide and choose a layout (Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content, etc.)
2. Type content directly into the placeholders provided by the layout
3. Do not delete placeholders and replace them with text boxes

If you received a presentation that uses custom text boxes:
1. You will need to set the reading order manually for each slide (see Step 3)
2. Or recreate the slides using proper layouts

Why it matters: Screen readers read slide content in the order items appear in the Selection Pane or Reading Order Pane. Custom text boxes are added in the order they were created — which has no relationship to visual layout or logical reading order.

Common error: Starting with a blank slide and adding text boxes and images manually. This is very common and almost always creates accessibility problems. Fix: Use the Layout menu to choose an appropriate slide structure before adding content.

Step 2: Give Every Slide a Unique, Descriptive Title

Every slide must have a title. Screen reader users navigate presentations by jumping from slide title to slide title — just as sighted readers scan slide headers. Without titles, blind and low-vision users cannot orient themselves in the presentation.

Requirements:
• Every slide gets a unique, descriptive title — even "simple" or "visual" slides
• Titles should describe the slide's content or purpose, not just number it
• If the slide design does not include a visible title placeholder, you can hide the title off-slide (move it outside the visible slide area) rather than deleting it

How to add a title:
1. If the slide has a title placeholder: click it and type the title
2. If the slide has no title placeholder: go to Insert > Text Box, type the title, move it off the slide, and then set it as the first item in reading order

How to check if a slide is missing a title:
Run the Accessibility Checker — it flags slides with missing titles.

Common error: Slides with titles that are identical across multiple slides ("Introduction," "Introduction 2") or slides where the title placeholder has been deleted and replaced with a text box. Fix: Give each slide a unique, meaningful title using the proper title placeholder.

Step 3: Set the Reading Order for Each Slide

The reading order determines the sequence in which a screen reader announces the content on each slide. In PowerPoint, the reading order is set through the Reading Order Pane (newer versions) or the Selection Pane (all versions), where items are listed in reverse order — the last item in the list is read first.

How to set reading order using the Reading Order Pane:
1. Go to View > Reading Order (if available in your version)
2. Drag items in the pane to set the logical reading sequence

How to set reading order using the Selection Pane:
1. Go to Home > Arrange > Selection Pane (or View > Selection Pane)
2. Items at the bottom of the list are read first; items at the top are read last
3. Drag items to set the order (reversed from what you want to announce)

Logic to follow:
• Title should be read first (placed at the bottom of the Selection Pane)
• Body content in the order it should be heard
• Footer and slide number last (placed at the top of the Selection Pane)
• Decorative elements should be at the top of the pane (read last) or marked as decorative so they are skipped

Common error: Slides with reading order that reflects the order items were inserted, not the order they should be read. Fix: Open the Selection Pane, review the order, and drag items to correct sequence.

Step 4: Add Alt Text to All Visuals

Every image, chart, SmartArt graphic, shape, screenshot, diagram, and video thumbnail on a slide needs alternative text — unless it is purely decorative.

How to add alt text in PowerPoint:
1. Right-click the image or visual
2. Select Edit Alt Text
3. Type a concise description in the alt text box
4. For decorative visuals: check Mark as decorative

Writing effective alt text for presentations:
• Describe what the visual shows and what it is meant to communicate in this slide
• For charts: summarize the key data point or trend ("Line chart showing a 35% decrease in service wait times from Q1 2023 to Q4 2024")
• For diagrams: describe the relationship or process shown
• For photos of people: describe the activity or context relevant to the slide (not personal identifying details)
• Keep alt text to one or two sentences

Common error: Grouping multiple objects (images + text + shapes) into a single group without alt text. Fix: Ungroup and add alt text to each meaningful element, or add alt text to the group as a whole that describes the complete visual unit.

Step 5: Use Sufficient Color Contrast

All text in your presentation must have a color contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background (normal text) or 3:1 (large text — approximately 18pt or 14pt bold and above).

High-risk situations in presentations:
• Dark text on dark image backgrounds (very common in stylized presentations)
• White text on a medium-blue or medium-green background (may not meet 4.5:1)
• Yellow or orange text on white
• Light gray text on white backgrounds (common in body text and speaker notes)
• Colored text in tables

How to check contrast:
1. Use the Colour Contrast Analyser (free tool): https://www.tpgi.com/color-contrast-checker/
2. Or run the Accessibility Checker (Step 9) — it flags some contrast issues
3. Note: The Accessibility Checker only checks text in solid opaque backgrounds; text over images requires manual checking

Using predesigned themes safely:
Built-in PowerPoint themes are generally designed with accessible color combinations. If you use a predesigned theme without customizing colors, you reduce your contrast risk. If you customize colors, always check contrast.

Common error: White text over a photographic image background. The contrast between white text and a varied photographic background cannot be predicted — some areas may pass, others fail. Fix: Add a solid or semi-transparent overlay behind text, or use a slide design that places text on a solid background.

Step 6: Do Not Rely on Color Alone

Color cannot be the only means of conveying information. This applies to:
• Highlighting or marking certain items as important
• Status indicators ("green = on track, red = delayed")
• Distinguishing between data series in a chart

Alternatives to color-only coding:
• Add text labels to color-coded items ("✓ On track," "✗ Delayed")
• Use both color and pattern/texture in charts
• Add a legend that describes both the color and the meaning
• Use bold or border to distinguish highlighted items

Common error: A pie chart where the only way to distinguish segments is by color, with a color-coded legend. Fix: Add data labels directly on each segment with the label and value; or use patterns in addition to colors.

Step 7: Make Animations and Transitions Accessible

Animations and transitions can create accessibility barriers if they are too fast, too complex, or strobe-like.

Requirements:
• Avoid animations that flash more than three times per second — this can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy (WCAG 2.3.1)
• Do not use rapid, blinking, or strobing effects
• Prefer simple fade or appear animations over complex spinning, swirling, or motion-path animations
• Respect prefers-reduced-motion — when presenting to an audience or sharing as a file, be aware that some users have motion sensitivity; offer a motion-free version if complex animations are central to the content
• Avoid auto-advancing slides — this removes user control over pacing; if auto-advance is used, provide a way to pause
• Ensure that content conveyed through animation is also available in a static form (e.g., the final state of an animated diagram includes all the information)

For presentations shared as files:
• Consider providing a version of the presentation with animations removed for users who will read it with a screen reader
• Or export to PDF as a non-animated version

Common error: Complex "fly-in" or "spin" animations on every bullet point. Fix: Use simple "Appear" or "Fade" animations, or use "With Previous" so all bullets appear at once.

Step 8: Caption All Embedded Video and Audio

Any video embedded in a PowerPoint presentation must have closed captions. Any audio-only content must have a transcript.

For prerecorded video:
• Include closed captions encoded in the video file before inserting it into PowerPoint
• PowerPoint for Windows supports separate caption files (.srt, .vtt) for some video formats
• Warning: If you use Compress Media or Optimize Media Compatibility, captions, subtitles, and multiple audio tracks may be removed
• Test captioning after any media optimization

For live presentations:
• Use Microsoft Teams or Zoom live captioning features
• Or provide a CART (Communication Access Realtime Translation) captionist
• See the Accessible Meetings Checklist for the ASL interpretation request process

For audio descriptions:
• If a video conveys visual-only information (diagrams, demonstrations, text on screen) without narration, it needs audio description
• Audio description narrates the visual content for blind and low-vision viewers
• Contact the DSD Equity Team for guidance on commissioning audio descriptions

Common error: Inserting a video without captions because "the video was created by someone else." Fix: All video embedded in DSD presentations must have captions regardless of origin; request captioned versions from vendors or caption them yourself.

Step 9: Run the Built-In Accessibility Checker

PowerPoint's Accessibility Checker runs automatically in the background and can be launched manually.

How to run it:
1. Go to Review > Check Accessibility
2. Review all items under Errors, Warnings, and Tips
3. Click each item to jump to the affected slide element
4. Follow the suggested fixes

What the PowerPoint Accessibility Checker finds:
• Slides with missing titles
• Images, shapes, and visuals with missing alt text
• Slides with possible reading order issues
• Tables without header rows
• Insufficient color contrast (for solid backgrounds)
• Small text sizes
• Animations that may be difficult for some users

What it does NOT find:
• Alt text quality (presence only, not accuracy)
• Color-over-image contrast
• Caption quality
• Reading order accuracy (flags "possible issues" but does not verify logical order)

Run the Accessibility Checker before every share, every export to PDF, and before every presentation.

Common error: Only running the Accessibility Checker at the very end of a complex presentation. Fix: Run it periodically as you build the presentation, especially after adding images or complex slide structures.

Step 10: Save Accessible PDFs from PowerPoint

When exporting a presentation to PDF for sharing, preserve the accessibility tags.

How to export:
1. Go to File > Save As or Export
2. Choose PDF (.pdf)
3. Click More options > Options
4. Check Document structure tags for accessibility
5. Click OK, then Save

Do NOT use Print to PDF — this strips all accessibility tags.

After exporting, open in Adobe Acrobat Pro and run the Accessibility Full Check to verify and fix any remaining issues.

Common Errors and How to Fix Them

Error — Impact — Fix

Custom text boxes on blank slides — Screen reader reads in wrong order — Recreate using built-in slide layouts
Slides with no title — Screen reader users cannot navigate — Add unique, descriptive title to every slide
Visuals with no alt text — Blind users miss the content — Right-click > Edit Alt Text > add description
Reading order not set — Content read in wrong sequence — Open Selection Pane and set correct order
Low contrast text over images — Low-vision users cannot read text — Add solid or semi-transparent overlay behind text
Color-only data labels in charts — Colorblind users cannot interpret chart — Add text labels or patterns in addition to color
Flashing or rapid animations — Can trigger seizures — Remove strobing effects; use simple Appear/Fade
No captions on embedded video — Deaf/HoH users miss audio content — Add captions to video before embedding
Print to PDF export — Creates inaccessible image-based PDF — Use File > Save As > PDF > check structure tags
Very small font sizes (under 18pt) — Hard to read for low-vision users — Increase font size; use 18pt or larger for slides

Where to Get Help

• Microsoft PowerPoint Accessibility Documentation: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/make-your-powerpoint-presentations-accessible-to-people-with-disabilities-6f7772b2-2f33-4bd2-8ca7-dae3b2b3ef25
• WebAIM PowerPoint Accessibility: https://webaim.org/techniques/powerpoint/
• Section508.gov — Creating Accessible Presentations: https://www.section508.gov/create/presentations/
• Colour Contrast Analyser: https://www.tpgi.com/color-contrast-checker/
• One DSD Equity Team: Contact for accessibility review support

Connection to DSD's Six Program Goals

DSD Program Goal — PowerPoint Accessibility Connection

Equity and inclusion — Presentations shared with or about people DSD serves must be accessible to all
Cultural and linguistic competence — Language identification and multilingual slide content requires proper settings
Olmstead implementation — Training about community integration must itself be accessible
Workforce development — Staff with disabilities need accessible training materials and meeting slides
Quality improvement — Accessible presentations are better structured and more effective for all audiences
Leadership and accountability — Leaders presenting to DSD staff model accessibility practices with every slide deck

Sources

• Microsoft — Make your PowerPoint presentations accessible: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/make-your-powerpoint-presentations-accessible-to-people-with-disabilities-6f7772b2-2f33-4bd2-8ca7-dae3b2b3ef25
• Section508.gov — Creating Accessible Presentations: https://www.section508.gov/create/presentations/
• WebAIM — Microsoft PowerPoint Accessibility: https://webaim.org/techniques/powerpoint/
• Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, W3C, December 2024: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
• DOJ ADA Title Two Web Accessibility Final Rule, April 2024: https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/

Accessibility is everyone's responsibility. When in doubt, ask people with disabilities what works for them.

fields.title: Supported Decision-Making Walk-Through
fields.summary: Supported Decision-Making (SDM) is a rights-based model in which people with disabilities keep their legal rights and make their own decisions, with assistance from trusted people of their choosing rather than having a guardian or legal substitute decision-maker make decisions for them. SDM is an alternative to guardianship — and increasingly a required alternative under federal law and disability rights frameworks.
fields.body:
Supported Decision-Making Walk-Through

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Methodology / Framework
Adapted from: UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006); National Resource Center for Supported Decision-Making; ACLU Disability Rights; 42 CFR §441.301 (HCBS Settings Rule); Minnesota Statutes
Library home: L07 Disability Services Practice Library
Companion to: T04_07 Person-Centered Planning; T04_09 LifeCourse Framework; T04_06 SAMHSA TIP

What this framework is

Supported Decision-Making (SDM) is a rights-based model in which people with disabilities keep their legal rights and make their own decisions, with assistance from trusted people of their choosing rather than having a guardian or legal substitute decision-maker make decisions for them. SDM is an alternative to guardianship — and increasingly a required alternative under federal law and disability rights frameworks.

Disability Rights New Jersey describes SDM (https://disabilityrightsnj.org/resource/supported-decision-making/) as grounded in self-determination: "the idea that people with disabilities have the right to make choices about their lives, including where they live, what they eat, how they spend their time, and how they spend their money."

The ACLU's guidance (https://www.aclu.org/issues/disability-rights/integration-and-autonomy-people-disabilities/supported-decision-making) summarizes the core distinction: in guardianship, another person makes choices for the individual; in supported decision-making, the individual makes their own choices, supported by trusted people who help them understand information, think through options, and communicate their decisions.

SDM does not require a formal legal agreement, though some states and contexts provide for SDM agreements. It can be as informal as an individual identifying trusted people who will help them make decisions — a friend who helps them understand medical information, a family member who helps them review lease agreements, a peer mentor who helps them advocate at planning meetings.

Why DSD uses this framework

DSD's services are primarily governed by the HCBS Settings Rule (42 CFR §441.301), which explicitly requires that DSD-funded services optimize "individual initiative, autonomy, and independence in making life choices." This is not aspirational language; it is a regulatory requirement that has real enforcement implications.

The disability rights movement — and federal policy reflecting decades of advocacy — has moved decisively toward recognizing that most people with disabilities, including those with significant intellectual or developmental disabilities, can and should make their own decisions with appropriate support. Guardianship — historically the default response to concern about decision-making capacity — has been extensively documented as overused, disproportionately imposed, and deeply harmful to the people it is intended to protect.

The ACLU (https://www.aclu.org/issues/disability-rights/integration-and-autonomy-people-disabilities/supported-decision-making) documents that "guardianship is a legal proceeding that strips an individual of multiple or ALL rights" and that "once a guardianship is created, it can be almost impossible to undo." DSD staff play a critical role in supporting SDM as an alternative and in ensuring that service systems do not inadvertently or deliberately steer people toward guardianship when SDM would meet their actual needs.

The core concepts (plain language with citations)

What supported decision-making actually looks like

SDM is, at its core, a description of what happens when people make decisions in the context of trusted relationships — which is how most human beings make important decisions, with or without a disability label. The ACLU explains (https://www.aclu.org/issues/disability-rights/integration-and-autonomy-people-disabilities/supported-decision-making): "people with disabilities have supporters who help them make their own choices. A person using supported decision-making appoints trusted advisors, such as friends, family, or professionals, to serve as supporters. The supporters help the person with a disability understand, make, and communicate her own choices."

Concrete examples:
• A person with an intellectual disability who wants to sign a lease agreement brings their sibling to read the contract with them and explain the terms. The sibling does not sign on their behalf; they help them understand what they are signing. The person signs.
• A person with a traumatic brain injury who has difficulty processing complex medical information brings a trusted friend to medical appointments who takes notes, asks clarifying questions, and helps the person recall what was discussed afterward. The person makes their own treatment decisions.
• A person with autism who has difficulty in meetings that move quickly has a peer mentor attend their service planning meetings, signal them when to slow down, and help them communicate their preferences clearly. The plan reflects their preferences.

SDM vs. guardianship — the critical distinction

Guardianship — Supported Decision-Making

A court determines the person lacks capacity to make decisions — The person retains decision-making capacity
A guardian makes decisions on the person's behalf — Supporters help the person make their own decisions
The person's legal rights are suspended or removed — The person's legal rights are preserved
Decision-making authority is transferred — Decision-making authority remains with the person
Often permanent and difficult to reverse — Can be adjusted as the person's support needs change
Strips personhood in significant ways — Affirms personhood and autonomy

It is important to note that guardianship is sometimes appropriate — in situations of genuine incapacity and where less restrictive alternatives have been inadequate. The problem is not guardianship per se; it is the overuse of guardianship as a default, the failure to explore SDM alternatives, and the frequent failure to review or terminate guardianship when it is no longer needed.

DSD's role is not to oppose guardianship categorically, but to ensure that SDM is always explored, that guardianship is not imposed as a default, and that every person in DSD services is supported to exercise the maximum decision-making authority consistent with their needs.

What decision-making support can look like

SDM supporters can provide different types of assistance, including:

• Information support: Helping the person understand complex information — medical, legal, financial, administrative — in accessible language and format.
• Communication support: Helping the person communicate their decision to others, including in formal settings.
• Processing support: Giving the person time and space to think through a decision, ask questions, and revisit if needed.
• Advocacy support: Helping the person ensure their preferences are heard and respected in institutional settings.
• Relationship support: Maintaining connection with people who know the person well and can help interpret their preferences when communication is complex.

Decisional capacity vs. competence

Decisional capacity is the functional ability to make a specific decision at a specific time — to understand relevant information, appreciate consequences, reason about options, and communicate a preference. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific: a person may have capacity for some decisions and not others, and may have capacity at some times and not others. Capacity is not a fixed trait.

Competence is a legal concept determined by a court. It is not synonymous with capacity.

DSD staff are not competence adjudicators. Their role is to support people in exercising their capacity, to adapt how information is presented to maximize understanding, and to ensure that service systems do not treat low verbal communication ability or behavioral expression as absence of preferences.

HCBS Settings Rule alignment

The HCBS Settings Rule explicitly requires that:
• Services support "individual initiative, autonomy, and independence in making life choices."
• The setting "optimizes individual initiative, autonomy, and independence."
• Rights are documented and can only be limited based on individual assessed need, with the limitation documented in the person-centered service plan and reviewed over time.

The NJ DDD guide (https://nj.gov/humanservices/ddd/assets/documents/providers/DDD-Provider-Guide-to-HCBS-Settings-Rule-Final.pdf) clarifies that "the HCBS Final Settings rule are designed to ensure that people with disabilities living in the community have access to the same kind of choice and control over their lives as those who do not receive Medicaid HCBS funding."

This means: restricting decision-making for a person receiving HCBS services is not a default; it requires specific, individualized, documented justification — and even then, the least restrictive approach must be used.

DSD staff role in supporting SDM

In planning meetings:
• Ask the person who they want to help them understand the plan and communicate their preferences — and make space for those people to be present.
• Present information in plain language, with visual supports if helpful, and with adequate time for the person to process.
• Never substitute a guardian's or family member's stated preferences for the person's own stated preferences without clear evidence that the person cannot form a preference.
• When a guardian is present, ensure the person's voice is still directly heard — not just the guardian's.

In daily support:
• Give the person real choices in daily life — not choices between two pre-approved options, but choices that reflect actual agency.
• Notice when the person is communicating a preference through behavior, not just words, and document it as evidence of their preferences.
• Support the person to practice and develop their decision-making over time. Decision-making is a skill, and it develops through supported practice.

In service design:
• Design service processes that assume the person has decision-making capacity unless specifically documented otherwise.
• Treat family and guardian input as supplementary to, not substitutive of, the person's own voice.
• Document instances where a person's stated preferences were honored and the outcome — to build an evidence base for SDM fidelity in DSD services.

What it looks like in DSD practice

Scenario 1 — Transition planning:
A young woman with Down syndrome is turning 21. Her parents want her to live in a group home. She has expressed — through conversation, through behavior at her current program, and through her relationship with a peer mentor — that she wants to live with a roommate in an apartment. A person-centered approach to this transition begins with her vision, supports her to articulate it clearly, and explores what SDM supports would help her navigate apartment living. It does not automatically defer to her parents' preference, even though they are well-intentioned and loving.

Scenario 2 — Medical decision:
A man with autism and limited verbal communication is being asked to consent to a dental procedure. The dental team assumes he cannot consent because he does not speak. His DSP, who knows him well, explains that he communicates through AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) and that he has strong preferences and fears around medical settings. The DSP facilitates a process in which the dental team uses pictures to explain the procedure, gives him ample time to process, and allows him to communicate consent through his device. He consents, with support.

Scenario 3 — Financial decision:
A person with a cognitive disability wants to spend their discretionary income on a specific hobby. Their guardian believes the money should be saved. A SDM framework asks: What does this person want? Has the guardian appropriately explained the financial implications? Is the person's preference informed? If the person understands the trade-off and still prefers to spend on their hobby, their preference should prevail for their own discretionary funds — this is their money, their decision, their life.

How to apply this in your role

As a DSP:
• Offer choices before acting on behalf of the person.
• When a person's preference is unclear, take time to learn it — through observation, through trying different communication approaches, through consulting with people who know them well.
• Resist the impulse to decide what is "better for" the person when that decision is theirs to make.

As a case manager:
• Before recommending guardianship, ask: "What SDM supports have we tried? What would help this person make this decision with support?"
• Document the decision-making support the person currently has and identify gaps.
• Include SDM goals in person-centered plans: "What decision-making skills and supports does this person want to develop?"

As a supervisor:
• Create a culture in which staff are recognized for supporting autonomy, not for making decisions on people's behalf.
• Address instances where staff make decisions for people without exhausting SDM options.

Common misconceptions

"SDM is only for people with mild disabilities." SDM applies across the disability spectrum. The form and intensity of support varies; the principle does not. Even people with the most significant disabilities have preferences — they communicate them through behavior, response, and relationship.

"If someone is under guardianship, SDM doesn't apply." Guardianship does not eliminate the person's preferences or DSD's obligation to support them in exercising as much autonomy as possible. Even people under guardianship have rights; guardianship does not give guardians unlimited authority.

"SDM means the person always gets what they want, regardless of safety." SDM includes honest information about risks and consequences. Supporters' role is to inform, not to override. And "safety" decisions in disability services have historically been overused to restrict autonomy. The standard is genuine risk, not discomfort with choice.

Connection to other frameworks

• Person-Centered Planning (T04_07): SDM is the rights framework; PCP is the planning process. Together they form the legal and practical architecture of self-determination in DSD services.
• LifeCourse Framework (T04_09): LifeCourse explicitly includes SDM as a life domain support strategy, particularly in the Safety/Security domain. The LifeCourse vision — "all people have the right to live, love, work, play" — is only realized when people can make their own decisions.
• Trauma-Informed Practice (T04_06): TIP's empowerment principle (Principle 5) is the experiential dimension of SDM's rights framework. Both insist that the person is the primary agent of their own life.
• Intersectionality (T04_11): Guardianship and SDM interact with race, gender, and class. Research documents that guardianship is disproportionately imposed on Black and Latino individuals with disabilities; this is an intersectional equity concern for DSD.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

DSD Goal — SDM Connection

Goal 1 — Eliminate Disparities — Disparate imposition of guardianship across racial and ethnic groups is a documented disparity. Centering SDM is a disparity-reduction strategy.
Goal 2 — Community Engagement — Genuine community integration is only possible when people have the autonomy to choose their community connections — which requires SDM supports, not guardian control.
Goal 3 — Hiring and Retention — Organizations that model respect for autonomy attract and retain staff who share that value.
Goal 4 — Learning and Development — SDM skills — for both people receiving services and DSD staff — are core competency development areas.
Goal 5 — Contracts and Procurement — DSD contractors are required to support SDM as part of HCBS compliance. Contract performance standards should include SDM fidelity.
Goal 6 — Communication and Accessibility — Accessible communication is a precondition for genuine SDM: a person cannot make informed decisions without accessible information.

When to escalate / where to refer

• For guardianship alternatives exploration: Connect with the person's attorney (if they have one), the Minnesota Disability Law Center, or Arc Minnesota.
• For information on SDM agreements in Minnesota: Contact the One DSD Resource Hub for current Minnesota-specific SDM resources.
• For HCBS Settings Rule compliance concerns: Escalate to your supervisor and program manager.
• For concerns about overriding a person's expressed preferences: Escalate to your supervisor; this is a rights concern and may require legal consultation.
• National Resource Center for Supported Decision-Making: https://supporteddecisionmaking.org

Reflective questions for your practice

1. In a recent service interaction, how many real choices did the person actually make — choices between options they generated, not choices from a pre-approved menu?
2. When was the last time you supported someone to make a decision you personally thought was unwise? What did you do?
3. If someone you support is under guardianship, how much do you know about what they want — separate from what their guardian wants?
4. What conditions in your service environment make it harder for people to exercise decision-making authority? What would it take to change them?
5. When you see a person behaving in a way that seems challenging or confusing, what is your first question — about what they are communicating, or about how to respond?

Sources

• Disability Rights New Jersey. (2025). Supported Decision-Making. https://disabilityrightsnj.org/resource/supported-decision-making/
• ACLU. (2025). Supported Decision Making & the Problems of Guardianship. https://www.aclu.org/issues/disability-rights/integration-and-autonomy-people-disabilities/supported-decision-making
• National Resource Center for Supported Decision-Making. https://supporteddecisionmaking.org
• Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (2014). HCBS Settings Rule. 42 CFR §441.301.
• NJ DDD. (2021). Provider Guide to HCBS Settings Rule. https://nj.gov/humanservices/ddd/assets/documents/providers/DDD-Provider-Guide-to-HCBS-Settings-Rule-Final.pdf
• LifeCourse Nexus. Supported Decision-Making in the Life Domains. https://www.lifecoursetools.com/lifecourse-library/exploring-the-life-domains/
• United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Article 12 — Equal recognition before the law. (2006).
• Shogren, K. A., et al. (2017). Self-determination and supported decision making. Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 55(1), 54–64.
• Bach, M., & Kerzner, L. (2010). A new paradigm for protecting autonomy and the right to legal capacity. Law Commission of Ontario.
