fields.title: CLAS Standards — Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services Walk-Through
fields.summary: The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care are a set of 15 action steps published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Minority Health (OMH) and available through Think Cultural Health (thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov) (https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas). The CLAS Standards were first published in 2000 and comprehensively updated in 2013 ("Enhanced CLAS Standards").
fields.body:
CLAS Standards — Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services Walk-Through

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Methodology / Framework
Adapted from: HHS Office of Minority Health (OMH); Think Cultural Health (thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov); National CLAS Standards (2013 Enhanced); CLAS Standards PDF (HHS/OMH)
Library home: L10 CLAS and Language Access Library
Companion to: T04_04 Cultural Humility; T04_15 Universal Design; T04_11 Intersectionality; T04_03 Hofstede Cultural Dimensions

What this framework is

The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care are a set of 15 action steps published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Minority Health (OMH) and available through Think Cultural Health (thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov) (https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas). The CLAS Standards were first published in 2000 and comprehensively updated in 2013 ("Enhanced CLAS Standards"). They were developed as a blueprint to help health and health care organizations — and by extension, human services organizations like DSD — provide services that are equitable, respectful, responsive to the cultural and linguistic diversity of the populations they serve.

As described by HHS OMH (https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas), "CLAS is a way to improve the quality of services provided to all individuals, which could ultimately help reduce health disparities. CLAS is about respect and responsiveness: Respect the whole individual and Respond to the individual's health needs and preferences."

The 15 CLAS Standards are organized around one Principal Standard and three thematic areas:
• Governance, Leadership, and Workforce (Standards 2–4)
• Communication and Language Assistance (Standards 5–8)
• Engagement, Continuous Improvement, and Accountability (Standards 9–15)

Why DSD uses this framework

DSD is a human services organization serving a population of remarkable linguistic and cultural diversity. Minnesota — and particularly the Twin Cities metropolitan area — is home to large Somali, Hmong, Karen, Latino, Oromo, and other language communities, as well as communities whose cultural relationship to disability, help-seeking, family, and government is substantially different from the dominant culture assumptions embedded in many service systems.

The CLAS Standards provide DSD with:
• A self-assessment framework for evaluating where DSD currently stands on culturally and linguistically appropriate service delivery.
• A roadmap for improvement organized across governance, communication, and continuous improvement dimensions.
• A legal and regulatory grounding for language access and cultural responsiveness — including the connection to Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and the Affordable Care Act's nondiscrimination provisions.
• A shared language for equity expectations that can be used consistently across DSD units, contracted providers, and community partners.

The CLAS Standards also reinforce DSD's own program goals, particularly Goal 1 (Eliminate Disparities), Goal 2 (Community Engagement), and Goal 6 (Communication and Accessibility).

The 15 CLAS Standards (plain language with DSD application)

Principal Standard

Standard 1 — Provide effective, equitable, understandable, and respectful quality care and services that are responsive to diverse cultural health beliefs and practices, preferred languages, health literacy, and other communication needs.

This is the overarching commitment from which all other standards flow. As stated by HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf), Standard 1 requires services that are effective (they work), equitable (they work for everyone), understandable (people can engage with them), and respectful (they honor the person's dignity and cultural identity).

For DSD: Every DSD service interaction is subject to Standard 1. The question is not whether DSD aspires to culturally responsive services — it is whether the actual service experience delivered to a Somali family, a Karen elder, a Native American person with a disability, and a monolingual Spanish speaker meets this standard as fully as it meets it for an English-speaking, acculturated, white family.

Theme 1 — Governance, Leadership, and Workforce (Standards 2–4)

Standard 2 — Advance and sustain organizational governance and leadership that promotes CLAS and health equity through policy, practices, and allocated resources.

CLAS implementation starts at the top. Governance and leadership that do not explicitly commit to, resource, and model cultural and linguistic responsiveness cannot produce it at the service delivery level. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that this commitment be expressed through policy, practice, and resource allocation — not just aspiration.

For DSD: DSD's six program goals — particularly Goal 1 and Goal 6 — are the governance-level expression of Standard 2. But governance commitment requires allocation: Are staff time and budget allocated for interpretation services? For cultural responsiveness training? For community partnership? If the commitment is not resourced, it is not real.

Standard 3 — Recruit, promote, and support a culturally and linguistically diverse governance, leadership, and workforce that are responsive to the population in the service area.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that the workforce reflect the linguistic and cultural diversity of the service population — not just at the entry level, but in governance and leadership.

For DSD: DSD's Goal 3 (Hiring and Retention) is the program-goal expression of Standard 3. A DSD workforce that does not reflect the communities it serves — in language, cultural background, and lived experience — will face persistent barriers to culturally responsive service delivery. Standard 3 also requires active recruitment, promotion, and retention — not just passive openness to diversity.

Standard 4 — Educate and train governance, leadership, and workforce in culturally and linguistically appropriate policies and practices on an ongoing basis.

Cultural and linguistic competence is not a one-time training event. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires ongoing education and training — because communities evolve, staff change, and competence must be developed, not assumed.

For DSD: This standard is the regulatory grounding for DSD's Goal 4 (Learning and Development) as it applies to cultural and linguistic responsiveness. The One DSD learning ecosystem — including all T04 methodology assets — is an expression of Standard 4. Training must be ongoing, not a one-time checkbox.

Theme 2 — Communication and Language Assistance (Standards 5–8)

Standard 5 — Offer language assistance to individuals who have limited English proficiency and/or other communication needs, at no cost to them, to facilitate timely access to all health care and services.

Language assistance is a legal right under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Executive Order 13166 (Improving Access to Services for Persons with Limited English Proficiency). HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that this assistance be offered at no cost to the individual.

For DSD: Language access is not optional and is not a special accommodation. DSD is legally required to provide interpretation and translation services to people with limited English proficiency. This includes spoken language interpretation and, where relevant, communication assistance for people who use AAC, sign language, or other non-verbal communication modalities.

Standard 6 — Inform all individuals of the availability of language assistance services clearly and in their preferred language, verbally and in writing.

People cannot use language assistance services they do not know exist. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires proactive communication of availability — not waiting for individuals to ask, which assumes they know the service exists and know how to request it.

For DSD: All DSD service entry points — intake processes, welcome materials, websites, first-contact communications — should clearly communicate that language assistance is available and how to access it. In the individual's preferred language.

Standard 7 — Ensure the competence of individuals providing language assistance, recognizing that the use of untrained individuals and/or minors as interpreters should be avoided.

Family members, friends, and children are not qualified interpreters. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that interpretation be provided by qualified, competent individuals — not by whoever happens to be present. Using a child to interpret for a parent in a disability services meeting is a confidentiality violation, a child protection concern, and an access failure.

For DSD: Qualified interpretation means interpreters who understand the relevant service context, are trained in professional interpretation ethics, and have demonstrated language competency. This is especially important in sensitive contexts (behavioral health, medical, legal) and for less commonly spoken languages where informal bilingualism may not be sufficient for accurate interpretation.

Standard 8 — Provide easy-to-understand print and multimedia materials and signage in the languages commonly used by the populations in the service area.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that written and multimedia materials be both linguistically translated and easy to understand — plain language is part of this standard.

For DSD: DSD's priority languages per the One DSD Program Charter are Spanish, Hmong, Somali, Karen, and Oromo. Core service materials — eligibility information, rights and responsibilities, service descriptions, planning process explanations — should be available in these languages in plain-language, culturally adapted form. Translation is not enough; culturally adapted communication is the standard.

Theme 3 — Engagement, Continuous Improvement, and Accountability (Standards 9–15)

Standard 9 — Establish culturally and linguistically appropriate goals, policies, and management accountability, and infuse them throughout the organization's planning and operations.

CLAS is not a silo; it must be integrated across DSD's planning and operations, not isolated in a diversity office or equity team. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that CLAS goals and accountability be embedded throughout.

For DSD: Cultural and linguistic responsiveness goals should appear in DSD's strategic plan, unit plans, supervisor performance expectations, and contractor performance standards — not only in the equity team's workplan.

Standard 10 — Conduct ongoing assessments of the organization's CLAS-related activities and integrate CLAS-related measures into measurement and continuous quality improvement activities.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires ongoing assessment — not a one-time baseline survey, but a continuous cycle of measurement, learning, and improvement. This includes CLAS-specific measures in DSD's quality improvement processes.

For DSD: CLAS self-assessment at regular intervals — using the Think Cultural Health CLAS self-assessment tool or DSD-adapted equivalents — provides the data that drives improvement.

Standard 11 — Collect and maintain accurate and reliable demographic data to monitor and evaluate the impact of CLAS on health equity and outcomes and to inform service delivery.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires demographic data collection sufficient to track disparities and service equity — including race, ethnicity, and language data.

For DSD: Demographic data collection is a prerequisite for disparity identification (Goal 1). Data that is not collected cannot be analyzed. DSD should collect, maintain, and use race, ethnicity, primary language, and disability type data at a level of granularity sufficient to identify disparities by community.

Standard 12 — Conduct regular assessments of community health assets and needs and use the results to plan and implement services that respond to the cultural and linguistic diversity of populations in the service area.

Community assets and needs assessment — conducted regularly, not only at program inception — is the CLAS foundation for community-responsive service design. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires that assessment results actually change what DSD does.

For DSD: Community needs assessment is part of DSD's community engagement practice. The assessment should identify community assets — not only needs — and should be conducted in partnership with communities, not just about them.

Standard 13 — Partner with the community to design, implement, and evaluate policies, practices, and services to ensure cultural and linguistic appropriateness.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires partnership — not consultation, not focus groups, but ongoing, genuine partnership in design, implementation, and evaluation.

For DSD: This is the CLAS expression of cultural humility's community partnership principle (T04_04). Genuine partnership means community organizations have real authority in shaping DSD services — not just advisory input that DSD may or may not use.

Standard 14 — Create culturally and linguistically appropriate processes to identify, prevent, and resolve conflicts, complaints, or grievances.

The grievance and conflict resolution process must itself be accessible. HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires processes that work across linguistic and cultural contexts.

For DSD: Can a Somali-speaking family who disagrees with their service plan navigate DSD's grievance process? In Somali? With interpretation? With cultural responsiveness? If not, Standard 14 is unmet.

Standard 15 — Communicate the organization's progress in implementing and sustaining CLAS to all stakeholders, constituents, and the general public.

HHS OMH (https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf) requires transparency — public reporting of progress, not internal-only reporting.

For DSD: DSD's annual reporting should include CLAS implementation progress, communicated in accessible language and in priority community languages where possible.

Using CLAS as a self-assessment framework

The CLAS Standards are most useful for DSD when applied as a structured self-assessment tool:

Step 1 — Baseline: For each of the 15 standards, where is DSD now? Use HHS's Think Cultural Health CLAS self-assessment (https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas) resources.

Step 2 — Gap identification: Which standards are partially or not met? For which populations, in which DSD programs or units?

Step 3 — Priority setting: Which gaps, if closed, would have the largest impact on equity? Prioritize Standards 5–8 (language assistance) as legally required floor; Standards 1, 9, 13 as organizational culture foundations.

Step 4 — Implementation planning: Assign clear responsibility, timeline, and resource allocation for closing each gap.

Step 5 — Continuous improvement: Repeat the assessment cycle annually; integrate CLAS measures into DSD's quality improvement system.

What it looks like in DSD practice

Standards 5–6 in action: A Hmong family contacts DSD about services for their adult child with a developmental disability. The first contact — phone call, website, or in-person — clearly communicates in Hmong that interpretation is available at no cost. The intake appointment includes a qualified Hmong-speaking interpreter as standard, not arranged in response to a request. This is Standards 5 and 6 met.

Standard 7 in action: A case manager is scheduling a planning meeting and learns that the family's teenage daughter is bilingual. The case manager arranges a qualified Somali-community interpreter through DHS language services rather than relying on the daughter — protecting the daughter from an inappropriate role and ensuring accuracy.

Standard 13 in action: DSD's community advisory structure for its waiver program includes compensated positions for representatives from Somali, Hmong, Karen, and Black disability advocacy organizations. These representatives co-design the waiver program's outreach strategy and provide ongoing feedback on cultural responsiveness. Their input results in actual program changes.

How to apply this in your role

As a DSP: Ensure that the people you support can communicate with their service system in their preferred language and format. If they cannot, escalate as an access barrier.

As a case manager: Use the 15 standards as a checklist for your caseload. Which families have language assistance? Which have never been told it is available?

As a supervisor: Include CLAS compliance in your team's quality review. Are language assistance services being offered proactively and consistently?

As a leader or program designer: Commission a CLAS self-assessment for your unit or program. Use the results to drive improvement planning.

Common misconceptions

"CLAS is a health care framework — not relevant to disability services." CLAS was developed in health and health care, but HHS explicitly applies it to all health and human services organizations. DSD is a human services organization subject to CLAS's principles and to the underlying legal frameworks (Title VI, Executive Order 13166) that CLAS implements.

"If we have interpretation services available, we're CLAS-compliant." Language assistance (Standards 5–8) is one of three themes. Governance, workforce, community engagement, continuous improvement, and accountability (Standards 2–4, 9–15) are equally required.

"CLAS is aspirational, not mandatory." Language access under Title VI and Executive Order 13166 is legally required for federally funded organizations. DSD is a federally funded state agency. Some CLAS standards are regulatory floors, not aspirational goals.

Connection to other frameworks

• Cultural Humility (T04_04): CLAS Standards 1, 3, 13 are institutional expressions of cultural humility's community partnership and institutional accountability principles.
• Universal Design (T04_15): Standards 8 and the communication theme broadly reflect universal design's mandate for accessible communication across diverse populations.
• Intersectionality (T04_11): CLAS implementation that attends to language but not disability, or to race but not language, is intersectionally incomplete. All 15 standards should be applied with an intersectional lens.
• Hofstede Cultural Dimensions (T04_03): Understanding cultural dimensions helps DSD implement Standards 1, 4, and 13 with substantive cultural knowledge, not just procedural compliance.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

DSD Goal — CLAS Connection

Goal 1 — Eliminate Disparities — CLAS is explicitly a health disparities reduction framework. All 15 standards, implemented with fidelity, are disparity-reduction strategies.
Goal 2 — Community Engagement — Standard 13 (partner with community to design, implement, and evaluate) is the CLAS articulation of genuine community engagement.
Goal 3 — Hiring and Retention — Standard 3 (recruit and retain diverse workforce) directly maps to Goal 3.
Goal 4 — Learning and Development — Standard 4 (ongoing education and training) maps directly to Goal 4 and is the regulatory grounding for DSD's learning ecosystem.
Goal 5 — Contracts and Procurement — CLAS standards can and should be embedded in DSD's contractor performance requirements — particularly language assistance and cultural responsiveness standards.
Goal 6 — Communication and Accessibility — Standards 5–8 are the CLAS framework's direct expression of communication and accessibility requirements.

When to escalate / where to refer

• For language access compliance questions: Contact DHS language services and DSD's legal and policy team. Language access under Title VI is a legal obligation.
• For CLAS self-assessment tools: HHS Think Cultural Health provides free resources at https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas
• For community partnership development: Contact the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant for existing community partnership frameworks and contacts.
• For language access complaints: Individuals who believe DSD has not provided required language assistance may file complaints with HHS Office of Civil Rights.

Reflective questions for your practice

1. Walk through the 15 CLAS Standards. For which of the three themes (Governance/Leadership/Workforce; Communication/Language Assistance; Engagement/Accountability) is your unit strongest? Where are the gaps?
2. The last time a person with limited English proficiency contacted your service area, what happened? Was language assistance offered proactively and at no cost?
3. Which communities in your service area are most underserved by DSD's current CLAS implementation? What would it take to close that gap?
4. How does "partnership" in Standard 13 differ from "consultation"? Is DSD's current community engagement structure partnership or consultation?
5. If DSD published its CLAS progress report publicly tomorrow, what would it show — and what would you want to be different about it?

Sources

• HHS Office of Minority Health. National CLAS Standards. https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards
• HHS Office of Minority Health. Think Cultural Health. https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas
• HHS / OMH. National Standards for CLAS in Health and Health Care. https://cccm.thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/PDF_Docs/CLASStandards.pdf
• HHS Office of Minority Health. (2013). National standards for culturally and linguistically appropriate services in health and health care: A blueprint for advancing and sustaining CLAS policy and practice. HHS/OMH.
• Betancourt, J. R., Green, A. R., Carrillo, J. E., & Ananeh-Firempong, O. (2003). Defining cultural competence: A practical framework for addressing racial/ethnic disparities in health and health care. Public Health Reports, 118(4), 293–302.
• U.S. Department of Justice. Executive Order 13166: Improving Access to Services for Persons with Limited English Proficiency. (2000).
• Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 42 U.S.C. §2000d.
• Office of Civil Rights, HHS. Guidance to Federal Financial Assistance Recipients Regarding Title VI Prohibition Against National Origin Discrimination Affecting Limited English Proficient Persons. (2003).

Always defer to the person in front of you. Frameworks describe patterns; people are individuals.

fields.title: MnCHOICES and Equitable Access to Services
fields.summary: MnCHOICES is the tool Minnesota uses to assess what long-term services and supports a person needs and to plan those supports with them. Counties, Tribal Nations, and managed care organizations use it for people of any age and any type of disability who need long-term services and supports.
fields.body:
MnCHOICES is the tool Minnesota uses to assess what long-term services and supports a person needs and to plan those supports with them. Counties, Tribal Nations, and managed care organizations use it for people of any age and any type of disability who need long-term services and supports.

How it works. A certified assessor meets with the person to learn about their needs, strengths, and preferences, and to talk through the supports that would help them live a good life. The assessment helps determine which programs and services the person is eligible for, and it helps connect them to those services. One assessment covers many programs, so people do not have to repeat the process again and again. There is no fee, and a person does not have to be enrolled in Medical Assistance to have an assessment.

Where equity comes in. An assessment is a gateway. If the process is hard to reach, hard to understand, or not offered in a person's language, some people get less than they are entitled to — and that shows up as a disparity. Equitable access means:
• Language access: interpretation and translated materials so people are assessed in the language they use.
• Cultural responsiveness: assessors who listen for how culture shapes what a good life and good support look like.
• Reaching people: making sure communities that have been underserved know about and can get an assessment.
• Consistent, person-centered practice: the same respectful, choice-driven process for everyone.

When you support someone through MnCHOICES, you are often standing at the door to their services. Hold it open, in their language, on their terms.

This is a working summary for staff. For current assessment policy, check DHS guidance or route the question to the consultant.

fields.title: Communicating with the Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Community
fields.summary: Communication access for people who are Deaf or hard of hearing is both a legal requirement and basic respect. A few practices make a real difference, and understanding a little about Deaf culture goes a long way.
fields.body:
Communication access for people who are Deaf or hard of hearing is both a legal requirement and basic respect. A few practices make a real difference, and understanding a little about Deaf culture goes a long way.

A note on culture and language. Many Deaf people, with a capital D, see themselves as part of a cultural and linguistic community whose language is American Sign Language, not as people with a medical loss. They often prefer identity-first language, Deaf person. Others, often those who are hard of hearing or who lost hearing later, may identify differently. Follow each person's own preference.

Key practices.
• Provide qualified interpreters for anything important, at no cost, and arrange them early. American Sign Language is its own language, not signed English, and a qualified interpreter matters.
• Do not rely on a family member or a child to interpret.
• When using an interpreter, look at and speak to the Deaf person, not the interpreter. Use you, not he or she.
• Offer real choices. Some people prefer interpreters, some video relay, some captioning, some writing back and forth. Ask what works for them.
• Face the person, keep your face visible, and speak naturally. Do not exaggerate or shout.
• Caption videos and provide transcripts.

What to avoid. Assuming everyone reads lips well, assuming written notes are always enough, or treating American Sign Language as a simplified version of English. None of those are true.

The respectful default. Ask the person how they prefer to communicate, and provide it. Access is not a favor; it is how the conversation becomes equal.

fields.title: EAT Step 4 Walk-Through — Explore Strategies and Options
fields.summary: IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.
fields.body:
EAT Step 4 Walk-Through — Explore Strategies and Options

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — EAT Walk-Through (Methodology Education, Not Analysis)
Adapted from: DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (Minnesota DHS) — Step 4: Benefits and Burdens (modification and strategy components)
Library home: L01 EAT Walk-Through Library
Companion to: T02_01 (EAT Overview), T02_04 (Step 3 Burdens/Benefits), T02_06 (Step 5 Implementation), T02_10 (IS/IS NOT)

IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.

What this step is for

After Step 3/4 has identified who benefits and who bears burdens, the analysis must generate options. This walk-through covers how the EAT approaches strategy development: how to generate alternatives, how to center the communities most affected in that process, and — critically — how to understand the difference between strategies that mitigate a disparity and strategies that eliminate its root cause.

Plain-language overview

Once the equity analysis has identified disparate impacts, the question becomes: What can be done, and which option most advances equity?

The DHS EAT Guide (https://mn.gov/dhs/) describes this as the moment where teams ask: "How can you modify the proposal to correct negative impacts and enhance positive impacts? Are there complementary strategies?" This is not just problem-solving — it is a disciplined process of generating, comparing, and prioritizing options through an equity lens.

The Race Forward Racial Equity Impact Assessment (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf) frames this as "examining alternatives or improvements": asking whether there are better ways to reduce racial disparities and what provisions could be changed or added to ensure positive impacts on racial equity and inclusion.

Walk-through (the methodology)

Generating alternatives

Strategy development in the EAT framework begins with generating a genuine range of options — not a single pre-selected solution with alternatives added to satisfy the process. A genuine alternatives process:

1. Starts from the burdens and benefits identified in Step 4. Every strategy option should respond directly to a specific finding. "We found that Karen-origin applicants abandon applications at three times the rate of English-speaking applicants; here are three strategies that could address that specific barrier."

2. Includes options at different levels of systemic depth. Some options modify the immediate policy or practice (surface-level). Others change the underlying process or infrastructure (structural). Others address the root conditions that create the disparity (transformational). The GARE Racial Equity Toolkit (https://belonging.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/ARCHIVE/gare-racial_equity_toolkit.pdf) emphasizes the distinction between transactional change (checkbox adjustments) and transformational change (authentic effort to address root causes). A good alternatives process includes options at both levels, so decision-makers can explicitly choose how deep to go.

3. Is generated with the communities most affected. The King County Equity Impact Review (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf) includes in Phase 3: "Include upstream alternatives (and related costs) that target root causes to eliminate disproportionate impact." Root-cause alternatives are often best identified by the communities experiencing the problem — not by program staff alone. This is why Step 3 (community engagement) must precede strategy development.

4. Names tradeoffs honestly. Every option has costs — financial, operational, political, or temporal. A strategy that would significantly reduce a disparity may require resources that are not currently budgeted, or may require changes that extend the timeline. Name these tradeoffs explicitly.

Centering communities most affected

"Centering" communities most affected means more than consulting them. It means:

• Using community-identified priorities as the primary criterion for evaluating strategy options, not the secondary criterion after organizational convenience.
• Returning proposed strategies to community members for review before finalizing them. "This is what we heard from you; this is the strategy we are proposing; does this reflect your priorities?"
• Including community members as co-designers of strategies where possible, not just validators of staff-designed options.
• Acknowledging explicitly when a preferred community strategy cannot be implemented due to legal, fiscal, or other constraints — and explaining why, rather than simply presenting a constrained option as if it were the only possibility.

Mitigation versus elimination: a critical distinction

This distinction is one of the most important — and most often collapsed — in equity strategy development.

Mitigation reduces the harm of a disparate impact without addressing its underlying cause. Example: adding a translation service to an application process that has structural barriers for immigrant communities reduces harm but does not eliminate the structural barrier.

Elimination addresses the root cause of the disparity. Example: redesigning the application process so that it does not require documentation that immigrant communities systematically lack — eliminating the structural barrier, not just reducing its impact.

Both mitigation and elimination strategies may appear in an equity analysis. The distinction matters for three reasons:

1. Mitigation strategies can normalize the disparity. If a program adopts translation services and considers the equity work done, it may never address the fact that the program itself was designed for a population that does not reflect the full served community. Mitigation can become an excuse for not pursuing elimination.

2. Elimination strategies are usually more resource-intensive. Changing the underlying policy or process takes more time, more political capital, and more organizational will than adding a complementary service. Decision-makers need to understand this tradeoff explicitly.

3. Communities experience the difference. Communities that bear the burden of a disparity can tell the difference between a program that addresses the root cause and one that adds a service layer on top of a broken foundation. Trust is built by moving toward elimination; it is eroded by repeated mitigation that never leads to change.

The EAT framework expects both types of strategies to be identified. The decision about which to pursue — or in what combination — is made by the team and leadership, not by this resource.

Prioritizing options

The King County Equity Impact Review (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf) provides useful criteria for prioritizing strategy options:

• What is the likelihood that this option will impact equity (high, medium, or low)?
• What is the cost of this action?
• What needs to happen to increase the feasibility of this action?
• What other resources are needed?
• Who will implement the action?
• What is the timing?

Equity-first prioritization means that options with the highest equity impact receive serious consideration even when they are more costly or more difficult — not automatic selection, but genuine evaluation.

Worked example fragment (anonymized, methodology illustration only)

Continuing the anonymized waiver program scenario:

After Step 4 identifies three primary burden areas (income documentation, language access, and immigration-related trust), the Equity Champion facilitates a strategy generation session that includes program staff and advocacy partners.

Options generated for income documentation burden:
1. Mitigation: Accept sworn affidavits of income from community-based organizations, while keeping the documentation requirement itself. (Reduces harm; does not eliminate structural barrier.)
2. Mitigation: Assign a dedicated "application navigator" staff position to assist applicants with documentation. (Reduces harm; addresses capacity barrier but not the policy itself.)
3. Elimination: Remove the income documentation requirement for HCBS waiver programs where income is not legally required for eligibility determination. (Addresses root cause; requires policy change and legal review.)

Community response: Advocacy partners indicate that Option 3 is strongly preferred and has been requested by communities for three years. Options 1 and 2 are appreciated but have been tried previously without significant impact on enrollment disparities.

Decision: Option 3 is recommended as the primary strategy, with Option 1 as an interim mitigation strategy during the policy-change process. Option 2 is not recommended due to resource constraints and evidence of limited effectiveness.

This resource walks through methodology only. The actual strategy development would be led by the Equity Champion and Equity Director.

IS / IS NOT

Strategy development IS — Strategy development IS NOT

Generating a genuine range of options at different levels of depth — Selecting a pre-determined solution and adding options for process compliance
Centered on community-identified priorities — Centered on organizational convenience
Explicit about the distinction between mitigation and elimination — Treating mitigation as sufficient when elimination is possible and needed
Honest about tradeoffs — cost, time, political difficulty — Presenting only the easiest option as if it were the most equitable
A collaborative process with affected communities — A staff-only exercise that is presented to communities after the fact

Common questions

What if the most equity-advancing strategy is fiscally impossible?
Name this constraint explicitly in the analysis. Document the recommended strategy, the fiscal constraint, and the gap between what equity requires and what is currently possible. This documentation serves two purposes: it provides an honest record of the decision, and it creates a basis for future resource requests. Equity constraints should be visible in the record, not quietly absorbed.

What if community members and program staff recommend different strategies?
This is a tension to surface, not to resolve by defaulting to staff preference. Bring the disagreement back to the Equity Director. Examine whether the program staff recommendation reflects genuine operational constraints or reflects a preference for less disruptive change. The EAT framework centers communities most affected — so when there is genuine disagreement, that principle guides the process.

How many strategy options are "enough"?
There is no set number. The goal is a genuine range that includes at least one option at each level of depth (surface, structural, root-cause). If all options are mitigation strategies, that is a finding worth naming — it means the analysis has not yet identified root-cause elimination options, and more work is needed.

Connection to DSD goals

DSD's commitment to transformational change — moving from transactional compliance to genuine systems-level equity advancement — is operationalized in this step. The distinction between mitigation and elimination is the distinction between checking a box and doing the work. DSD's six organizational goals require elimination strategies, not just mitigation.

When to escalate / where to refer

• If no elimination strategy can be identified: escalate to your Equity Director. The absence of a viable elimination strategy is a finding that should be documented and escalated, not quietly dropped.
• If community members and program staff are in significant disagreement about strategies: escalate to your Equity Director for structured resolution.
• If a recommended strategy would require changes to policy above the program area's authority: escalate to the appropriate level of DHS leadership, with a clear equity analysis supporting the recommendation.

Reflective questions

1. Think about a change your program area made in the last two years. Was it a mitigation strategy or an elimination strategy? How do you know?
2. What would it mean for your team to genuinely center community priorities in strategy development — not just invite community input, but let it drive the options selected?
3. Have you ever seen a mitigation strategy that worked so well it prevented the organization from pursuing elimination? What did that look like?
4. What root causes of disparity in your program area have been identified but never fully addressed? What would elimination look like?
5. What makes a strategy option "realistic" — and whose definition of realistic is being used?

Sources

• DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/) (primary source, Step 4 modification and complementary strategies)
• Racial Equity Impact Assessment Guide — Race Forward (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf) (section 8: examining alternatives or improvements)
• King County Equity Impact Review — Phase 3: Analysis and Decision Process (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf)
• Racial Equity Toolkit — GARE, via Othering and Belonging Institute (https://belonging.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/ARCHIVE/gare-racial_equity_toolkit.pdf) (transformational vs. transactional change)
• One DSD Program Charter v1.1 (one-dsd-program-charter)

Always defer to the person in front of you.

Ask: What is the cost of this action?
Ask: What needs to happen to increase the feasibility of this action?
Ask: What other resources are needed?

Ask: What is the timing?
Ask: What if the most equity-advancing strategy is fiscally impossible?

fields.title: RMHF — Relational-Cultural Theory and Multicultural Humility Framework
fields.summary: The Relational-Cultural Theory and Multicultural Humility Framework (RMHF), as used in DSD's learning ecosystem, brings together two connected frameworks:
fields.body:
RMHF — Relational-Cultural Theory and Multicultural Humility Framework

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Methodology / Framework
Adapted from: Judith V. Jordan, Ph.D.; Jean Baker Miller, M.D.; Irene Stiver; Janet Surrey (Wellesley Centers for Women / Stone Center); Tervalon & Murray-García; David Sue (multicultural humility)
Library home: L08 Emotional Intelligence Library; L03 IDI-Informed Intercultural Development Library
Companion to: T04_04 Cultural Humility; T04_05 Goleman EI; T04_06 SAMHSA TIP; T04_11 Intersectionality

What this framework is

The Relational-Cultural Theory and Multicultural Humility Framework (RMHF), as used in DSD's learning ecosystem, brings together two connected frameworks:

Relational-Cultural Theory (RCT) was developed by Jean Baker Miller, M.D., Judith V. Jordan, Ph.D., Irene Stiver, and Janet Surrey at the Wellesley Centers for Women (formerly the Stone Center) beginning in the 1970s and 1980s. RCT proposes that humans — contrary to dominant psychological models emphasizing individual autonomy and separation — grow and develop through connection, and that the quality and character of relationships are the primary vehicle of psychological health and development throughout life.

Multicultural Humility, as a framework applied alongside RCT, extends the relational focus to the cultural and power dimensions of helping relationships — recognizing that therapeutic, supervisory, and service relationships occur within cultural, historical, and systemic power contexts that are not optional or incidental but fundamental to what happens in those relationships.

The Wellesley Centers for Women describes RCT's development (https://www.wcwonline.org/JBMTI-Site/the-development-of-relational-cultural-theory) as emerging from the observation that existing psychological theories (Freudian, object relations, Eriksonian) described human development in ways that centered the experiences of white, Western, middle-class men, and that pathologized relationality (particularly in women and non-Western cultures) as immaturity or dependence.

Why DSD uses this framework

DSD staff build relationships with people with disabilities, families, colleagues, and communities — relationships that are the primary vehicle of effective service delivery, just as RCT suggests they are the primary vehicle of human development. The quality of those relationships is not a soft peripheral concern; it is the core mechanism through which good outcomes are produced or not.

RCT, paired with multicultural humility, gives DSD a framework for:
• Understanding why relationships in DSD work feel meaningful or hollow, effective or stuck.
• Recognizing the power dynamics embedded in service relationships and addressing them constructively.
• Building organizational cultures where staff can thrive and grow — because growth happens in connection.
• Centering the relational quality of service delivery as a primary quality standard, not a secondary nicety.

The core concepts (plain language with citations)

Relational-Cultural Theory: Core Propositions

1. Humans grow through connection, not separation.

The dominant model in Western psychology — from Freud through Erikson — treated healthy human development as a progression toward increasing separation, autonomy, and independence. RCT challenges this: as described by Beyond Intractability (https://www.beyondintractability.org/essay/relational-cultural-theory), RCT proposes that "human beings grow and develop in the context of relationships and that psychological health is characterized by increasing complexity of connection rather than separation and increasing self-sufficiency."

For DSD: This means that services oriented solely toward individual independence may be misoriented. Connection — to family, community, peers, supporters — is not a developmental stepping stone to be transcended; it is a lifelong condition of human wellbeing. The Disability Justice principle of interdependence (T04_12) converges here.

2. Growth-fostering relationships have specific qualities.

RCT identifies five good things (https://cupofpeace.com/?p=186) that people in growth-fostering relationships experience:
• Zest: Increased energy and vitality.
• Action: Movement toward change and engagement.
• Knowledge: Increased self-understanding and understanding of others.
• Worth: A sense of increased self-worth.
• Connection: Desire for more connection.

When a service relationship produces these five outcomes, it is a growth-fostering relationship in the RCT sense. When it does not — when a service interaction leaves a person feeling diminished, more isolated, or more confused — the relationship may be what RCT calls a "disconnection."

For DSD staff: Audit your service relationships against these five outcomes. After an interaction with you, does the person feel more energized, more capable, more worthwhile, more connected? If not, what is producing the disconnection?

3. Disconnections are inevitable and can be repaired.

RCT does not assume that growth-fostering relationships are always harmonious. Disconnections — moments of misunderstanding, hurt, power differential assertion, or failure to be seen — are inevitable in all relationships. What distinguishes growth-fostering relationships is not the absence of disconnection but the capacity for repair: the ability to acknowledge the disconnection, understand what happened from both perspectives, and restore connection.

Cup of Peace describes (https://cupofpeace.com/?p=186) the three phases of healing: joining through truth (confronting the dysfunctional pattern directly), skill-building (developing communication, boundary, and empathy skills), and ongoing maintenance (relational mindfulness and mutual growth).

For DSD: Service relationships will have disconnections. A supervisor who dismisses a concern, a case manager who misunderstands a family's priorities, a DSP who does not notice that their communication style is not landing — these are disconnections. The professional response is not to pretend they didn't happen but to repair: to acknowledge, understand, and restore.

4. Mutual empathy is possible across power differentials.

A central tension in applying RCT to service relationships is that genuine mutuality — both people affecting and being affected by the relationship — is complicated by the power differential inherent in professional service relationships. RCT does not require that the power differential disappear; it requires that it be named, acknowledged, and navigated with integrity.

Judith V. Jordan's work (https://www.wcwonline.org/JBMTI-Site/Founding-Scholars/judith-v-jordan) explores the concept of mutual empathy as a condition of relational growth — not that the staff member becomes the client, but that both are genuinely present in the relationship, that the staff member's genuine care and genuine uncertainty are visible, and that the person being served is not positioned as an object of professional expertise.

5. Cultural context is not incidental; it is relational.

RCT began as a challenge to the cultural assumptions of mainstream psychology — specifically, the assumption that the white, Western, male developmental trajectory was universal. Multicultural humility, integrated into RCT, extends this challenge: every relationship is culturally embedded, every relationship involves different positions within systems of power, and ignoring these dimensions does not make them disappear — it just makes them invisible to the professional while remaining very visible to the person being served.

Multicultural Humility within RMHF

Multicultural humility, as articulated by Sue, Rasheed & Rasheed (2016) and integrated with RCT by Jordan and others, brings three core orientations to helping relationships:

1. Cultural humility in the relationship:
Not just knowledge about culture (cultural competence), but genuine openness, curiosity, and not-knowing — the willingness to be taught by the person about their own cultural context rather than presuming the professional's cultural knowledge is sufficient.

2. Awareness of power dynamics:
Every helping relationship involves power — professional authority, institutional backing, resource control. Multicultural humility requires naming this power, examining how it operates in the relationship, and working to use it in service of the person rather than in service of the professional's comfort or the institution's efficiency.

3. Social justice commitment:
Multicultural humility requires recognizing that individual helping relationships exist within systemic contexts that produce the conditions requiring helping. A culturally humble helper does not only help individuals navigate unjust systems; they work to change those systems.

How RCT and multicultural humility connect in DSD

The integration of RCT and multicultural humility produces a framework for DSD service relationships that holds simultaneously:
• The relational quality of the interaction (Does this produce growth-fostering connection?)
• The cultural dimension of the interaction (How is cultural context shaping what each person experiences in this relationship?)
• The power dimension of the interaction (What does the power differential in this relationship require of the professional?)
• The systemic dimension of the interaction (What structural conditions are shaping what is possible in this relationship, and what responsibility does DSD have to change those conditions?)

What it looks like in DSD practice

Growth-fostering service relationships:
A case manager who has worked with the same family for three years reflects that after every planning meeting, the mother seems more capable of articulating her son's needs and more confident in navigating systems. This is RCT's five good things — zest, action, knowledge, worth, connection — in a service relationship. The case manager has been a growth-fostering presence.

Repairing disconnections:
A DSP misunderstands a communication from the person they support — interprets a behavioral signal as agitation when it was actually excitement — and responds in a way that escalates the situation rather than resolving it. Later in supervision, with support, the DSP acknowledges the misread to the person directly: "I got that wrong yesterday, and I'm sorry. I want to learn to understand you better." This repair strengthens the relationship rather than ending it.

Mutual empathy across power differentials:
A supervisor conducting a performance review acknowledges their own uncertainty: "I'm not always sure I see everything that's happening for you in this work. Can you help me understand what this past month has been like?" This is mutual empathy — not pretending the power differential doesn't exist (the supervisor is still the supervisor), but genuinely seeking to understand and be affected by the other person's experience.

Cultural humility in the relational frame:
A DSD program manager notices that their supervision style — direct, agenda-driven, task-focused — is not working well with a staff member from a cultural background that emphasizes relational connection before task engagement. Rather than attributing the friction to the staff member, the manager reflects on their own relational assumptions and adjusts their approach: they begin meetings with genuine relationship-building conversation before turning to the agenda.

How to apply this in your role

As a DSP:
• Before service interactions, ask: "How can I be genuinely present with this person today — not managing them, but actually connecting?"
• After service interactions, ask: "Did this person seem more or less connected to me after our interaction? If less, what happened?"
• Practice repair: when something goes wrong in a service relationship, address it directly and gently rather than moving on as if it didn't happen.

As a supervisor:
• Create the conditions for growth-fostering supervision: psychological safety, genuine curiosity about staff experience, willingness to be affected by what they share.
• Name power dynamics in supervision: "I hold authority in this relationship, and I want to use it in your service, not against you."
• Model relational repair: when you get something wrong with a staff member, acknowledge it.

As a leader:
• Assess organizational culture through an RCT lens: Does the organizational culture of DSD produce growth-fostering conditions for staff? Or conditions of chronic disconnection?
• Use multicultural humility in leadership: be genuinely uncertain, genuinely curious, genuinely willing to be taught.

Common misconceptions

"RCT is just about being nice and warm." RCT is analytically rigorous and includes clear thinking about power, disconnection, and the conditions of growth-fostering connection. It is not a mandate for constant positivity.

"Multicultural humility means I can't have professional expertise." Multicultural humility is about how expertise is held and applied — with openness and curiosity, not with presumptuous certainty. Expertise and humility coexist.

"RCT is only relevant for therapy, not disability services." RCT's core insight — that humans grow through connection — applies to every helping relationship, including DSP-person, case manager-family, and supervisor-staff relationships.

"This is too soft for the real challenges of DSD work." The relational quality of service delivery has direct, measurable impacts on trust, engagement, outcomes, and equity. Relational practice is as rigorous and as important as any technical practice.

Connection to other frameworks

• Emotional Intelligence (T04_05): Goleman's domains of social awareness and relationship management are the EI dimensions most directly supported by RCT. RCT provides the relational theory; EI provides the competency framework.
• Cultural Humility (T04_04): Multicultural humility within RMHF is an extension and deepening of cultural humility practice into the relational frame.
• Trauma-Informed Practice (T04_06): Growth-fostering connections and the capacity for relational repair are exactly what TIP's safety, trustworthiness, and collaboration principles require.
• Intersectionality (T04_11): RCT's attention to how power dynamics shape relationships must be deepened by intersectional analysis of which power dimensions are operating in any specific relationship.
• Person-Centered Planning (T04_07): Genuinely person-centered planning requires the relational presence that RCT describes — being genuinely curious about and moved by the person's experience, not processing them as a case.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

DSD Goal — RMHF Connection

Goal 1 — Eliminate Disparities — Disconnected, power-unaware service relationships reproduce disparities. Growth-fostering, culturally humble relationships are a mechanism for disparity reduction.
Goal 2 — Community Engagement — Genuine community partnership requires relational qualities — mutual empathy, repair capacity, cultural humility in the relationship — that RMHF describes.
Goal 3 — Hiring and Retention — Staff retention is shaped by the quality of supervisory and organizational relationships. RCT provides a framework for understanding why staff stay or leave.
Goal 4 — Learning and Development — Growth happens in relationship. Learning and development programs that create growth-fostering conditions will produce better developmental outcomes for staff.
Goal 5 — Contracts and Procurement — Authentic community partnership relationships — as distinct from extractive consultant relationships — require the mutual respect and cultural humility that RMHF describes.
Goal 6 — Communication and Accessibility — Communication that is relationally grounded — attentive to the other person's experience, transparent, responsive to feedback — is more accessible across cultural and disability contexts.

When to escalate / where to refer

• For RCT-informed supervision training: Contact the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant; RCT-based supervision is a recognized model in social work and human services education.
• For relational repair in conflict situations: Consult with your supervisor and HR; some relational ruptures require mediation beyond one-on-one repair.
• For multicultural humility in clinical relationships: Refer to behavioral health consultation and multicultural clinical supervision resources.
• For Wellesley Centers for Women resources: https://www.wcwonline.org

Reflective questions for your practice

1. After your most recent service interaction, did the person seem more energized, more capable, more worthwhile — or less? What drove that outcome?
2. When have you experienced a disconnection in a service relationship — a misunderstanding or failure of connection — and successfully repaired it? What made the repair possible?
3. In your supervision relationships — whether you are the supervisor or the supervisee — do you experience the five good things of a growth-fostering relationship?
4. What power dynamics are present in the service relationship you find most complex right now? Have you named them? How do they affect what is possible in the relationship?
5. What would it look like for your team or unit to create genuinely growth-fostering conditions — not just for the people you serve, but for each other?

Sources

• Jordan, J. V. (Ed.). (1997). Women's growth in diversity: More writings from the Stone Center. Guilford Press.
• Jordan, J. V., Kaplan, A. G., Miller, J. B., Stiver, I. P., & Surrey, J. L. (1991). Women's growth in connection: Writings from the Stone Center. Guilford Press.
• Miller, J. B. (1976). Toward a new psychology of women. Beacon Press.
• Wellesley Centers for Women. The Development of Relational-Cultural Theory. https://www.wcwonline.org/JBMTI-Site/the-development-of-relational-cultural-theory
• Wellesley Centers for Women. Judith V. Jordan, Ph.D. https://www.wcwonline.org/JBMTI-Site/Founding-Scholars/judith-v-jordan
• Beyond Intractability. Relational-Cultural Theory: Fostering Healthy Coexistence. https://www.beyondintractability.org/essay/relational-cultural-theory
• Cup of Peace. (2025). Relational Cultural Theory and Psychological Development. https://cupofpeace.com/?p=186
• Sue, D. W., Rasheed, M. N., & Rasheed, J. M. (2016). Multicultural social work practice: A competency-based approach to diversity and social justice. Wiley.
• Tervalon, M., & Murray-García, J. (1998). Cultural humility versus cultural competence. Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, 9(2), 117–125.
• Jordan, J. V. (2010). Relational-cultural therapy. American Psychological Association.

fields.body:
Worked Example — Communication and Outreach Decision Walk-Through

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — EAT Walk-Through (Methodology Education, Not Analysis)
Adapted from: DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (Minnesota DHS) — all six steps, applied to a hypothetical communication and outreach scenario
Library home: L01 EAT Walk-Through Library
Companion to: T02_01 through T02_10 (all EAT walk-throughs), T02_11, T02_13 (other worked examples)

IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This is an anonymized hypothetical example demonstrating the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses on real DSD programs, real communities, or real data. All names, figures, and scenarios are illustrative. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.

What this step is for

This worked example applies all six steps of the EAT to a second hypothetical scenario: an information campaign reaching diverse communities, including communities with disabilities and communities defined by cultural intersections. It demonstrates how equity analysis applies to communication and outreach decisions — not just service design — and how disability and cultural identities intersect in ways that communication strategies must account for.

Plain-language overview

Hypothetical scenario: Benefits Enrollment Awareness Campaign — Reaching Underserved Eligible Populations

[Note: All details in this scenario are hypothetical and constructed for methodology illustration only. They do not represent any real DSD program, real data, or real community conditions.]

A DSD program area responsible for a benefits enrollment program identifies a persistent gap: significant numbers of eligible individuals are not enrolled. Preliminary data suggests that the gap is concentrated in specific communities — people with certain types of disability, recent immigrants, and communities with lower English proficiency. The program area is developing a new outreach and communication campaign to increase enrollment among these underserved eligible populations.

Walk-through (the methodology)

Before Step 1: Equity Lens Needs Assessment

Questions asked:
• What is the proposal? A new outreach campaign targeting underserved eligible populations for a benefits enrollment program.
• Is this new or a modification? New targeted campaign, not previously analyzed.
• Who is affected? Eligible individuals who are not currently enrolled — concentrated in communities with disabilities, limited English proficiency, and recent immigrant/refugee backgrounds.
• CLAS, workforce, contracting? Yes — CLAS standards are central: the campaign must be culturally and linguistically appropriate to reach its target populations.
• Timeline? Campaign is planned to launch in three months. Timeline negotiated to four months to allow for meaningful community input before finalization.

Needs Assessment conclusion: Equity Analysis Track. Full six-step process.

Step 1: Frame the Decision/Issue

Proposal: Design and implement a targeted outreach and communication campaign to enroll eligible individuals from underserved communities in [anonymized benefits program].

Internal impact: Affects program outreach staff; communication team; interpreter and translation service coordination; potential caseload increase if campaign succeeds.

External impact: Affects eligible individuals not currently enrolled, concentrated in disability communities, immigrant/refugee communities, and communities with limited English proficiency. Families and caregivers are also affected.

Intended community result: Eligible individuals who are currently not accessing benefits they are entitled to become enrolled. The enrollment gap between currently served and underserved eligible populations narrows.

Intended organizational outcome: Program enrollment increases; documented enrollment gap by race and disability status narrows; campaign reach metrics show engagement with previously unreached communities.

Disparity domains: Income (benefits access), health (if program is health-adjacent), disability-specific service access, language access.

Key questions surfaced at Step 1:
• What are the barriers keeping eligible individuals from enrolling — and do those barriers differ by community?
• Is the campaign designed to address barriers, or only to increase awareness? (Awareness alone may not address barriers to enrollment.)
• How does disability intersect with cultural and linguistic identity in this population? (A Deaf Somali-origin person faces access barriers that are not captured by disability data alone, or by language access data alone.)

Stakeholders identified for Step 3: Disability advocacy organizations (including Deaf-specific, intellectual/developmental disability, and physical disability organizations); immigrant and refugee serving organizations; CECLC; interpreter services staff; community health workers.

Step 2: Gather Data and Engage Community (Data component)

Quantitative data gathered (hypothetical figures for illustration):
• Current enrollment demographics: 34% of enrolled individuals are people of color; the eligible population in the region is estimated at 51% people of color. (Hypothetical enrollment gap for illustration.)
• By disability type: cognitive and developmental disabilities are underrepresented in enrollment relative to physical disabilities (hypothetical).
• By language: Somali-primary-language and Karen-primary-language households are enrolled at significantly lower rates than Spanish-primary-language and English-primary-language households (hypothetical).
• By immigration status: Recent arrivals (within 5 years) are enrolled at one-third the rate of long-term residents (hypothetical).

Data gaps identified:
• Enrollment data does not capture intersection of disability type and racial/ethnic identity — making it impossible to see whether the underrepresentation of cognitive/developmental disability populations is concentrated in communities of color.
• No data exists on why individuals are not enrolled — no application-abandonment tracking, no "never applied" survey data.
• Previous outreach campaigns did not track reach by community, making it impossible to know whether prior campaigns reached or missed these communities.

Plan for gaps: Community listening sessions will fill the "why not enrolled" gap. Add campaign reach tracking by language and community in the new campaign design.

Step 3: Community Engagement

[Community engagement is the responsibility of DSD program areas and the CECLC. This section illustrates the methodology only.]

Engagement conducted (hypothetical methodology illustration):

Working with the CECLC and disability advocacy partners, the Equity Champion organizes four listening sessions:

• Session 1: Somali-origin community members, including individuals with disabilities; held in Somali, with a trained disability-services interpreter.
• Session 2: Deaf community members; conducted in American Sign Language with a certified interpreter.
• Session 3: Cognitive and intellectual disability advocacy partners, including self-advocate participants.
• Session 4: Karen-origin community health workers, who serve as trusted intermediaries.

Key findings from engagement (hypothetical):
• Somali-origin participants: Primary barriers are distrust of government data sharing, concerns about immigration-related consequences of registration, and cultural stigma around disability identity that affects willingness to self-identify as eligible.
• Deaf community: Previous communications about this program were not in ASL — they were in written English, which is inaccessible to Deaf community members for whom English is a second language. Deaf community members had simply not encountered accessible information about eligibility.
• Cognitive and developmental disability self-advocates: Application process requires reading and writing at a level that is inaccessible without significant support; caregiver-assisted application creates privacy and autonomy concerns.
• Karen-origin community health workers: Trust in the program exists among their client communities — the gap is awareness, not distrust. Community health workers could serve as outreach ambassadors if properly trained and compensated.

Step 4: Identify Burdens, Benefits, and Disparities

Benefits of proposed campaign:
• Increased awareness of the program among communities currently unaware of it (particularly for Karen-origin communities where awareness, not trust, is the barrier).
• Increased enrollment among all targeted communities if barriers are addressed.

Burdens and disparate impacts identified:

1. Communication accessibility gap (Deaf community): A campaign that does not include ASL video content will fail to reach Deaf community members who are not strong English readers. This is not a minor oversight — it is a complete access failure for this community.

2. Trust and immigration-related fear (Somali-origin community): A campaign that does not explicitly address data sharing and immigration-related concerns may increase awareness but will not increase enrollment. Fear is the primary barrier, not information.

3. Cognitive accessibility gap (cognitive/developmental disability community): A campaign designed for general audiences will not be accessible to individuals with cognitive and intellectual disabilities. Easy-read materials and person-centered application support are not a nice-to-have; they are a prerequisite for this community.

4. Disability-cultural intersection gap: The intersection of disability identity with Somali-origin cultural context creates a specific barrier (stigma around disability identification) not captured in either disability data or cultural competency data alone. The campaign must be designed for this intersection explicitly.

Modifications recommended:

• Campaign materials must include ASL video versions (not just captions — ASL is a distinct language from English).
• Campaign materials must include explicit, plain-language statements about data use limitations and what the program does and does not share with other government agencies.
• Easy-read versions of all campaign materials required, co-designed with cognitive and intellectual disability self-advocates.
• Campaign for Somali-origin communities designed in partnership with trusted Somali-origin community leaders, not by DSD communications staff alone.

Complementary strategies:

• Karen community health worker outreach ambassador program: train and compensate community health workers to conduct peer outreach; provide application support for their client networks.
• Application support navigator service: individuals who initiate an application can request a trained navigator to assist them through the process.

Step 5: Implementation Planning

Strategy — Action/Task — Person Responsible — Deadline — Resources

ASL video campaign materials — Hire Deaf-owned production company; cast Deaf presenters; finalize script in ASL — Communications Lead + CECLC — 8 weeks before launch — Budget: [amount for production]; CECLC coordination
Immigration and data-sharing communication — Draft plain-language statements with OGC review; have translated by bilingual community partners — Communications Lead + OGC — 6 weeks before launch — OGC review time; translation honoraria
Easy-read materials — Co-design with self-advocate advisory group; print and distribute — Training Coordinator + self-advocate partners — 8 weeks before launch — Design budget; self-advocate compensation
Karen community health worker program — Train 4 CHWs; provide program materials in Karen; establish referral protocol — CECLC Lead — 4 weeks before launch — CHW compensation; materials translation
Application navigator service — Designate 2 staff as navigators; train on application process and cultural context — Program Lead — 2 weeks before launch — Existing staff time; 8-hour training

Feasibility test: Realistic: Yes, with timeline extension achieved. Adequately funded: Partially — ASL video production requires new budget approval. Personnel: CECLC capacity is at limit; may need to prioritize CHW program and delay some activities. Data collection and community engagement: Yes — tracking plan designed below.

Step 6: Monitor, Evaluate, Adjust

Quantity: Campaign reach by community (tracked through language of first contact, community partner referrals, CHW outreach logs); applications initiated by community.

Quality: Completion rate of applications by community; navigator service utilization by community; ASL video view counts; easy-read material request counts.

Is anyone better off? Enrollment by community 6 months post-campaign; enrollment gap compared to pre-campaign baseline; disaggregated by disability type and race.

Pre-specified adjustment trigger: If Somali-origin enrollment has not increased by 15% at 90-day review, convene trust and data-sharing communication review with Somali-origin advocacy partners.

Feedback loop: CHW ambassador monthly report; advocacy partner check-ins at 60 days; client application experience survey at 30 days (in Somali, Karen, ASL video, easy-read, and English).

IS / IS NOT (for this worked example)

This worked example IS — This worked example IS NOT

A methodology illustration for a communication and outreach decision — Analysis of any real DSD outreach campaign or real community data
A demonstration of disability-cultural intersectionality in practice — A characterization of any real community's actual barriers or experiences
A teaching tool for how to apply the EAT to outreach decisions — A template that can be used without a real equity analysis

Common questions

Does every outreach campaign require a full Equity Analysis?
The Equity Lens Needs Assessment determines this. A minor update to an existing communication (changing a deadline, updating a phone number) likely does not. A new campaign targeting underserved communities, as in this example, is more likely to warrant the Analysis Track. Consult your Equity Director.

The disability-cultural intersection seems very specific. How do we address it without expertise in both areas?
This is exactly why the EAT requires genuine community engagement rather than staff-designed analysis. The intersection of disability identity with Somali-origin cultural context cannot be understood from the outside by staff who do not share those identities. It must be learned through engagement with Somali-origin community members who have disabilities, or with community advocates who support them. The methodology does not require you to have the expertise — it requires you to engage the people who do.

Connection to DSD goals

Communication and outreach are not separate from equity work — they are equity work. A campaign that reaches only some eligible communities while missing others reproduces the enrollment disparities that the program exists to address. The EAT applied to outreach decisions ensures that communication strategy advances DSD's equity goals rather than inadvertently deepening existing gaps.

Sources

• DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/) (primary source)
• Racial Equity Impact Assessment Guide — Race Forward (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf)
• King County Equity Impact Review (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf)
• DHS Equity Policy — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/assets/equity-policy_tcm1053-646921.pdf) (CLAS standards requirements)
• One DSD Program Charter v1.1 (one-dsd-program-charter)

fields.summary: Treat cultural knowledge as a way to ask better questions, not as a shortcut to certainty. Examine assumptions, invite correction, share decision-making power, and keep accountability visible in the work.

fields.title: Equity Review Checklist
fields.summary: Use this checklist when you are creating or revising a policy, program, practice, communication, or decision. It is a quick equity scan, a way to catch problems before they reach the people we serve. For significant decisions, use the full Equity Analysis Toolkit; this checklist is the everyday version.
fields.body:
Use this checklist when you are creating or revising a policy, program, practice, communication, or decision. It is a quick equity scan, a way to catch problems before they reach the people we serve. For significant decisions, use the full Equity Analysis Toolkit; this checklist is the everyday version.

Who is affected.
• Have I named who this affects, including communities that are often underserved?
• Have I looked at impacts by race, disability, language, age, and geography, not just on average?
• Have I involved the people most affected, or at least sought their perspective?

Access and fairness.
• Can people with disabilities use this fully, including the appeal or exception path?
• Is it available and understandable in the languages people use?
• Is it written in plain language at about an eighth-grade level?
• Does any requirement screen people out for reasons unrelated to the goal?

Burdens and benefits.
• Who benefits from this, and who carries the burden or cost?
• Could this widen an existing gap, even unintentionally?
• What is the worst-case impact on the most vulnerable person it touches?

Follow-through.
• How will we know if this is working or causing harm?
• Who owns fixing it if a problem shows up?
• Is there a clear, fair way for someone to raise a concern?

If any answer gives you pause, slow down and address it before moving ahead. A few minutes here prevents a real harm later. When in doubt, ask the consultant.
