fields.title: National CLAS Standards: A Quick Guide for DSD Staff
fields.summary: The National CLAS Standards are 15 standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health. They help health and human services reduce disparities by making sure services respond to each person's culture, language, and communication needs.
fields.body:
The National CLAS Standards are 15 standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health. They help health and human services reduce disparities by making sure services respond to each person's culture, language, and communication needs.

There is one Principal Standard and 14 supporting standards, grouped into three themes.
• The Principal Standard: provide services that are effective, equitable, understandable, and respectful, and that fit each person's cultural beliefs, preferred language, health literacy, and communication needs.
• Governance, leadership, and workforce: make CLAS a leadership priority, build a workforce that reflects the people we serve, and train staff on an ongoing basis.
• Communication and language assistance: offer language help at no cost, tell people it is available in their language, use qualified interpreters (never children or family members), and provide easy-to-understand materials in the languages people use.
• Engagement, improvement, and accountability: build CLAS into planning and operations, collect demographic data, partner with the community, and report progress.

How to use CLAS in your work.
• Ask about and record language preference, and arrange a qualified interpreter as soon as a need shows up.
• Plan translation and interpretation into the budget and timeline from the start, not as a special request later.
• Test materials at a plain-language reading level and offer them in the languages your service area uses.
• Bring community members in as partners early, not as reviewers of a near-final draft.

CLAS is not a checklist you finish once. It is a standard you keep, because the people we serve speak many languages and hold many cultures, and equitable service means meeting them there.

For the full standards, see the HHS Office of Minority Health at thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas.

fields.title: Using Cultural Briefs: A Starting Point, Not the Last Word
fields.summary: Cultural briefs, sometimes called cultural briefs, are short orientations to a community's general patterns, history, and common practices. They are useful, and they are also incomplete by design. A brief can help you ask better questions and avoid obvious missteps. It can never tell you about the actual person in front of you. Held the right way, briefs help. Held the wrong way, they become stereotypes.
fields.body:
Cultural briefs, sometimes called cultural briefs, are short orientations to a community's general patterns, history, and common practices. They are useful, and they are also incomplete by design. A brief can help you ask better questions and avoid obvious missteps. It can never tell you about the actual person in front of you. Held the right way, briefs help. Held the wrong way, they become stereotypes.

What a cultural brief is, and is not.
• It is a starting point, a way to orient before an interaction, not a script.
• It is general, describing patterns that many, not all, members of a community may share.
• It is non-comprehensive by design. No brief captures a whole community, and every community holds enormous internal diversity.
• It is not validity. Fluency about a community is not the same as authority from it. The community, and the individual, remain the real experts.

How to use a brief well, in context.
• With person-centered practice. Start from what this person wants and how they describe themselves. The brief orients you; the person directs you. When the two differ, the person wins.
• With intercultural communication. Use the brief alongside cultural humility. Approach with curiosity, hold your assumptions loosely, and let the person correct you.
• With service delivery. Treat a brief as background for designing respectful, accessible service, not as a checklist of traits to apply to everyone from a group.
• With community engagement. Briefs are informed by, and stay accountable to, community voice. When a brief and a community's own description differ, the community's voice carries more weight.

The trap to avoid. Never let a brief flatten a person into a category. A Somali elder, a second-generation Somali college student, and a recently arrived Somali family share a label and little else. The brief is a door into curiosity, not a box to put people in.

The rule of thumb. A brief should make you ask more questions, not fewer. If it ever makes you feel you already know someone before you have met them, set it down and ask.

fields.title: Accessible Communications Checklist
fields.summary: A checklist for accessible communications across all DSD channels — email, DSD web pages, social media, video, audio, and imagery. This resource covers the accessibility requirements specific to each channel and the cross-cutting practices that apply everywhere. It is organized by channel for ease of use.
fields.body:
Accessible Communications Checklist

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Accessibility
Library home: L09 Accessibility & Plain Language Library
Companion to: WCAG 2.2 AA Flagship Module; Plain-Language Style Guide for DSD; Accessible Meetings Checklist; Effective Communication for People with Communication Disabilities
Standards reference: WCAG 2.2 AA; §508 Rehabilitation Act; Title II ADA; Minnesota Human Rights Act (MHRA)

What this is

A checklist for accessible communications across all DSD channels — email, DSD web pages, social media, video, audio, and imagery. This resource covers the accessibility requirements specific to each channel and the cross-cutting practices that apply everywhere. It is organized by channel for ease of use.

Why this matters for DSD

Communications are how DSD reaches staff, clients, community partners, and the public. When communications are not accessible:

• Staff and clients with visual disabilities cannot access visual-only content
• People who are deaf or hard of hearing cannot access audio or video content without captions
• People with cognitive disabilities are excluded by dense, jargon-heavy communications
• People with motor disabilities who use keyboard-only navigation cannot interact with inaccessible web forms, links, or social media
• People with low vision cannot read low-contrast text on social media graphics or email templates

The DOJ's 2024 Title II ADA Final Rule extends accessibility requirements to websites, mobile apps, social media posts, and other digital content. DSD's Resolution 26 requires WCAG 2.2 AA compliance for all digital content.

Channel 1: Email Accessibility

Email is DSD's primary internal communication channel and a key channel for client and partner communication.

Checklist: Accessible Email

Structure and format:
• [ ] Use a clear, specific subject line that tells the reader what the email is about and what action (if any) is required ("Action required: Submit your updated service plan by October 15")
• [ ] Put the most important information first — use the inverted pyramid (conclusion first, detail second)
• [ ] Use short paragraphs (3–5 sentences)
• [ ] Use bullet lists for three or more items
• [ ] Use plain language — grade 8 reading level for broad audiences
• [ ] Use a readable, sans-serif font (Arial, Calibri, Verdana) at 11–12pt minimum
• [ ] Avoid decorative or background images in email templates

Links:
• [ ] All hyperlinks use descriptive text — not "click here," not raw URLs
• [ ] Hyperlink text describes the destination or action ("Download the accessible meeting guide," "View the DSD event calendar")

Images and graphics:
• [ ] All images in emails have alt text
• [ ] Decorative images are marked as decorative (blank alt text in HTML: alt="")
• [ ] Do not send critical information as an image only — if you include a text image (poster, flyer), also include the same information as plain text in the email body

Color and contrast:
• [ ] Text has sufficient contrast against the email background (4.5:1 for normal text)
• [ ] Color is not used as the only indicator of importance or status
• [ ] Do not use colored text as the only way to highlight important information — use bold, bullets, or a clear statement

Attachments:
• [ ] All attachments are in accessible formats (accessible Word or accessible tagged PDF — not scanned PDFs)
• [ ] Attachment names are descriptive ("DSD_WCAG_Checklist_2025.pdf" is better than "Checklist.pdf" or "Final_v3_FINAL.pdf")

Common errors:
• Sending a flyer or announcement only as an image, with no plain-text equivalent — the image is invisible to screen readers
• Using red text as the only way to mark urgent content — colorblind users miss it
• Attaching scanned PDFs — inaccessible to all assistive technology

Channel 2: DSD Web Pages

DSD maintains web pages for program information, resources, and public communications. All DSD web content must meet WCAG 2.2 AA.

Checklist: Accessible Web Pages

Structure:
• [ ] Every page has a unique, descriptive page title (visible in browser tab)
• [ ] Content is organized with heading hierarchy (H1 for page title, H2 for major sections, H3 for subsections)
• [ ] Skip-to-main-content link at the top of every page (allows keyboard users to bypass navigation)
• [ ] Consistent navigation in the same location across all pages

Text and content:
• [ ] Plain language — grade 8 reading level for public-facing pages
• [ ] All acronyms defined on first use
• [ ] All link text is descriptive and makes sense out of context
• [ ] No "click here" or raw URL link text
• [ ] All language changes (from English to another language) marked in HTML (lang attribute)

Images and media:
• [ ] All images have alt text
• [ ] Decorative images have empty alt text (alt="")
• [ ] All videos have closed captions
• [ ] Pre-recorded videos have audio description if visual content is not conveyed in the narration
• [ ] Audio-only content has a text transcript

Color and contrast:
• [ ] Normal text: 4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum
• [ ] Large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold): 3:1 minimum
• [ ] UI components (buttons, form fields, icons): 3:1 minimum
• [ ] Color not used as the only indicator

Forms:
• [ ] All form fields have visible, descriptive labels
• [ ] Error messages identify the field with the error and explain how to fix it
• [ ] Required fields identified with text (not only with a color or asterisk — include "required" in text)
• [ ] Forms can be completed by keyboard only
• [ ] No timed form sessions without warning and extension option

Focus and keyboard navigation:
• [ ] All interactive elements reachable by keyboard (Tab key)
• [ ] Focus indicator is visible on all interactive elements
• [ ] No keyboard traps (Tab can always escape any interactive component)
• [ ] Focused element is not hidden by sticky headers or footers (WCAG 2.4.11)
• [ ] Logical tab order follows visual layout

Touch targets:
• [ ] Interactive elements are at least 24×24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8); aim for 44×44px
• [ ] Sufficient spacing between touch targets to prevent mis-taps

Common errors:
• PDFs linked from web pages that are not accessible — all linked documents must meet accessibility standards
• Forms that time out without warning — a user with a disability may need more time to complete a form
• Icons without labels — a user cannot understand an icon-only button with a screen reader unless it has a text label or aria-label

Channel 3: Social Media Accessibility

DSD's social media presence reaches the public, community partners, and the broader DSD service community. Social media posts must be accessible.

Checklist: Accessible Social Media

Images and graphics:
• [ ] All images posted on social media include alt text (most platforms support this natively)
• [ ] Text-heavy graphics (announcements, event information, quotes) include the same text in the post caption, so screen reader users get the content even if the image alt text is insufficient
• [ ] Infographics include a link to the same information in plain-text format (web page, document)

Adding alt text on common platforms:
• Twitter/X: Click the "Add description" option on uploaded images before posting
• Facebook/Meta: Tap the edit icon on images; select "Alt text" and type description
• LinkedIn: Alt text is added after upload in the edit menu
• Instagram: Go to "Advanced settings" before posting; tap "Write alt text"

Video:
• [ ] All videos posted on social media have closed captions
• [ ] Auto-generated captions are reviewed and corrected for accuracy before posting
• [ ] Videos that rely on visual content for meaning include audio description or text description in the post

Hashtags:
• [ ] Hashtags use CamelCase (capitalize the first letter of each word): #AccessibilityMatters, not #accessibilitymatters — screen readers read CamelCase hashtags as distinct words rather than a string of merged letters
• [ ] Limit the number of hashtags per post — multiple consecutive hashtags at the end of a post are disruptive to screen reader users

Emoji:
• [ ] Use emoji sparingly — screen readers read each emoji's full name ("sparkles," "red heart," "party popper")
• [ ] Do not use emoji to replace words or as the only indicator of meaning
• [ ] Do not stack multiple emoji in a row — each is read aloud

Text in posts:
• [ ] Plain language — clear, concise, grade 8 or lower
• [ ] All links are embedded with descriptive text where the platform allows
• [ ] Avoid ALL CAPS — screen readers read ALL CAPS letter by letter in some configurations

Common errors:
• Posting a graphic with event information (date, time, location, RSVP) without including that information in the text of the post — the graphic is invisible to screen readers
• Using hashtags in all lowercase (#disabilityawareness) — screen readers read this as one word
• Auto-posting video without reviewing captions for accuracy

Channel 4: Video Captioning

All video content DSD produces, commissions, or distributes must be captioned.

Checklist: Accessible Video

Closed captions (required):
• [ ] All prerecorded video has closed captions
• [ ] Captions are accurate (not only auto-generated without review)
• [ ] Captions identify speakers when there are multiple speakers ("[Name]:") or use separate captions per speaker
• [ ] Captions include relevant sound effects ("[phone rings]," "[applause]")
• [ ] Captions are synchronized with audio
• [ ] Caption text is readable (sufficient contrast, adequate font size — WCAG recommends minimum 22px caption text in video)

Auto-caption review process:
1. Generate auto-captions in your platform (Teams, Zoom, YouTube, etc.)
2. Download the caption file (SRT or VTT format)
3. Review for accuracy — correct names, technical terms, acronyms, and Hmong/Somali/Spanish/Karen/Oromo terms that auto-captioning struggles with
4. Upload the corrected caption file before publishing

Open captions vs. closed captions:
• Closed captions can be toggled on/off by the viewer — preferred for most uses
• Open captions are burned into the video and always visible — useful for social media where auto-captioning is unreliable or when you cannot guarantee the viewer will enable captions

Audio description (when needed):
• [ ] If the video relies on visual content not described in the narration (on-screen text, diagrams, demonstrations), add audio description
• [ ] Audio description is a narration track that describes visual content during natural pauses in the audio
• [ ] Contact the DSD Equity Team for guidance on commissioning audio descriptions

Transcripts:
• [ ] Provide a text transcript for all prerecorded video — particularly for screen reader users and Braille display users who may prefer reading to watching
• [ ] Transcript includes all spoken words, speaker identifications, and descriptions of relevant audio and visual content

Live video:
• [ ] All live-streamed meetings and events use live captioning (Teams or Zoom live captions, or CART)
• [ ] Live captions are clearly visible and have sufficient contrast
• [ ] Sign language interpreter visible and in an accessible format for live events

Channel 5: Audio Content

DSD may produce podcasts, audio recordings of meetings, or audio-only training materials.

Checklist: Accessible Audio

• [ ] All audio content has a text transcript
• [ ] Transcript is in an accessible document format (not a scanned PDF)
• [ ] Transcript is published alongside the audio on the same page or in the same communication
• [ ] Audio has no background music that competes with speech for listeners using hearing aids or cochlear implants
• [ ] Volume is consistent — no sudden loud segments
• [ ] Speakers identify themselves at the start of audio ("This is [Name]")

Channel 6: Accessible Imagery

Images used in all DSD communications must be inclusive and have meaningful alt text.

Checklist: Accessible Imagery

Alt text:
• [ ] All informational images have meaningful alt text
• [ ] Alt text describes what is in the image and why it is relevant — not just "person" or "group photo"
• [ ] Decorative images have empty alt text

Representation:
• [ ] Images of people reflect the diversity of DSD's staff and client community — including people with visible disabilities
• [ ] Avoid stock photos that portray disability in a stereotypical, pitying, or sensationalized way
• [ ] Center dignity — people in images are portrayed as whole, active, and capable
• [ ] For images of specific people: obtain consent; do not use images of clients who have not consented to appear in DSD communications

Alt text for diverse representation images:
• Describe the activity, context, or setting relevant to the communication — not personal characteristics unless they are directly relevant
• Do not describe race, disability, or other personal characteristics unless that is the point of the image

Cross-Cutting Practices for All Communications

Regardless of channel, every DSD communication must:

1. Use plain language — grade 8 reading level for client-facing content
2. Not rely on color alone — add text, pattern, or symbol alongside any color coding
3. Meet contrast requirements — 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI elements
4. Include alt text for images — concise and meaningful
5. Caption all audio and video — not just the important parts
6. Use descriptive link text — no "click here"
7. Provide multiple ways to access information — link from email to web page; include plain text version alongside graphics
8. Test before publishing — run the Accessibility Checker; check contrast; test keyboard navigation on web content

Where to Get Help

• Section508.gov — Creating Accessible Communications: https://www.section508.gov/create/
• WebAIM — Email Accessibility: https://webaim.org/techniques/email/
• WebAIM — Social Media Accessibility: https://webaim.org/
• W3C WAI — Video Captions Tutorial: https://www.w3.org/WAI/media/av/captions/
• Colour Contrast Analyser: https://www.tpgi.com/color-contrast-checker/
• One DSD Equity Team: Accessibility review and consultation

Connection to DSD's Six Program Goals

DSD Program Goal — Accessible Communications Connection

Equity and inclusion — Communications that exclude people with disabilities contradict DSD's equity mission
Cultural and linguistic competence — Multilingual communities need accessible formats across all languages
Olmstead implementation — Community integration depends on accessible information reaching people in accessible forms
Workforce development — Internal communications must be accessible for staff with disabilities
Quality improvement — Accessible communications reduce confusion, callbacks, and service errors
Leadership and accountability — Leaders ensure all team communications meet accessibility standards before publishing

Sources

• Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, W3C, December 2024: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
• DOJ ADA Title Two Web Accessibility Final Rule, April 2024: https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/
• Section508.gov — Creating Accessible Documents and Content: https://www.section508.gov/create/
• W3C WAI — Making Audio and Video Media Accessible: https://www.w3.org/WAI/media/av/
• WebAIM — Email Accessibility: https://webaim.org/techniques/email/
• Microsoft — Accessible Social Media: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/accessibility
• Twitter/X Accessibility: https://help.twitter.com/en/using-twitter/picture-descriptions

Accessibility is everyone's responsibility. When in doubt, ask people with disabilities what works for them.

fields.title: Change Management: Bringing People Along
fields.summary: Change management is how you help people through a change so it actually sticks. A good idea can fail simply because the people affected were not brought along. Equity work is full of change, so this is a core skill.
fields.body:
Change management is how you help people through a change so it actually sticks. A good idea can fail simply because the people affected were not brought along. Equity work is full of change, so this is a core skill.

Why change is hard. People do not resist change so much as they resist loss, uncertainty, and feeling done to instead of done with. Most resistance is information: it tells you something about what people fear or do not yet understand.

What helps change take hold.
• Make the case. Explain why the change matters and what happens if nothing changes, in plain language.
• Involve people early. People support what they help shape. Bring affected staff and communities in before the plan is final.
• Be honest about the trade-offs. Name what is hard or uncertain. Trust grows when you do not oversell.
• Support the transition. Give people training, time, and a place to ask questions and make mistakes.
• Close the loop. Show what you heard and what you changed because of it. Silence reads as not listening.
• Expect a dip. Things often feel worse before they feel better. Plan for it so it does not derail the work.

Lead with respect. Change done to people breeds resistance. Change done with people builds ownership. The difference is whether they had real voice along the way.

Go at the speed of trust. Sustainable change moves only as fast as people can come with you.

fields.title: Allyship Archetypes
fields.summary: This resource introduces the allyship archetype framework — drawing on the work of Karen Catlin and related research — to help DSD staff identify how they currently practice allyship, what other archetypes are available, and how to build a sustained, role-appropriate allyship practice. It addresses the difference between performative and sustained allyship and connects allyship to DSD's specific context.
fields.body:
What this is for

This resource introduces the allyship archetype framework — drawing on the work of Karen Catlin and related research — to help DSD staff identify how they currently practice allyship, what other archetypes are available, and how to build a sustained, role-appropriate allyship practice. It addresses the difference between performative and sustained allyship and connects allyship to DSD's specific context.

Why this matters in DSD work

Allyship is a behavioral commitment — a practice of using one's own access, influence, and credibility in service of people from marginalized communities. At DSD, allyship is both a workforce equity practice (how majority-group staff support colleagues from marginalized communities) and a service quality practice (how staff support equitable access and experience for the people DSD serves).

The challenge with allyship as a concept is that it is often understood as a status ("I am an ally") rather than as a practice ("I practice allyship"). Status claims without behavioral follow-through are at best insufficient and at worst harmful — they create the impression of support without its substance. The archetype framework is useful precisely because it moves from identity to behavior: what do allies actually do?

Core concepts

The allyship archetype framework

Karen Catlin's work on better allyship identifies seven archetypes of ally action (noting that the nine-archetype formulation referenced in the task spec aggregates related types):

1. The Sponsor
A sponsor uses their access to opportunity and decision-making to create opportunities for people from marginalized communities — advocating for someone's promotion, recommending them for projects, ensuring their name is in the room when decisions are made.

At DSD: A supervisor who advocates for a staff member from an underrepresented community to lead a high-visibility project when that opportunity might otherwise not have gone to them.

2. The Champion
A champion publicly advocates for the value and contributions of marginalized colleagues — crediting their work, naming their contributions in meetings, and speaking positively about them to people with influence.

At DSD: A senior leader who explicitly names and attributes the contributions of staff from marginalized communities rather than allowing those contributions to go unrecognized.

3. The Amplifier
An amplifier ensures that marginalized voices are heard in group settings — repeating and attributing an idea that was overlooked when raised by a marginalized colleague, inviting quieter voices to contribute, and interrupting dominant voices when they are crowding out others.

At DSD: A meeting facilitator who notices that a particular voice has been repeatedly overlooked and specifically invites that person to share their perspective.

4. The Advocate
An advocate works in systemic and structural ways to create more equitable conditions — not only supporting individuals but working to change policies, practices, and processes that produce inequitable outcomes.

At DSD: A program manager who examines a hiring process, identifies bias-producing elements, and advocates for structural changes rather than only trying to support individual candidates from marginalized communities.

5. The Scholar
A scholar takes responsibility for their own education — reading, listening, learning, and staying current on the experiences and perspectives of communities they want to ally with, rather than expecting those community members to educate them.

At DSD: A staff member who regularly reads literature by and about the communities DSD serves, who completes the CQ learning library materials, and who follows equity scholarship in disability and cultural communities.

6. The Confidant
A confidant creates a safe relationship in which colleagues from marginalized communities can express concerns, experiences, and emotions without filtering for the dominant-group audience — a person who listens without defensiveness, keeps confidences, and doesn't need the experience translated into language that's comfortable for them.

At DSD: A trusted peer who colleagues know they can talk to honestly about their experience of DSD's organizational culture without the conversation being repeated or used against them.

7. The Upstander
An upstander intervenes when they witness harm — using calling in, calling out, or the 5 Ds bystander framework to address discriminatory language, microaggressions, or exclusionary behavior in real time.

At DSD: A staff member who, in a team meeting, gently corrects a colleague who has used outdated or harmful language to refer to a disability community member.

(Note: Catlin's framework names seven archetypes; some formulations aggregate or add archetypes. The core categories above reflect the primary behavioral types.)

Finding the right archetype for the moment

Effective allyship is situationally appropriate — what is needed in a specific moment determines which archetype is most useful:

• In a meeting where a colleague's voice is being overlooked: Amplifier
• In a performance review season: Sponsor or Champion
• After witnessing harmful language: Upstander
• In designing a hiring process: Advocate
• In a learning conversation about a community you serve: Scholar
• When a colleague from a marginalized community needs to vent: Confidant

No single archetype is more valuable than others — the combination is what produces a comprehensive allyship practice. Staff who practice only one archetype miss the others. Staff who cycle through all seven are practicing sustained allyship.

Sustained allyship practice

Allyship is a practice, not an identity. The move from "I am an ally" to "I practice allyship consistently" is the critical shift. Practice implies:

• Regularity: allyship that only happens when it's visible or convenient is not sustained
• Learning: allyship requires ongoing education about the experiences and needs of the communities you ally with — education that comes primarily from listening and reading, not from expecting community members to teach you
• Accountability: sustained allies ask for feedback on their allyship — not from community members as a burden, but from trusted sources who will tell them the truth
• Repair: sustained allies acknowledge when they have caused harm, and repair it — not defensively, not performatively, but genuinely

Centering those most affected. The quality of allyship is evaluated not by the ally's intentions but by its impact on the people the ally is trying to support. What do colleagues and community members from marginalized communities actually experience when you practice allyship? That experience — not your assessment of your own intentions — is the measure.

Allyship and power

Allyship is most meaningful at the intersection of difference and power. Staff with racial majority privilege can ally with colleagues and community members from racially marginalized communities. Staff without disabilities can ally with disabled colleagues and the people DSD serves. LGBTQ+ -inclusive staff can ally with LGBTQ+ colleagues and community members.

This does not mean that people from one marginalized community cannot ally with people from another — they often can, and those forms of allyship are valuable. It means that allyship is most powerful when the person practicing it has relevant access, privilege, or influence that they are willing to use in service of equity.

Practical application

Identify your current archetype. Look at the seven archetypes. Which one are you most consistently practicing? Which are you not practicing at all? Why?

Choose one underdeveloped archetype to build. Identify one specific archetype you rarely or never practice and identify one concrete, time-bound action you will take in that archetype role in the next month.

Audit your allyship for impact. Ask a trusted colleague from a community you ally with: "What do you experience as supportive from me, and where do I miss?" This feedback is the calibration mechanism for allyship practice.

Practice the Scholar archetype regularly. Identify one resource — a book, an article, a CQ guide, a podcast — by or about a community DSD serves that you will engage with in the next month. Make this a regular practice.

Build the Confidant relationship deliberately. If you have colleagues from marginalized communities who trust you with their honest experiences, protect that trust scrupulously. If you don't, examine why and what might build it.

Common challenges

"I don't want to overstep." Allyship practiced carefully — with attentiveness to what is actually needed, with genuine listening, and with willingness to hear "that wasn't helpful" — is rarely overstepping. The more common failure is understep: doing nothing because of fear of doing the wrong thing.

"I'm from a marginalized community myself; does this apply to me?" Yes. Allyship is available to and important from everyone. Your own marginalization in one dimension does not exempt you from practicing allyship in dimensions where you have more access or privilege.

"I'm afraid of getting it wrong." You will get it wrong sometimes. The response to getting it wrong is what matters: acknowledge, learn, repair, continue. The alternative — disengagement to avoid mistakes — is not allyship.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

Sustained allyship from DSD staff builds the inclusive workplace culture that DSD's program goals require, and demonstrates to the communities DSD serves that the organization's equity commitments are practiced by the people who work there.

Connection to other leadership competencies

• Calling In vs. Calling Out (Asset 27): The Upstander archetype in practice
• DEAI Integration Across Leadership (Asset 24): Allyship is DEAI at the relational level
• Inclusive Supervision Foundations (Asset 9): Supervisors who ally with their staff build more inclusive teams

Reflective questions

1. Which of the seven allyship archetypes do you practice most consistently? Which do you never practice?
2. Think of a colleague from a marginalized community at DSD. What does your allyship look like in practice for that person? What would they say about its impact?
3. When was the last time you practiced the Scholar archetype — reading, listening, or learning about a community you serve or work alongside? What did you learn?
4. What is the form of allyship most needed in your current work context? Who needs it and from whom?
5. What would sustained allyship look like as a regular practice — not a single act, but an ongoing, monthly, weekly commitment?

Sources

• Catlin, K. (2019). Better allies: Everyday actions to create inclusive, engaging workplaces. Better Allies Press. https://betterallies.com (https://betterallies.com)
• Forbes / Kratz, J. (2024). 7 research-backed allyship archetypes every leader needs to practice. https://www.forbes.com/sites/juliekratz/2024/01/07/7-research-backed-allyship-archetypes-every-leader-needs-to-practice/ (https://www.forbes.com/sites/juliekratz/2024/01/07/7-research-backed-allyship-archetypes-every-leader-needs-to-practice/)
• Brown, B. (2018). Dare to lead: Brave work. Tough conversations. Whole hearts. Random House.
• One DSD L01 Massive DEIA Multimedia Resource Library. One DSD People, Equity and Culture Program.
• One DSD L05 Inclusive Leadership Library. One DSD People, Equity and Culture Program.

fields.title: EAT Overview Walk-Through — What the Equity Analysis Toolkit Is and How It Works
fields.summary: IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.
fields.body:
EAT Overview Walk-Through — What the Equity Analysis Toolkit Is and How It Works

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — EAT Walk-Through (Methodology Education, Not Analysis)
Adapted from: DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (Minnesota DHS) + Government Alliance on Race and Equity (GARE) Racial Equity Toolkit
Library home: L01 EAT Walk-Through Library
Companion to: T02_02 through T02_14 (all EAT walk-throughs)

IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.

What this step is for

This overview gives every DSD staff member a foundation for understanding what the Equity Analysis Toolkit (EAT) is, what it is not, how its two tracks work, and how it connects to the Equity Lens Needs Assessment. You do not need to be an equity specialist to read and use this walk-through. It is designed for any DSD staff member who will encounter, support, or contribute to an equity analysis process.

Plain-language overview

The DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit is a structured, step-by-step process for examining how proposed policies, programs, practices, plans, and budget decisions affect communities — and particularly communities that have historically experienced inequities. It is the primary tool Minnesota DHS uses to ensure that equity is not an afterthought but is built into decision-making from the beginning.

As the DHS Equity Policy (https://mn.gov/dhs/assets/equity-policy_tcm1053-646921.pdf) makes clear, a formal equity analysis is required for all actions that have prolonged or long-term impact and that are scheduled for approval at the supervisor, director, deputy commissioner, or commissioner level. The toolkit gives staff the framework to do that work — or to understand the work being done around them.

The toolkit functions in two ways simultaneously. It is a process — a series of structured events that produces more equitable decisions. It is also a result — the modifications that communities actually feel and experience when equity analysis is done well. This dual nature is important: completing the paperwork is not the goal. The goal is better outcomes for people.

Walk-through (the methodology)

The six-step process

The EAT is organized around six sequential steps. Each step builds on the last. The six steps are:

Step 1 — Set Desired Results and Outcomes (Frame the Decision/Issue). Start by articulating clearly what decision is being made or what issue is being examined. Define who the decision affects, what the intended results are in the community, and which disparity domains are in scope. Shared understanding at Step 1 is foundational — if team members disagree about what is being decided, the analysis will diverge at every subsequent step.

Step 2 — Data. Gather both quantitative and qualitative data about racial demographics, existing disparities, and the root causes of inequities in the area being examined. Disaggregate data by race wherever possible. Identify data gaps honestly and develop plans to fill them.

Step 3 — Engaging Communities. Community engagement is not optional. The EAT Guide is explicit: "It is not enough to consult data or literature to assume how a proposal may impact a community. Communities know what they need." This step requires genuine engagement with the communities most affected — not token representation, but meaningful participation.

Step 4 — Benefits and Burdens. Use what you learned in Steps 2 and 3 to assess who benefits and who bears burdens from the proposed action. Surface unintended consequences. Identify how the proposal can be modified to reduce negative impacts and expand positive ones.

Step 5 — Implementation. Describe a plan with four elements: the strategy (how you will mitigate unintended consequences or expand positive impact), specific actions, the person responsible for each action, and the deadlines and resources required. Test the plan for feasibility.

Step 6 — Accountability, Communication, and Evaluation. Make the work ongoing. Document impacts. Evaluate whether anticipated outcomes are being achieved. Create feedback loops with communities. Iterate and adjust.

The two tracks

The DHS Equity Lens Needs Assessment (a decision tree) determines which of two tracks is appropriate for a given decision:

Equity Analysis Track. This is the full, intentional examination. It involves all six steps in depth, meaningful community engagement, comprehensive data gathering, and a full Equity Impact Statement. The Analysis Track is used when a decision has significant, prolonged impact on communities experiencing inequities. Per the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (https://mn.gov/dhs/), the Analysis Track is most valuable when applied early — at the very beginning of a decision process, not at the end.

Equity Scan Track. This is a shorter, more targeted tool. It is used when: (a) a process, project, or program has already been fully analyzed and is being re-reviewed, or (b) when a shortened timeline makes a full analysis impossible. The Scan is not a shortcut to avoid rigor; it is a calibrated tool for specific circumstances. If you are unsure which track applies, consult your Equity Director or Specialist before proceeding.

The Equity Lens Needs Assessment

The Equity Lens Needs Assessment is a decision tree that lives at the very front of the EAT process. You complete it before you begin the six steps. It helps you determine:

• Whether an equity analysis is required at all for this decision
• Which track (Analysis or Scan) is appropriate given the scope, timeline, and impact area of the decision
• What level of staffing and community engagement the process will require

Think of the Needs Assessment as the scoping tool. It sets the frame for everything that follows. Without it, teams often jump into analysis work without agreement on depth, track, or scope — which leads to inconsistent results and community disengagement.

Key impact areas the toolkit addresses

According to the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (https://mn.gov/dhs/), every analysis should consider impact across three focus areas at minimum:

• Workforce and Leadership Development — how the decision affects the availability and productivity of health and human service workers
• Contracting and Procurement — how the decision ensures inclusion of historically marginalized populations
• CLAS Standards — how the decision ensures effective, equitable, understandable, and respectful care and services responsive to diverse cultural health beliefs, preferred languages, health literacy, and communication needs

Worked example fragment (anonymized, methodology illustration only)

A DSD program area is considering a change to its intake process for a waiver program. The program lead is unsure whether a full Equity Analysis or an Equity Scan is appropriate.

The program lead completes the Equity Lens Needs Assessment. The decision tree reveals: the change will affect thousands of individuals across multiple demographic groups, will persist for at least three years, and involves a program area with documented racial disparities in enrollment. The Needs Assessment points to the Equity Analysis Track.

The program lead now knows the scope: full six-step process, meaningful community engagement, disaggregated data, and a completed Equity Impact Statement before the change goes to leadership for approval.

This resource walks through methodology only. The actual analysis would be conducted by the program lead's Equity Champion working with the DHS Equity Director for that work area.

IS / IS NOT

The EAT IS — The EAT IS NOT

A structured, six-step methodology for examining equity impacts — The "answer" to inequities — it reveals them; it does not automatically fix them
A process and a result — A full stop of a process or a reason to delay indefinitely
Best used early — at the beginning of a decision — Only applicable at the beginning (ongoing evaluation is part of the process)
Conducted with diverse perspectives and stakeholders — A substitute for authentic community engagement
A way to ensure racial equity impacts are at the core of decision-making — A separate "add-on" to normal work
A tool for raising the voice of marginalized communities — A tool for creating token representation
An authentic effort to prevent institutional racism and identify options to remedy inequities — A checkbox activity
Required for major decisions per DHS Equity Policy — Optional or advisory only

Common questions

Who is responsible for conducting the equity analysis?
Your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area conducts and oversees the analysis. Your role as a staff member is to understand the process, contribute your knowledge of the affected communities and programs, and support the analysis — not to conduct it independently.

What if time is short and the deadline is real?
The EAT Guide recommends negotiating the timeline first. If the timeline cannot be moved due to external factors, contact your Equity Director or Specialist. They can help you determine whether the Equity Scan Track applies, or whether modifications to the full Analysis are appropriate. Using the toolkit "mid-late in a process" is not a reason to skip it — but it does reduce its effectiveness, which is why applying it early matters.

What if there are data gaps?
This is expected. Both quantitative and qualitative data matter. When quantitative data is absent or incomplete, qualitative data (community testimony, focus group input, staff observations) can speak to subpopulations and nuance. Document the gap and develop a plan to improve data collection going forward.

What are "disparity domains"?
The DHS EAT Guide defines disparity domains as areas where documented differences in health and life outcomes are linked to social, economic, or environmental disadvantage. Domains include: education, employment, income, health, housing, transportation, justice, public safety, institutional systems change, employee engagement and belonging, built environment, neighborhood, and social and community context. Your analysis identifies which domains the proposed action touches.

Connection to DSD goals

DSD's six organizational goals anchor all equity work. The EAT is the mechanism through which those goals move from aspiration to action. The ADSA strategy (https://mn.gov/dhs/) connects DSD's program-level decisions to DHS's broader population-level outcomes — and the EAT is the structured tool that surfaces whether a given decision advances or undermines those connections.

The EAT also connects directly to the Equity Cascade Crosswalk, which maps how individual decisions trace upward through DSD's six goals to ADSA strategy to DHS outcomes. Walk-through asset T02_14 covers this traceability in detail.

When to escalate / where to refer

• If you are unsure whether a decision requires an equity analysis: contact your work area's Equity Director or Specialist.
• If the Equity Lens Needs Assessment indicates the Analysis Track and you need support: refer to your Equity Champion or the One DSD Equity Team.
• If a community engagement component is needed: refer to DSD program areas and the CECLC (Community Engagement, Cultural and Linguistic Competency). Community engagement is not a function this resource performs; it is DSD's collective responsibility.
• If you have questions about Tribal Nations-specific equity implications: refer to the ADSA Tribal Collective. Per Charter v1.1 Article 13 (one-dsd-program-charter), tribal content is handled by the ADSA Tribal Collective — this resource does not advise on tribal-specific equity analysis practices.

Reflective questions

1. Think of a recent decision in your work area. At what point in that process was equity formally considered? Would earlier application of the EAT have changed the process or the outcome?
2. What is the difference between using the EAT as a process tool and using it as a result-producing tool? How does your team currently think about it?
3. Who in your work area is your Equity Champion or Equity Director contact? Do you know how to reach them?
4. What data about the communities your programs serve do you have ready access to? Where are the gaps?
5. The EAT is designed to be adapted — not a one-size-fits-all template. What adaptations might your program area need?

Sources

• DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/) (primary source)
• DHS Equity Policy — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/assets/equity-policy_tcm1053-646921.pdf)
• Racial Equity Toolkit — Government Alliance on Race and Equity (GARE), via Othering and Belonging Institute (https://belonging.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/ARCHIVE/gare-racial_equity_toolkit.pdf)
• Racial Equity Impact Assessment Guide — Race Forward (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf)
• King County Equity Impact Review Tool (https://cdn.kingcounty.gov/-/media/king-county/depts/dph/documents/safety-injury-prevention/emergency-preparedness/cre/equity-impact-review-tool.pdf)
• One DSD Program Charter v1.1 (one-dsd-program-charter)
• One DSD Content Map and Gap Analysis v1.0 (../content_map_and_gap_analysis_v1.md)

Always defer to the person in front of you.

fields.summary: IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. fields.body:
EAT Step 6 Walk-Through — Monitor, Evaluate, Adjust

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — EAT Walk-Through (Methodology Education, Not Analysis)
Adapted from: DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide (Minnesota DHS) — Step 6: Accountability, Communication, and Evaluation
Library home: L01 EAT Walk-Through Library
Companion to: T02_01 (EAT Overview), T02_06 (Step 5 Implementation), T02_10 (IS/IS NOT)

IMPORTANT — Scope of this resource: This walks staff through the methodology of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. It does not perform equity analyses. Actual equity analyses are conducted by the appropriate authorities — your Equity Champion, the One DSD Equity Team, or the DHS Equity Director for your work area.

What this step is for

Step 6 is the step most likely to be skipped — and the one whose absence most undermines the equity work that preceded it. Without monitoring and evaluation, a program can implement an equity analysis recommendation, declare success, and never learn that the change did not produce the intended results, or produced new disparities, or helped some communities while leaving others behind. This walk-through teaches staff how the EAT approaches monitoring, evaluation, feedback loops, and iteration discipline.

Plain-language overview

Step 6 of the EAT asks: Are we achieving what we said we would achieve — for all communities, not just on average?

The DHS EAT Guide (https://mn.gov/dhs/) describes Step 6 as "accountability, communication, and evaluation of results" and is clear that the equity analysis process is ongoing: "Using the tool at different phases helps identify and implement new opportunities for advancing equity." This is not a one-time activity that concludes when the implementation plan is complete. It is a continuing discipline.

The Race Forward Racial Equity Impact Assessment (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf) frames success indicators as the final question of any equity analysis: "What are the success indicators and progress benchmarks? How will impacts be documented and evaluated? How will the level, diversity and quality of ongoing stakeholder engagement be assessed?"

Walk-through (the methodology)

Outcome tracking: the three levels of performance measurement

The EAT Guide specifies that performance level measures respond to three levels:

1. Quantity: How much did we do? This is the baseline measure — how many people received the service, how many applications were processed, how many training sessions were delivered. Quantity measures tell you the volume of activity. They are necessary but not sufficient for equity evaluation.

2. Quality: How well did we do it? Quality measures assess whether the service was delivered consistently, accessibly, and responsively. For equity purposes, quality must be assessed disaggregated by race — a service delivered consistently to white clients but inconsistently to Black clients has a quality equity problem even if its aggregate quality score is high.

3. Is anyone better off? This is the equity question. Did the communities that bore the greatest burden before the change experience improvement? Are the people most affected by the proposal — the communities identified in Step 1 and engaged in Step 3 — experiencing better outcomes? Are disparities narrowing? This third level is the one most equity analyses never reach because the data systems to answer it do not exist or have not been disaggregated.

For each of the three levels, the EAT expects tracking disaggregated by race. An equity analysis that monitors "overall" outcomes without disaggregation cannot tell whether the change helped or harmed the communities it was designed to benefit.

Feedback loops

Feedback loops are mechanisms through which communities experiencing the change can report back on whether it is working for them. The EAT Guide requires that implementation include "ongoing data collection, public reporting, and community engagement." A feedback loop is the community engagement component of Step 6.

Effective feedback loops:

• Are accessible to the communities most affected. A feedback survey that is only in English, only online, and requires thirty minutes to complete will not reach the communities with the highest barriers. Design feedback mechanisms that match the access patterns of the communities you are trying to hear from.
• Are responsive. If community feedback is collected but does not inform any decisions, communities will stop providing it. Close the loop: share back what you heard, what you decided, and why.
• Are ongoing. A one-time post-implementation survey is not a feedback loop. Feedback loops are regular touchpoints — quarterly check-ins, standing agenda items in community partner meetings, annual community surveys — that create a continuous channel for community voice into program evaluation.
• Are disaggregated. Feedback from community members should be analyzed by community to identify whether different groups are experiencing different outcomes. Aggregate satisfaction scores mask community-specific concerns.

Community feedback mechanisms

The King County Equity Impact Review (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf) frames Phase 5 (Ongoing Learning) as: "Evaluate whether your action appropriately responds to community priorities and concerns. Learn with the community to adjust your action as their priorities and concerns shift. Communicate progress to all stakeholders. Plan to include community feedback into future planning."

In DSD's context, community feedback mechanisms might include:

• Standing advisory groups representing communities most affected by a change, with regular meeting cadences and documented feedback processes
• Community-based organization partner check-ins, where advocacy partners who participated in Step 3 are invited to report on community experience of the implementation
• Client satisfaction surveys, disaggregated by race and primary language
• Formal community listening sessions at six-month and annual intervals post-implementation
• Grievance and complaint tracking, disaggregated by community, with analysis for patterns that suggest systemic implementation failures

Iteration discipline

Iteration discipline means committing in advance to a process for adjusting the implementation based on what monitoring and evaluation reveal — and then actually following through. The EAT Guide asks: "Are you achieving anticipated outcomes? Do you have a plan to course-correct if needed?"

Iteration discipline requires:

1. Pre-specified adjustment triggers. Before implementation begins, define what evidence would trigger a course-correction review. Example: "If the enrollment gap between Somali-origin and white applicants has not narrowed by 10 percentage points within 12 months, we will convene a review." Without pre-specified triggers, teams wait for a crisis instead of proactively adjusting.

2. A designated review body. Who reviews monitoring data and decides whether adjustment is needed? The Equity Director, the Equity Committee, or a designated implementation team should be specified in the implementation plan. Without a named body, review does not happen.

3. A documented adjustment process. When monitoring data triggers a review, what happens? Who is involved? What decision-making authority exists? How are communities engaged in the adjustment? Document this process in Step 5 so it is ready when Step 6 requires it.

4. Honest reporting. "We are not achieving our equity targets" is a finding that must be reported — to Equity Directors, to division leadership, and to the communities affected. The temptation to report only positive progress is real; the EAT framework requires honest reporting, even when the news is difficult.

The ongoing nature of Step 6

The EAT Guide states that "the equity analysis process is ongoing. Using the tool at different phases helps identify and implement new opportunities for advancing equity." This means Step 6 is not a conclusion — it is a transition to the next iteration of the process. What monitoring reveals in Step 6 may trigger a new Step 1 — a re-framing of the issue in light of what was learned. Or it may trigger a new Step 4 — generating new strategies because the original strategies did not produce the intended equity impact.

The EAT is a cycle, not a linear sequence with a defined end. Programs and policies change over time. Communities change. The data environment changes. Equity analysis that treats the toolkit as something to be "completed" rather than as an ongoing practice will miss the opportunities for course-correction that Step 6 is designed to surface.

Worked example fragment (anonymized, methodology illustration only)

Continuing the anonymized waiver program scenario at 12 months post-implementation:

The Equity Champion conducts the first annual monitoring review.

Quantity: Applications processed increased by 22%. Somali-origin applications increased by 31% — the targeted community is engaging more.

Quality: Error rates on income documentation processing decreased overall. However, Karen-origin applications are experiencing a higher rate of processing delays — a new disparity not present before the change.

Is anyone better off? Somali-origin enrollment increased; the documentation disparity is narrowing. Karen-origin enrollment has not improved, and a new processing-delay disparity has emerged.

Feedback loop findings: Community-based organization partners report that Karen-origin applicants are encountering a specific staff training gap — case managers were trained on the new income documentation alternatives but not on the application navigator service that was designed to support Karen-origin applicants.

Adjustment triggered: Pre-specified trigger met (Karen-origin processing delays exceeding threshold). Review convened. New action added to implementation plan: targeted staff training on application navigator service for Karen-origin applicants; monthly processing-time monitoring added for Karen-origin applications specifically.

This resource walks through methodology only. The actual monitoring and evaluation would be conducted by the Equity Champion and Equity Director.

IS / IS NOT

Step 6 IS — Step 6 IS NOT

Ongoing monitoring at three levels: quantity, quality, is anyone better off? — A one-time post-implementation survey
Disaggregated evaluation — by race, not just in aggregate — Aggregate outcome reporting that masks community-specific results
Community feedback mechanisms that are accessible and responsive — A feedback form that communities cannot access or that never influences decisions
Iteration discipline with pre-specified adjustment triggers — Waiting for a crisis before reviewing whether implementation is working
Honest reporting of equity target progress (or non-progress) — Only reporting when results are positive
A transition to the next cycle of equity analysis — The final step that "completes" the process

Common questions

What if monitoring reveals that the implementation is not working?
Document the finding, trigger the pre-specified adjustment review, and convene the designated review body. Do not delay reporting because the news is difficult. The EAT framework expects this — implementation without monitoring is just hope, not equity work.

How long does Step 6 monitoring last?
For as long as the policy or program exists. Step 6 is not a temporary phase; it is the ongoing operational posture. The monitoring cadence may change over time — more frequent early in implementation, less frequent once stable patterns are established — but it does not end.

Who has access to monitoring data?
The Equity Director, the Equity Committee, division leadership, and the communities affected. The EAT Guide is explicit that the Equity Impact Statement and monitoring results should be shared with stakeholders and posted on SharePoint. Monitoring data is not an internal document for program staff only.

Connection to DSD goals

Step 6 is where DSD's equity commitments become verifiable. DSD's six organizational goals are not just aspirational — they are measurable. Step 6 is the mechanism through which the organization knows whether its equity work is producing the outcomes it committed to. Without Step 6, DSD cannot honestly report whether equity is advancing or stalling.

When to escalate / where to refer

• If monitoring data reveals that equity targets are not being met and adjustment within the program area's authority is insufficient: escalate to division director with specific findings and resource implications.
• If community feedback reveals significant concerns not captured in quantitative monitoring data: convene the review body and involve the communities in the adjustment process.
• If monitoring reveals that a policy change has produced new disparities not present before the analysis: initiate a new Step 1 framing to address the new disparity.

Reflective questions

1. Think of a program your area runs. Do you currently have monitoring measures that are disaggregated by race? If not, what would it take to add them?
2. What is the difference between a feedback mechanism and a feedback loop? Does your program area close the loop with communities after gathering feedback?
3. Have you ever seen a program course-correct based on equity monitoring data? What made the adjustment possible?
4. What would "pre-specified adjustment triggers" look like for a major program in your area? What evidence would you specify as the threshold for a review?
5. What does ongoing equity analysis look like in a program area that does not have dedicated equity staff time?

Sources

• DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit Guide — Minnesota DHS (https://mn.gov/dhs/) (primary source, Step 6)
• Racial Equity Impact Assessment Guide — Race Forward (https://www.raceforward.org/sites/default/files/RacialJusticeImpactAssessment_v5.pdf) (section 10: identifying success indicators)
• King County Equity Impact Review — Phase 5: Ongoing Learning (https://blog.homelessinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/King-County-Equity-Impact-Review-checklist_Mar2017.pdf)
• Racial Equity Toolkit — GARE, via Othering and Belonging Institute (https://belonging.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/ARCHIVE/gare-racial_equity_toolkit.pdf)
• One DSD Program Charter v1.1 (one-dsd-program-charter)

Always defer to the person in front of you.
