fields.title: Microsoft Word Accessibility Checklist
fields.summary: A step-by-step checklist for creating accessible Microsoft Word documents. This checklist covers every major accessibility requirement — from document title and language settings through heading structure, images, tables, links, color contrast, and the built-in Accessibility Checker. It also covers how to export accessible PDFs from Word.
fields.body:
Microsoft Word Accessibility Checklist

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Accessibility
Library home: L09 Accessibility & Plain Language Library
Companion to: WCAG 2.2 AA Flagship Module; PDF Accessibility Checklist; Plain-Language Style Guide for DSD
Standards reference: WCAG 2.2 AA; §508 Rehabilitation Act; Title II ADA; Microsoft Accessibility documentation

What this is

A step-by-step checklist for creating accessible Microsoft Word documents. This checklist covers every major accessibility requirement — from document title and language settings through heading structure, images, tables, links, color contrast, and the built-in Accessibility Checker. It also covers how to export accessible PDFs from Word.

Use this checklist every time you create or update a Word document that will be shared with colleagues, clients, or the public — including reports, policy summaries, training materials, meeting agendas, and letters.

Why this matters for DSD

Word documents are the most common document format in DSD operations. Policy summaries, training materials, case-related letters, meeting agendas, and reporting templates are all typically created in Word. If these documents are not accessible:

• Staff and clients who use screen readers (due to vision disabilities) cannot read them
• People using Braille displays cannot navigate them
• People with low vision who use magnification software encounter poorly structured content
• People with cognitive disabilities encounter dense, unstructured walls of text
• When documents are converted to PDF for sharing, the inaccessibility carries over

Under the DOJ's 2024 Title II ADA Final Rule, documents — including Word files — that provide access to programs or services must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. DSD's own Resolution 26 sets WCAG 2.2 AA as the operating standard. The two frameworks overlap significantly for documents; this checklist addresses both.

The core requirements

Accessible Word documents must:
1. Have a meaningful document title
2. Have the correct language set
3. Use built-in heading styles (not manually bolded text)
4. Include alt text for every informational image
5. Use accessible table structure with header rows
6. Use built-in list formatting (not manually typed dashes or bullets)
7. Use descriptive, meaningful link text
8. Meet color contrast requirements (4.5:1 for text)
9. Not rely on color alone to convey information
10. Pass the built-in Accessibility Checker

Step-by-Step Checklist

Step 1: Set the Document Title

A document title is different from the file name. It is the name embedded in the document properties that screen readers announce when the document opens.

How to set it:
1. Go to File > Info
2. In the Properties panel (right side), find Title
3. Type a clear, descriptive title (example: "2025 DSD Equitable Engagement Plan")
4. Click back into the document to save

Why it matters: Screen readers announce the document title when a user opens the file. A title of "Document1" or a vague file name tells blind and low-vision users nothing about what they are reading.

Common error: Leaving the title blank or using the file name. Fix: Always set a meaningful title in document properties before sharing.

Step 2: Set the Document Language

Word uses language settings to tell screen readers how to pronounce content. Without it, a screen reader may use the wrong language synthesizer.

How to set it:
1. Select all text (Ctrl+A)
2. Go to Review > Language > Set Proofing Language
3. Select the primary language (e.g., English (United States))
4. Click OK
5. If the document contains sections in another language, select that text separately and set its language

Why it matters: Screen readers switch pronunciation engines based on language settings. Incorrect settings cause mispronunciation that makes content incomprehensible for blind users.

Common error: Using the default language setting without verifying it. Fix: Always verify and set language explicitly, especially in documents created from templates.

Step 3: Use Built-In Heading Styles

Headings are the most important navigation tool for screen reader users. Screen readers can jump from heading to heading, allowing users to scan and navigate a document without reading every word.

What this means in practice:
• Do not create the appearance of a heading by making text bold and large
• Use the built-in styles in the Home tab: Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3, etc.
• Use only one Heading 1 per document (the document title, if it is in the body)
• Use Heading 2 for major sections, Heading 3 for subsections
• Do not skip heading levels (do not jump from Heading 1 to Heading 3)
• Keep heading text concise and descriptive — screen reader users hear the heading and decide whether to jump into that section

How to apply a heading style:
1. Select the heading text
2. In the Home tab > Styles group, click the appropriate heading level

Keyboard shortcut: Alt+H, L to open the Styles gallery

Why it matters: Without headings, a screen reader user must listen to every word of a long document to find what they need. With headings, they can navigate directly to the section they want. This is the same as visual skimming for sighted readers.

Common error: Manually formatting text to look like a heading (bold, large font, centered) without using the Heading style. Fix: Select all such text and apply the appropriate Heading style from the Styles gallery.

Step 4: Add Alt Text to All Images

Every image, chart, SmartArt graphic, shape, screenshot, and embedded visual in a Word document needs alternative text (alt text) unless it is purely decorative.

How to add alt text:
1. Right-click the image
2. Select Edit Alt Text
3. Type a concise description in the alt text field
4. For decorative images: check Mark as decorative

Writing good alt text:
• Be concise — most alt text should be one or two sentences
• Describe what the image shows and why it is there (its purpose in the document)
• Do not begin with "image of" or "picture of" — screen readers already announce it is an image
• For charts and graphs: describe the key finding or trend, not just "a bar chart"
• Good: "Bar chart showing program enrollment increased by 22% between 2022 and 2025"
• Not helpful: "Bar chart"
• For images that contain text: repeat the text in the alt text field
• For logos: describe the logo and the organization it represents

Why it matters: Screen reader users cannot see images. Alt text provides the equivalent information in a form they can access. Missing alt text leaves a gap in the document's content.

Common error: No alt text on charts, screenshots, or icons. Fix: Run the Accessibility Checker (Step 10) to find all images missing alt text, then add descriptions.

Step 5: Make Tables Accessible

Tables are challenging for screen readers when they are complex or improperly structured. The key principle: use tables only for tabular data, and keep them simple.

Requirements:
• Every table must have a header row that labels the columns
• Do not use merged cells, split cells, or nested tables — they break the reading order for screen readers
• Do not use tables for layout (positioning content visually) — use column layouts, text boxes, or section breaks instead
• Avoid fixed-width tables when documents will be viewed on mobile devices
• Ensure tables have enough contrast between cell backgrounds and text

How to set a header row:
1. Click anywhere in the table
2. Go to the Table Design tab
3. In Table Style Options, check Header Row
4. In the first row, type your column headings

How to repeat headers on multiple pages:
1. Select the header row
2. Go to Table > Properties > Row tab
3. Check Repeat as header row at the top of each page

Why it matters: Without a header row, screen readers read tables cell by cell without context. A user in cell D4 of a table has no way to know which column or row they are in. Header rows give that context.

Common error: Using a table for visual layout (e.g., putting two images side by side). Fix: Use columns, text boxes, or side-by-side paragraph layout instead.

Step 6: Use Built-In List Formatting

Lists are one of the most effective accessibility and plain-language tools. But lists made by manually typing dashes, asterisks, or numbers are not recognized as lists by screen readers.

How to create accessible lists:
1. Click where you want the list to start
2. Go to Home tab
3. Click Bullets (for unordered lists) or Numbering (for ordered lists)
4. Type each list item and press Enter

Requirements:
• Use numbered lists when the order matters (steps, instructions, ranked items)
• Use bulleted lists when the order does not matter
• Do not insert a plain paragraph in the middle of a list — some screen readers will miscount the items
• Keep list items parallel in structure (all start with a verb, or all are noun phrases, etc.)

Why it matters: Screen readers announce "list of N items" when entering a properly formatted list and "leaving list" when exiting. This orientation helps users understand structure. Manual lists (dashes, asterisks) are read as individual characters or plain text with no structural signal.

Common error: Creating lists by typing dashes or numbers manually. Fix: Delete the manual formatting and use the built-in Bullets or Numbering buttons.

Step 7: Write Descriptive Link Text

Every hyperlink in a Word document must convey the purpose of the link from the link text alone — without needing to read the surrounding sentence.

Requirements:
• Do not use vague link text: "click here," "learn more," "see this," "read more"
• Do not use raw URLs as link text unless the URL itself is meaningful: "https://www.section508.gov/develop/universal-design/" is not meaningful link text
• Do use the destination's title or a clear description: "Download the WCAG 2.2 Checklist (PDF, 12 pages)"
• Add ScreenTips for additional context when helpful

How to edit link text:
1. Select the text you want to link
2. Go to Insert > Link (or right-click > Edit Hyperlink)
3. In Text to display, type the descriptive text
4. In Address, paste the URL
5. Click OK

Why it matters: Screen reader users often browse links as a list, out of context from the surrounding text. When every link says "click here," users cannot determine where each link goes. Descriptive link text is also a plain-language practice that benefits all readers.

Common error: Pasting raw URLs as link text. Fix: Always replace the raw URL with a descriptive phrase that indicates the destination.

Step 8: Meet Color Contrast Requirements

Text must have sufficient contrast against its background to be readable by people with low vision and color vision deficiencies.

WCAG 2.2 AA requirements:
• Normal text (under 18pt regular or 14pt bold): 4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum
• Large text (18pt regular or 14pt bold and above): 3:1 contrast ratio minimum
• UI components and graphical objects: 3:1 contrast ratio minimum

Common high-risk situations in Word documents:
• Light gray text on white background (common in templates)
• Yellow or light text on white backgrounds
• Red or green used for status — many people with color blindness cannot distinguish these
• Colored text in tables with colored cell backgrounds

How to check contrast:
1. Use the free Colour Contrast Analyser tool (https://www.tpgi.com/color-contrast-checker/)
2. Or run the Accessibility Checker (Step 10), which flags some contrast issues

How to fix contrast problems:
1. Select the text with insufficient contrast
2. Go to Home > Font Color
3. Choose a darker color that meets the 4.5:1 ratio
4. Or change the background to a lighter or darker shade

Requirements beyond contrast:
• Do not use color as the only way to convey information (e.g., "items marked in red are overdue")
• Add a secondary indicator: bold text, an icon, a label, a note

Common error: Using light gray text (#999999 on white) for captions or secondary information. This common design choice fails the 4.5:1 requirement. Fix: Use #767676 or darker on white.

Step 9: Create Accessible PDFs from Word

When you export a Word document to PDF, the accessibility of the PDF depends on the accessibility of the source Word document. Fixing accessibility in Word is easier and more reliable than fixing it in Acrobat after the fact.

Best practice: Make the Word document fully accessible before exporting.

How to export an accessible PDF from Word:
1. Go to File > Save As or Export
2. Choose PDF (.pdf) as the format
3. Click More options (or Options in the dialog)
4. Check Document structure tags for accessibility
5. Check Document properties (if available)
6. Click OK, then Save

Do NOT use Print to PDF — this method strips accessibility tags and creates an image-based PDF that is not accessible.

After exporting:
• Open the PDF in Adobe Acrobat Pro
• Run the Accessibility Full Check (Tools > Accessibility > Full Check)
• Fix any remaining issues in Acrobat
• Verify tab order in forms
• Add bookmarks if the document is long (Acrobat can create them from heading structure)

Why it matters: A "Save As PDF" export that does not preserve tags creates a PDF that is essentially a picture of the document — screen readers cannot read it, and it cannot be navigated by keyboard.

Common error: Using Print to PDF or exporting without checking the "document structure tags" option. Fix: Always use File > Save As or Export > PDF, and always check the accessibility tagging option.

Step 10: Run the Built-In Accessibility Checker

Microsoft Word's built-in Accessibility Checker runs automatically in the background and can also be run manually. It finds the most common accessibility errors and explains how to fix them.

How to run it:
1. Go to Review > Check Accessibility
2. The Accessibility pane opens on the right
3. Review each item under Errors, Warnings, and Tips
4. Click each item to jump to its location in the document
5. Follow the suggested fixes

What the Accessibility Checker finds:
• Missing alt text on images
• Tables with no header row
• Merged or split cells in tables
• Insufficient color contrast
• Missing document title
• Slides with no reading order (in PowerPoint)
• Links with non-descriptive text

What the Accessibility Checker does NOT find:
• All heading structure problems (it checks for some but not all)
• Language settings issues
• Quality of alt text (it checks for presence, not meaning)
• All color-coding problems
• Reading level or plain language issues

The Accessibility Checker is a starting point, not the finish line. Run it, fix all Errors and most Warnings, and then do a manual review using the checklist steps above.

Common error: Treating a green "no issues" result as full accessibility compliance. Fix: Use the Accessibility Checker as a baseline, then manually check headings, language, alt text quality, and link text.

Step 11: Spacing and Typography for Accessibility

Typography choices affect readability for people with dyslexia, low vision, and cognitive disabilities.

Recommendations:
• Use sans-serif fonts: Arial, Calibri, Verdana — these are generally more readable on screen than serif fonts
• Set body text at 11–12pt minimum; 14pt for materials intended for older adults or people with low vision
• Set line spacing to at least 1.15 — 1.5 is better for readability
• Leave at least 6–12pt spacing between paragraphs
• Do not justify text (full justification creates uneven word spacing that is difficult for people with dyslexia)
• Use left-aligned text for body content
• Avoid ALL CAPS for body text — use bold for emphasis instead
• Avoid excessive italics — reserve for titles, terms, or occasional emphasis

Common Errors and How to Fix Them

Error — Impact — Fix

No document title in properties — Screen reader announces file name — File > Info > Properties > set Title
Language not set — Wrong pronunciation for screen readers — Review > Language > Set Proofing Language
Headings created by bold+large font — No navigation structure for screen readers — Apply built-in Heading styles from the Styles gallery
Images with no alt text — Screen reader users miss the content — Right-click image > Edit Alt Text > add description
Merged cells in tables — Screen reader loses count in table — Remove merged cells; use simple table structure
No table header row — Screen reader cannot identify columns — Table Design > Table Style Options > Header Row
Non-descriptive links ("click here") — Screen reader link list is meaningless — Rewrite link text to describe destination
Light gray or low-contrast text — Text invisible to low-vision users — Darken text color to achieve 4.5:1 ratio
Color used alone for status — Colorblind users miss meaning — Add bold, icons, or text labels alongside color
"Print to PDF" export — Creates inaccessible image-based PDF — Use File > Save As > PDF > check structure tags
Manually typed dashes as bullets — Not recognized as lists by screen readers — Use built-in Bullets/Numbering formatting

Cultural and linguistic competence — Language settings enable screen readers to serve multilingual users correctly
Olmstead implementation — Plain, accessible documents support people exercising informed choices
Workforce development — Accessible training materials support staff with vision, cognitive, and motor disabilities
Quality improvement — Accessible documents are better structured and easier for all readers
Leadership and accountability — Leaders model accessible document practices and require them from their teams

fields.title: Calling In vs. Calling Out
fields.summary: This resource distinguishes between calling in and calling out as approaches to addressing harm in the workplace — and provides the 5 Ds bystander intervention framework as a practical tool for DSD staff. It addresses when each approach is appropriate, how to use them effectively, and how to respond well when you are the one being called in or out.
fields.body:
What this is for

This resource distinguishes between calling in and calling out as approaches to addressing harm in the workplace — and provides the 5 Ds bystander intervention framework as a practical tool for DSD staff. It addresses when each approach is appropriate, how to use them effectively, and how to respond well when you are the one being called in or out.

Why this matters in DSD work

DSD staff operate in environments where discriminatory language, microaggressions, implicit bias, and inequitable behavior do occur — in meetings, in case discussions, in supervisory relationships, and in interactions with external partners. Staff who witness harm face a choice about whether and how to respond. This resource provides frameworks for making that choice with intention and effectiveness.

The ability to address harm when you see it — as a bystander, as a peer, or as a leader — is a core DEAI competency. Staff who cannot or will not address harm when they witness it contribute to the culture that permits it.

Core concepts

Calling out: what it is and when it applies

Calling out is a public naming of harmful behavior — a direct statement in the moment, directed at the harm-doer, in the presence of others. Its purpose is to stop harmful behavior immediately and to signal to everyone present that the behavior is unacceptable.

When calling out is appropriate:
• The harm is ongoing and requires immediate interruption — particularly if someone's physical or psychological safety is at risk
• Previous private conversation (calling in) has not produced change
• The harm-doer is not a trusted relationship — calling in requires some degree of trust and rapport
• The public nature of the calling out serves an accountability or community-norm function

How to call out effectively:
• Be brief and direct: "That comment was harmful. We don't use that language here."
• Focus on the behavior, not the person's character
• Don't debate — the purpose of a calling out is to stop the behavior, not to win an argument
• Follow up later privately if the relationship permits

Limitations of calling out:
• Public shame rarely produces lasting behavior change
• It can end conversations that need to continue
• It can harm the person calling out (particularly if they're from a marginalized community and the harm-doer has more organizational power)
• It does not address the underlying beliefs or patterns that produced the behavior

Calling in: what it is and when it applies

Calling in is a private, relational approach to addressing harm — a conversation in which a person who has caused harm is invited to understand the impact of their words or actions and to take responsibility for changing them. It is most effective with trusted community members who have demonstrated willingness to grow.

Calling in was developed by human-rights practitioners as an alternative to public call-out culture — not to excuse harm, but to create conditions in which genuine learning and behavior change are more likely.

When calling in is appropriate:
• The harm-doer is someone with whom you have some relationship and basis for trust
• The harm does not require immediate public interruption
• Your goal is lasting behavior change, not only cessation in the moment
• The person has shown prior willingness to examine their behavior

How to call in effectively:
• Choose a private, calm moment — not in the heat of the original incident
• Name the specific behavior and its impact: "When you said X, the impact was Y. I want to talk with you about it."
• Ask questions that help the person understand their own thinking: "What were you trying to communicate?" "How do you think that landed for [person affected]?"
• Listen genuinely — calling in is a conversation, not a lecture
• Connect to shared values: "I know you care about equity. I want to help you understand how this moment wasn't aligned with that."

The limits of calling in:
• It is labor-intensive, and that labor often falls disproportionately on people from marginalized communities
• It assumes capacity for learning and change that not everyone has
• It is not appropriate when the harm is severe, when the person's power over you creates risk, or when good-faith change has been refused multiple times

Choosing between calling in and calling out

The choice between calling in and calling out is not binary — it is situational. Factors to consider:

• Who was harmed, and what do they need? The person harmed has the most important perspective on what response is appropriate. If they are present, follow their lead.
• What is the nature of the relationship? Calling in requires relationship; calling out does not.
• What is the severity? More severe harm warrants more direct and potentially more public response.
• What is your own capacity? You are not obligated to address every instance of harm in every moment. Choosing when and how to respond is itself a judgment call.
• What is the power dynamic? Calling out someone who has significant power over you carries real risk. This is a real constraint, not a failure of courage.

The 5 Ds bystander framework

When witnessing harm directed at someone else — harassment, discrimination, microaggression, or more explicit harm — the 5 Ds framework (developed by Hollaback! and widely used in bystander intervention training) provides practical options:

Distract: Interrupt the situation indirectly — change the subject, ask an unrelated question, make a commotion. This disrupts the harm without direct confrontation.

Delegate: Identify someone with more authority, standing, or capacity to intervene — a supervisor, a security person, a colleague with a closer relationship to the harm-doer — and ask them to intervene.

Document: If it is safe to do so and someone else is already helping the person being harmed, document the situation — take notes on what was said and done, when, and who was present. Documentation belongs to the person harmed; share it only with their permission.

Delay: Check in with the person who was harmed after the incident: "I saw what happened. I'm sorry that happened to you. Is there anything I can do?"

Direct: Address the harm-doer directly — calmly, briefly, and focused on the behavior: "That's not okay" or "Please stop."

Key principle: The 5 Ds are not a hierarchy from safest to most courageous. They are a toolkit. You choose based on your assessment of what will be most effective and least harmful in the specific situation. You can combine strategies, and you can adjust as the situation develops.

Responding when you are called in or out

Being called in or out is uncomfortable. Your first response will likely be defensive — this is a normal human reaction. How you manage that response determines whether you grow from the experience.

When you are called in:
• Pause before responding
• Listen to understand, not to rebut
• Acknowledge the impact — not "I didn't mean to hurt you" but "I hear that what I said was hurtful"
• Reflect afterward: what happened, and what will you do differently?

When you are called out:
• Resist the urge to explain or justify in the moment — focus on stopping the behavior
• Acknowledge the feedback with genuine respect: "Thank you for naming that"
• Process your reaction privately later — with a trusted colleague, in your journal, in supervision

Practical application

Practice the language. Out loud, to yourself or a trusted colleague, practice the phrases: "That comment was harmful." "I want to talk with you privately about what you said." "Is there anything I can do?" Until the language is habitual, the moment will feel too fast.

Assess your own pattern. When you witness harm, what do you typically do — act, hesitate, avoid? What factor most influences your choice? Is that factor aligned with your values?

Build calling-in relationships. Identify one or two trusted colleagues with whom you could have a genuine calling-in conversation — people who would tell you when your behavior has caused harm, and people you could tell the same.

Use the 5 Ds as a pre-commitment. Before you're in a situation where you witness harm, pre-commit to which D you'll try first. Research shows that advance planning increases the likelihood of intervention.

Common challenges

"It's not my job to correct people." In a workplace committed to equity, everyone has some responsibility for the culture. This doesn't mean you must address every instance of harm in every moment — it means developing the habit of thoughtful, occasional intervention.

"I'm afraid of how the person will react." This is a real concern. The 5 Ds framework specifically includes options that don't require direct confrontation. Choose the approach that balances effectiveness with safety.

"The person who caused harm is my supervisor." Power dynamics are real constraints on calling in and calling out. The 5 Ds' Delegate option — identifying someone with standing and authority — is often the most appropriate path when the harm-doer has power over you.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

• Inclusive workforce culture: The degree to which DSD staff address harm when they witness it shapes the inclusivity of DSD's workplace
• Community responsiveness: These skills apply in community and external relationships, not only internally

Connection to other leadership competencies

• Allyship Archetypes (Asset 28): The Upstander archetype is grounded in calling in/out practice
• DEAI Integration Across Leadership (Asset 24): Calling in/out is DEAI in relational practice
• Inclusive Supervision Foundations (Asset 9): Supervisors who call in and out model the culture they're trying to build

Reflective questions

1. Think of a time you witnessed harm in a professional setting and did not address it. What prevented you from acting? What would you do differently?
2. Think of a time you were called in or out. What was your internal reaction? What was your behavioral response? What did you learn?
3. Which of the 5 Ds do you most naturally gravitate toward? Which do you most rarely use? What does that pattern tell you?
4. Who in your professional life would you call in if they caused harm — and why do you trust them enough for that conversation?
5. What is the harm most frequently witnessed in your work environment that is least often addressed? What would it take for it to be addressed?

Sources

• University of New Mexico Health Sciences. (n.d.). Calling in vs. calling out. https://hsc.unm.edu/medicine/education/leo/_media/quarterly-reports/leo-toolkit_calling-in-vs-calling-out.pdf (https://hsc.unm.edu/medicine/education/leo/_media/quarterly-reports/leo-toolkit_calling-in-vs-calling-out.pdf)
• American Psychological Association. (n.d.). Bystander intervention tip sheet. https://www.apa.org/pi/health-equity/bystander-intervention (https://www.apa.org/pi/health-equity/bystander-intervention)

fields.title: PDF Accessibility Checklist
fields.summary: A step-by-step checklist for creating and verifying accessible PDF documents. This checklist covers tagged PDFs, reading order, alternative text, form accessibility, language settings, bookmarks, table structure, and how to use the Acrobat Pro Accessibility Checker. It also explains the difference between converting an accessible Word document to PDF versus building an accessible PDF from scratch, and the relative advantages of each approach.
fields.body:
PDF Accessibility Checklist Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Accessibility Library home: L09 Accessibility & Plain Language Library Companion to: WCAG 2.2 AA Flagship Module; Microsoft Word Accessibility Checklist; Microsoft PowerPoint Accessibility Checklist Standards reference: WCAG 2.2 AA; §508 Rehabilitation Act; Title II ADA; PDF/UA (ISO 14289); Adobe Acrobat accessibility documentation What this is A step-by-step checklist for creating and verifying accessible PDF documents. This checklist covers tagged PDFs, reading order, alternative text, form accessibility, language settings, bookmarks, table structure, and how to use the Acrobat Pro Accessibility Checker. It also explains the difference between converting an accessible Word document to PDF versus building an accessible PDF from scratch, and the relative advantages of each approach. Use this checklist whenever you create a PDF that will be shared with colleagues, clients, or the public — including fact sheets, reports, policy documents, forms, and training materials. Why this matters for DSD PDF is the most widely used format for sharing finalized documents in government and human services. DSD shares PDFs for intake forms, policy summaries, program guides, reports, and public-facing materials. If a PDF is not accessible: • People who use screen readers (due to visual disabilities) may hear garbled text, incorrect reading order, or silence • People who use Braille displays cannot navigate untagged PDFs • People who use keyboard navigation cannot tab through forms or navigate headings • Scanned PDFs (image-only PDFs) are effectively invisible to all assistive technology Under the DOJ's 2024 Title II ADA Final Rule, PDFs that provide access to programs or services must be accessible. DSD's Resolution 26 requires WCAG 2.2 AA compliance, which for PDFs means meeting the PDF/UA standard (ISO 14289) and WCAG success criteria applicable to documents. Critical distinction: Not all PDFs are created equal. A PDF exported from a properly accessible Word document is far more accessible than a PDF created by scanning a paper document. A scanned PDF is an image — it has no text that can be read, only a picture of text. The core requirements Accessible PDFs must: 1. Be tagged (contain document structure tags) 2. Have a logical reading order 3. Include alternative text for all images and non-text content 4. Have the document language identified 5. Have a meaningful document title 6. Include bookmarks for navigation in longer documents (15+ pages) 7. Have accessible table structure (tagged rows and header cells) 8. Have all form fields labeled and logically tabbed 9. Not be security-restricted in ways that block assistive technology 10. Pass the Acrobat Pro Accessibility Full Check Step-by-Step Checklist Step 1: Understand What "Tagged PDF" Means PDF tags are the structural backbone of an accessible PDF. They work like HTML tags in a web page — they tell screen readers what each element is (heading, paragraph, list item, table cell, image, form field) and in what order to read them. An untagged PDF: • Has no structural information • Screen readers must guess the reading order from visual position (often incorrectly) • Cannot be navigated by headings, tables, or form fields • Cannot be reflowed for readability on mobile or zoom A tagged PDF: • Has a tag tree defining every element's type and reading order • Can be navigated by headings, lists, tables, and links • Can be reflowed on mobile and zoom settings • Can be read accurately by screen readers and Braille displays How to check if a PDF is tagged: 1. Open the PDF in Acrobat Pro 2. Go to File > Properties > Description tab 3. Under Security (or Description), look for "Tagged PDF: Yes" 4. Or run the Accessibility Checker — it will flag "Tagged PDF" as an error if untagged Common error: Sharing a PDF without checking whether it is tagged. Fix: Always verify tagged status before distributing any PDF. Step 2: Create Accessible PDFs — The Best Method The best method for creating accessible PDFs is to start with an accessible Word (or other Office) document and export it as a tagged PDF. This approach works because: • Word's heading styles become PDF heading tags • Word's table structure becomes PDF table tags • Alt text in Word becomes alt text in the PDF • Language settings carry over • Lists become tagged list items Step-by-step export from Word: 1. Make the Word document fully accessible (complete the Word Accessibility Checklist first) 2. Go to File > Save As or Export > choose PDF 3. Click More options > Options 4. Check Document structure tags for accessibility 5. Check Document properties (to carry over title, language, author) 6. Click OK > Save 7. Open the resulting PDF in Acrobat Pro and run the Full Accessibility Check (Step 9) Do NOT use these methods: • Print to PDF — strips all tags; creates an image-based PDF • Screenshot to PDF — creates a pure image; completely inaccessible • Scanning a paper document to PDF — creates an image-based PDF; must be OCR'd and then tagged Step 3: Fix Scanned or Untagged PDFs If you have a PDF that was created by scanning or is otherwise untagged, you can still make it accessible — but it requires more work. For scanned PDFs (image-only): 1. Open in Acrobat Pro 2. Go to Tools > Scan & OCR > Recognize Text 3. Run OCR to convert the image to searchable text 4. Then proceed with the tagging process below For untagged PDFs: 1. Open in Acrobat Pro 2. Go to Tools > Accessibility > Make Accessible (Action Wizard) 3. Follow the guided workflow 4. Or use Tools > Accessibility > Add Tags to Document for a faster (less controlled) approach 5. After auto-tagging, use the Reading Order tool to verify and correct the tag structure Note: Automated OCR and auto-tagging are starting points, not finished products. Always verify the result manually. Step 4: Set Reading Order Even in tagged PDFs, the reading order may not match the visual presentation — especially in multi-column layouts, sidebars, callout boxes, or complex table-heavy documents. How to check and fix reading order in Acrobat Pro: 1. Go to View > Show/Hide > Navigation Panels > Tags 2. Open the Tags panel — this shows the tag tree in reading order 3. Or go to Tools > Accessibility > Reading Order 4. Use the Touch Up Reading Order tool to verify the sequence 5. Drag tags in the Tags panel to reorder them What good reading order looks like: • Document heading, then subheadings and body text in logical top-to-bottom, left-to-right order • For multi-column layouts: first column complete, then second column — not alternating line by line • Sidebars and callout boxes either integrated logically or read as distinct sections • Page numbers, headers, and footers either at the end or marked as artifacts Marking page furniture as artifacts: Headers, footers, page numbers, and decorative elements that are not content should be marked as "artifacts" so screen readers skip them. 1. Open the Tags panel 2. Find the element (usually a tag labeled "," "

," or similar) 3. Right-click > Change Tag to Artifact Common error: Multi-column documents read left-to-right across both columns line by line, rather than completing the left column before the right. Fix: Use the Touch Up Reading Order tool to set the correct reading sequence. Step 5: Add Alt Text to All Images Images in a PDF must have alternative text in the PDF tag structure. How to add alt text in Acrobat Pro: 1. Open the Tags panel (View > Show/Hide > Navigation Panels > Tags) 2. Find the image tag (usually labeled

fields.title: Goleman Emotional Intelligence for DSD Leaders
fields.summary: Emotional Intelligence (EI) is the capacity to recognize, understand, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others — and to use that capacity to guide thought and action effectively, especially in relationships and complex social situations. The concept was popularized and operationalized by psychologist and science journalist Daniel Goleman beginning with his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ and developed further in the leadership-focused Primal Leadership (2013, with Boyatzis and McKee).
fields.body:
Goleman Emotional Intelligence for DSD Leaders

Resource type: Tier 1 Flagship — Methodology / Framework
Adapted from: Daniel Goleman (1995, 1998, 2013); Goleman, Boyatzis & McKee (2013); Richard Boyatzis
Library home: L08 Emotional Intelligence Library
Companion to: T04_04 Cultural Humility; T04_06 SAMHSA Trauma-Informed Practice; T04_14 RMHF

What this framework is

Emotional Intelligence (EI) is the capacity to recognize, understand, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others — and to use that capacity to guide thought and action effectively, especially in relationships and complex social situations. The concept was popularized and operationalized by psychologist and science journalist Daniel Goleman beginning with his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ and developed further in the leadership-focused Primal Leadership (2013, with Boyatzis and McKee).

Goleman's framework organizes EI into four domains and twelve competencies, as described at DanielGolemanEI.com (https://danielgolemanemotionalintelligence.com/ei-overview-the-four-domains-and-twelve-competencies/):

Domain 1 — Self-Awareness
• Emotional Self-Awareness: Recognizing one's own emotions and their impact.

Domain 2 — Self-Management
• Emotional Self-Control: Managing disruptive emotions and impulses.
• Adaptability: Flexibility in response to changing circumstances.
• Achievement Orientation: Striving to improve or meet a standard of excellence.
• Positive Outlook: Seeing the positive in people and situations.

Domain 3 — Social Awareness
• Empathy: Sensing others' emotions and perspectives.
• Organizational Awareness: Reading the organization's social networks and currents.

Domain 4 — Relationship Management
• Influence: Inspiring and moving others.
• Coach and Mentor: Supporting others' development.
• Conflict Management: Navigating disagreements productively.
• Teamwork: Collaborative contribution to shared goals.
• Inspirational Leadership: Guiding with a compelling vision.

Goleman's research, summarized in the Disruptive Leadership Institute's overview (https://www.disruptiveleadership.institute/goleman_emotional_social_intelligence/), argues that EI — far more than IQ or technical skill — predicts professional effectiveness and organizational success, particularly at leadership levels.

Why DSD uses this framework

DSD staff at every level — from DSPs in direct support to supervisors, program managers, and senior leaders — operate in emotionally complex environments. They work with people facing disability, loss, family stress, institutional barriers, and sometimes historical trauma. They carry the emotional weight of that work. They manage conflict, provide difficult feedback, navigate bureaucratic frustration, and sustain relationships with people in acute need.

Without emotional intelligence, this work is unsustainable and inequitable. Without self-awareness, staff cannot recognize when their own emotional reactions are shaping service interactions in ways that harm the people they serve. Without empathy, they cannot genuinely center the person they are supporting. Without relationship management skills, they cannot maintain the trust relationships on which effective services depend.

The EI framework also directly supports DSD's equity goals: research consistently shows that leaders with higher EI create more psychologically safe, inclusive, and equitable workplaces. Staff who feel recognized and understood are more likely to stay, to grow, and to carry the organization's mission with fidelity.

The core concepts (plain language with citations)

Domain 1 — Self-Awareness

Self-awareness is the foundation of EI. Goleman's research finds (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/four-domains-emotional-intelligence-daniel-goleman) it is the most critical domain, because without accurate self-knowledge, the other domains are unreliable.

Self-awareness means knowing your emotional states — what you are feeling, when you are feeling it, and why. It means understanding how your emotions affect your behavior, your decisions, and other people. It means recognizing your triggers — the situations that reliably produce disproportionate or misdirected emotional reactions.

For DSD leaders and staff, self-awareness includes:
• Knowing when you are burned out and acknowledging it, rather than pushing through.
• Recognizing when frustration with a bureaucratic system is bleeding into frustration with the person you are serving.
• Noticing when your discomfort with a family's choices is being expressed as professional concern about their decisions.
• Understanding the ways your own cultural background shapes your emotional responses to the people you work with.

Emotional self-awareness is the foundation for cultural humility (T04_04): you cannot examine your cultural assumptions without first being able to notice your emotional reactions to cultural difference.

Domain 2 — Self-Management

Self-management is the ability to regulate your emotional responses, rather than being controlled by them. This is not suppression — the research evidence on emotional suppression is clear that it is both unhealthy and counterproductive. Self-management is the capacity to experience an emotion, name it accurately, and choose how to respond to it rather than simply reacting from it.

Key self-management competencies in DSD work:
• Emotional Self-Control: Staying professional under pressure without denying the pressure exists. A supervisor receiving a complaint from a family member who is angry can hold their own emotional response steady without either becoming defensive or becoming mechanical.
• Adaptability: Changing course when circumstances change — a service plan that is not working, a new challenge a person presents, a team's shifting needs.
• Positive Outlook: Finding the genuine strengths and possibilities in difficult situations. Not toxic positivity — acknowledging what is hard — but not catastrophizing either.

The Ohio 4-H Emotional Intelligence background document (https://ohio4h.org/sites/ohio4h/files/imce/Emotional%20Intelligence%20Background.pdf) describes self-management as the domain that "allows us to take the 'raw' emotional material of self-awareness and use it constructively."

Domain 3 — Social Awareness

Social awareness is the outward-facing dimension: the capacity to sense what others are feeling and to read social situations accurately.

• Empathy: Not sympathy (feeling for), but empathy (sensing the emotional experience of another person from inside their perspective). This is the core relational skill of DSD work. Genuine empathy enables staff to understand what a service interaction feels like from the person's perspective, not just the staff member's.
• Organizational Awareness: Understanding the informal currents, relationship networks, and power dynamics of an organization. For DSD supervisors and leaders, this means knowing which teams are under stress before it becomes a crisis, recognizing the informal channels through which equity issues are being processed, and reading the organization's readiness for change.

Empathy in DSD is not just interpersonal; it has structural implications. Structural empathy — the capacity to understand how institutional structures feel from the inside of the communities they affect — is what turns policy intentions into policy outcomes.

Domain 4 — Relationship Management

Relationship management is the integration of the other three domains into action. As described by Ohio 4-H (https://ohio4h.org/sites/ohio4h/files/imce/Emotional%20Intelligence%20Background.pdf), "Relationship management can be used to influence those around us to make a good decision. We can sense other's reactions to the situation and fine-tune our response to move the interaction in a positive direction."

For DSD leaders, relationship management competencies include:
• Coach and Mentor: Supporting staff's emotional and professional development over time, not just managing performance events.
• Conflict Management: Navigating the inevitable conflicts — between family members' wishes and professional judgment, between staff's needs and organizational demands, between communities' expectations and policy constraints — without escalation or avoidance.
• Inspirational Leadership: Sustaining team commitment to DSD's mission through the daily experience of institutional friction, bureaucratic constraint, and the weight of people's unmet needs.

The leader-emotional-labor connection

Human services work is emotional labor — the management of feeling to fulfill the emotional requirements of a role. DSPs manage their emotional responses to support people through distress, loss, frustration, and resistance. Supervisors manage their own emotional responses while holding the emotional experiences of their teams. Leaders manage the emotional culture of entire organizations.

Emotional labor without emotional intelligence is unsustainable. It produces burnout, secondary traumatic stress, compassion fatigue, and — when staff are operating from unmanaged emotional exhaustion — poor service quality and equity failures.

DSD's EI framework addresses this directly: developing EI is not a luxury for leaders; it is a structural condition for a sustainable, equitable workforce. Organizations with emotionally intelligent leaders have lower turnover, higher staff wellbeing, better service quality, and more equitable outcomes.

How EI shows up in DSD work

Self-Awareness in a service interaction: A DSP notices mid-conversation that they are feeling impatient with a person who communicates slowly. They pause, name the impatience internally, recognize that it belongs to them and not to the person, and consciously reset — slowing their own pace, asking an open question, and listening.

Self-Management under organizational pressure: A supervisor receives word that a staff member has filed a complaint. Their first reaction is defensiveness. They notice the defensiveness, take a breath, and before responding to the complaint, ask themselves: "What does this person need me to understand? What might I be missing about their experience?"

Empathy in community partnership: A program manager preparing to present a service design change to a community advisory board pauses before the meeting to ask: "How might this change look from the families' perspective? What are they afraid of? What have they been promised before that didn't materialize?"

Conflict management in a team: An Equity Champion navigates a team disagreement about whether a service practice is culturally appropriate. Rather than taking a side, they help the team slow down, articulate what each position is protecting, and identify what additional information would help them decide.

How to apply this in your role

As a DSP or direct-support staff:
• Practice naming your emotional reactions internally before they become behavioral reactions externally.
• Use empathy as a deliberate professional tool: before entering an interaction, ask "What might this person be feeling right now? What would I want from someone in this situation?"
• Know your burnout signs. Name them to your supervisor before they become service-quality failures.

As a supervisor or manager:
• Create conditions for staff to develop EI, not just exercise it. Reflective supervision, psychological safety, and modeled self-disclosure are the conditions.
• Use the four-domain frame in performance conversations: "Where is this person's self-awareness? What would help their empathy? What relationship-management skill does this situation require?"
• Monitor your team's emotional culture, not just their outputs.

As a senior leader:
• Recognize that organizational culture is set by leader behavior, not leader policy. Your emotional self-management in difficult moments shapes the team's emotional culture.
• Build EI assessment into leadership development and promotion considerations — not as a checkbox, but as a genuine developmental investment.

Common misconceptions

"EI is just being nice." EI includes conflict management, adaptability, and organizational awareness — none of which are synonymous with niceness. High-EI leaders can deliver difficult feedback, enforce accountability, and navigate conflict — more effectively than low-EI leaders, not less.

"You either have it or you don't." EI is developable. Research supports that EI competencies respond to deliberate practice, coaching, and feedback.

"EI is about suppressing emotions." Self-management is not suppression. Research consistently shows that emotional suppression is counterproductive. EI is about recognizing and thoughtfully channeling emotions, not eliminating them.

"Men don't do EI." EI is not gender-typed. Research shows no consistent gender difference in overall EI scores; what varies is which specific competencies individuals develop. The framing of EI as "soft" or feminine is a cultural, not an empirical, claim.

Connection to other frameworks

• Cultural Humility (T04_04): Self-awareness and empathy are the emotional foundations of cultural humility practice. You cannot hold your own cultural assumptions accountable without noticing your emotional reactions to cultural difference.
• Trauma-Informed Practice (T04_06): Trauma-informed leadership requires the self-management to remain present with difficult disclosures, the empathy to understand trauma responses without pathologizing them, and the relationship management to rebuild trust after ruptures.
• Person-Centered Planning (T04_07): Genuine person-centeredness requires empathy — the ability to understand what a person actually wants, not what the staff member projects onto them.
• RMHF (T04_14): Relational-Cultural Theory's emphasis on growth-fostering relationships parallels Goleman's relationship management domain — both identify relationships as the site of human development and wellbeing.

Connection to DSD's six program goals

DSD Goal — EI Connection

Goal 1 — Eliminate Disparities — Empathy — structural and interpersonal — is what enables staff to recognize how services feel from the perspective of communities experiencing disparities.
Goal 2 — Community Engagement — Relationship management competencies (influence, coach/mentor, conflict management) are what makes community partnership possible at scale.
Goal 3 — Hiring and Retention — Organizational awareness and EI leadership are primary predictors of whether staff stay. Low-EI leadership is a retention risk.
Goal 4 — Learning and Development — EI is both a learning goal (developing EI competencies) and a condition for learning (psychological safety requires emotionally intelligent leadership).
Goal 5 — Contracts and Procurement — EI leadership in procurement means genuine listening to community partners, not extractive consultation.
Goal 6 — Communication and Accessibility — Empathy and social awareness are the EI foundations of accessible communication — understanding how your message lands, not just what you intend.

When to escalate / where to refer

• For EI-informed supervision tools: Consult the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant and the L08 Emotional Intelligence Library.
• For secondary traumatic stress or burnout concerns: Refer to your organization's EAP (Employee Assistance Program), HR, and your supervisor. Secondary traumatic stress is a recognized occupational risk in disability services.
• For team EI development: Contact the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant for available learning resources and coaching pathways.

Reflective questions for your practice

1. What are your most reliable emotional triggers in DSD work — the situations that consistently produce a disproportionate or misaligned emotional reaction?
2. When was the last time you made a decision in a service context that you later realized was shaped by your emotional state rather than the person's needs?
3. What does your team's emotional culture feel like right now? How much of that is shaped by your own emotional modeling?
4. When you experience empathy in a service interaction, what does it actually feel like in your body and your mind — and what do you do with it?
5. What is one EI competency you want to develop this year, and what would development look like in concrete practice?

fields.title: Accessibility and Accommodations
fields.purpose: Practical guidance for designing accessible meetings, documents, digital experiences, communications, and workplace accommodations.
fields.quickAnswer: Build access into the work from the beginning. Ask what people need, use accessible formats and communication methods, test the result, and provide a clear way to request another format.
actionSteps: Identify the people, setting, technology, and access needs.
Offer an accessible way to request accommodations without unnecessary disclosure.
Use headings, meaningful links, alt text, captions, transcripts, keyboard access, readable contrast, and plain language as applicable.
Test with accessibility tools and, when possible, people who use the relevant access method.
Fix barriers and document the accessible alternative and owner.

Start by identify the people, setting, technology, and access needs.

For division leadership, use Accessibility and Accommodations to identify the workplace condition, involve affected staff, test an improvement, and monitor impact; set direction, allocate resources, name accountable owners, and review outcome patterns. Start by offer an accessible way to request accommodations without unnecessary disclosure.

Start by use headings, meaningful links, alt text, captions, transcripts, keyboard access, readable contrast, and plain language as applicable.

Start by test with accessibility tools and, when possible, people who use the relevant access method.

fields.quickAnswer: A healthy workplace is built through protection from harm, connection, work-life harmony, mattering, growth, worker voice, and equity. Address organizational conditions rather than placing responsibility only on individuals.
actionSteps: Listen to staff and examine workload, safety, inclusion, and role clarity.
Protect confidentiality and distinguish support from clinical care.
Address harmful conduct and structural causes promptly.
Increase autonomy, connection, recognition, development, and access where possible.
Measure conditions and outcomes and hold leaders accountable for improvement.

roleApplications.application: For all staff, use Workplace Culture and Well-Being to choose the relevant guidance, verify fit and currency, and apply it to the work product; use the guidance in the immediate task, check impact and access, and ask for help when authority is unclear. Start by listen to staff and examine workload, safety, inclusion, and role clarity.

For facilitators learning leads, use Workplace Culture and Well-Being to draft, structure, test, and distribute communication in usable formats; build the guidance into preparation, practice, debrief, access checks, and follow-up. Start by protect confidentiality and distinguish support from clinical care.

For program service staff, use Workplace Culture and Well-Being to identify affected communities, plan accessible influence, and report what changed; apply the guidance in the person-specific workflow, explain options accessibly, and document the next step. Start by address harmful conduct and structural causes promptly.

limitations: Do not replace official legal, policy, clinical, supervisory, program, or Tribal authority.
Do not infer an individual's identity, preferences, needs, or experience from group-level information.
State uncertainty, use current authoritative sources, and escalate when the decision exceeds the user's role.
